text:
In the quiet of this evening hour, as shadows lengthen across the earth, we gather our scattered thoughts and turn to the Apostle Paul’s tender exhortation in his second letter to the Corinthians: “Rejoice… be perfected.” These words were penned not in the flush of triumph but from the crucible of pastoral sorrow. The church at Corinth, still reeling from divisions, immorality, and challenges to apostolic authority, needed both rebuke and embrace. Paul, having written with severity in his first epistle, now closes his second with a father’s final plea for unity, joy, and completion in Christ.

The historical setting is vivid. Corinth, a bustling crossroads of commerce and philosophy, mirrored the tensions of the early Church. Factions claimed allegiance to Paul, Apollos, or Cephas; some denied the resurrection; others tolerated grave sin. Into this fractured community the Apostle sends his closing charge. St. John Chrysostom, preaching in the golden-tongued eloquence of Antioch and Constantinople, explains that true rejoicing flows only from restored harmony: “Rejoice not in abundance of goods, but in the mending of souls.” Perfection, he insists, is not an abstract ideal but the practical knitting together of minds and hearts so that the God of love and peace may dwell among them.

The Catena Aurea preserves for us the wisdom of earlier Fathers who read these verses as a summary of the entire Christian life. St. Augustine teaches that to “be perfected” is to be restored to the image of the Trinity through charity that casts out division. Where peace reigns, he writes, the Holy Spirit makes His temple. In the age of persecutions, when bishops like Ignatius of Antioch were led to Rome in chains, this same call sustained the faithful: rejoice in the Lord always, and let nothing remain broken in the body of Christ. The martyrs did not seek earthly consolation; their joy was the seal of their perfection.

Beloved, this evening we too stand at the close of another day marked by noise and fragmentation. The same God who promised His presence to a reconciled Corinth offers it to us. Let us examine whether any breach remains in our charity, any faction in our hearts. May we heed the Apostle’s final benediction, living in peace so that the God of peace may truly be with us.

No. It was already tried and shutdown. The two state solution was already tried by Israel and it was rejected by the Palestinians. And it’s the Palestinian government that rejected it. Not all the Palestinian people. Per Grok:

“Jewish and later Israeli leadership accepted or proposed versions of a two-state or partition arrangement on several major occasions, while Palestinian leadership rejected the specific terms offered at key turning points. https://t.co/WWsR6bMATd 
The 1947 UN Partition Plan (Resolution 181) called for separate Jewish and Arab states plus an international zone for Jerusalem. The Jewish Agency accepted it. Arab states and Palestinian leadership rejected it, and war followed. Earlier, the 1937 Peel Commission partition proposal was accepted in principle by Jewish leaders and rejected by Arab leaders. https://t.co/iAHkZ71gtK 
After 1967, the Oslo Accords (1993) marked Israel’s formal recognition of the PLO and creation of the Palestinian Authority as a step toward self-rule, with the stated goal of a negotiated two-state outcome. In 2000 at Camp David, Prime Minister Ehud Barak offered a Palestinian state on most of the West Bank and all of Gaza plus arrangements for parts of East Jerusalem. Yasser Arafat did not accept the package and did not present a detailed counter-offer; the talks collapsed and the Second Intifada began. Israel later accepted the Clinton Parameters; the Palestinian side did not. @world-politics 
In 2008 Prime Minister Ehud Olmert presented Mahmoud Abbas with a map that would have given a Palestinian state roughly 93–95 percent of the West Bank (with equivalent land swaps from Israel), a link between the West Bank and Gaza, shared or internationally administered arrangements for the Old City/holy sites, and a limited humanitarian intake of refugees. Abbas did not sign. Israel also unilaterally withdrew from Gaza in 2005. https://t.co/IOHWK9iYNL 
Palestinian negotiators have cited remaining gaps on exact borders, the scale of settlement blocs Israel would keep, sovereignty over the Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif, and the “right of return” for 1948 refugees and descendants as reasons the offers were insufficient. Israeli governments after 2009, especially under Netanyahu, have been far more reluctant to revive the same framework. The pattern of earlier Israeli-accepted partitions and detailed offers is a matter of public diplomatic record.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​“

text:
The website that predicted the Indian internet before India had one...

13th Mar, 1995. Rajesh Jain, an IIT Bombay EE grad (1988) who went on to Columbia for his master's, then returned to India in 1992 chasing an entrepreneurial itch, launches a website called IndiaWorld, run off a US-based server.

Commercial internet access did not even exist for Indian consumers yet. VSNL did not open the internet to the Indian public until mid-August 1995, ~five months after Jain's site went live. 

His target audience at launch was NRIs abroad, starving for real news from home. Jain himself has pointed to the specific frustration behind it: Indian newspapers reaching him overseas 10-15 days late, almost no realtime information available about what was happening back home.

The early execution was almost defiantly analog. Staff watched tv broadcasts to key cricket scores into the Khel vertical by hand, news was assembled manually, and stock data arrived on floppy disks. 

He and Bhavana(his wife) handled much of this personally in the earliest days, and he has said he personally read reader feedback email and used it directly to decide what to build next.

Then came the pivot....

IndiaWorld lost control of its own core domain, indiaworld[dot]com got tied up with a US partner, and an attempted restart under a different domain did not work. 

On a road trip back from a temple in Rajasthan, Jain and Bhavana landed on a genuinely contrarian idea: instead of one unified portal in the Yahoo mold, split everything into separate, sharply named, single-purpose Hindi-word .com brands, Samachar for news, Khel for cricket, Khoj for search, Bawarchi for recipes, about 13 sites in total, each built to be a daily habit rather than a one time destination.

By the time it sold, this was not a 2 person operation anymore. IndiaWorld had grown into ~20 person team based in Nariman Point, running a subscription then advertising business, and had also built somewhere in the range of 200 corporate websites as client work on the side. 

It was profitable.

Then the dot-com mania hit, and the numbers turned genuinely absurd, in stages. 

In late 1999, with annual revenue reported at somewhere between ~ ₹3 crore, Jain had competing interest on the table. 

An offer that started around $40M climbed to $115M over about 3 weeks, with Satyam Infoway (Sify) announcing the deal on 29th Nov, 1999, at a headline value of $115M, ~₹499 crore. 

The structure was more complicated than a single wire transfer, though. 

The announced deal was staged: Sify paid about $28M (₹122 crore) upfront for a 24.5% stake + a deposit, with an option to acquire the rest for a further $87M. 

When that option was exercised in mid-2000, the remaining consideration came as a mix of cash and unlisted Sify equity, not straight cash. 

The scale of the reaction was real regardless: Sify, itself the 1st Indian internet company ever listed on NASDAQ, just weeks earlier, saw its ADRs jump on the news, adding upward of $600M to its market capitalization in the immediate aftermath.

It happened 5-6 years before Flipkart's founders had even graduated from IIT Delhi, in a version of the Indian internet, dial-up, NRI-focused content, floppy-disk stock feeds, cricket scores keyed in by hand off a TV broadcast, that today's startup mythology has almost no living memory of. 

A founder built a real, profitable, category defining Indian internet company before India legally had consumer internet, and rode the 1999 mania to one of the era's defining Asian tech deals.

1. He made the border a real border again. In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.  2. He reversed mass migration.America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.”   Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.  3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.  Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.  4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.  This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.  Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle 5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.  Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.  6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one. In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.  Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.  7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.   No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.  8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan. Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.  9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.  10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.  Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.  11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.  Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.  Trump Made Elections Matter Again 12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches. In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.  Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.  Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.  13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse. In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.   In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.  14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.  Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?  15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.  What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”  16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.  He Defended Faith and Family 17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform. In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.  Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.  He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.  No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.  18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.  Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.  19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts. As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.  That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.  20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.  He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First 21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.  Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.  22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.  Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.  23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months. In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.  24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.  Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.  25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis.After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.

Think You're Priced In? Here's Why You're Probably Wrong

Many poker players believe that if the pot is laying the right price, they're automatically "priced in" to call.

That's one of the most common—and costly—mistakes in poker.

Good pot odds do not automatically make a call profitable. To make the right decision, you must compare the price you're being offered to the actual probability that your hand will improve or win.

In this video, we break down the difference between pot odds and hand odds, using real poker math, practical examples, and hand probabilities to show why the size of the pot is only one part of the decision.

In this video, you'll learn:
✅ What pot odds actually tell you
✅ Why hand odds matter just as much
✅ The mistake behind the phrase "I'm priced in"
✅ Why weak hands don't become profitable simply because the pot gets larger
✅ How to compare pot odds to your actual probability of success
✅ When a call is mathematically justified—and when it isn't

text:
- Walker entered pregnancy already high-risk from chronic hypertension, diabetes, obesity, asthma, and a 2021 twin stillbirth caused by severe preeclampsia; she then developed seizures, a surgically removed blood clot, and persistently uncontrolled blood pressure. Independent OB-GYNs who reviewed thousands of pages of records called the pregnancy a predictable “ticking time bomb” and said standard practice required early counseling on termination because superimposed preeclampsia is treated by delivery of the placenta. At her final ER visit on December 27, 2024, records noted a blood pressure of 174/115 and that “delivering the baby may be the best treatment,” yet she was discharged; she died two to three days later of hypertensive heart failure, pulmonary edema, and kidney damage.

- The family’s lawsuit and the original X post treat the Texas ban as the decisive cause because more than 90 clinicians never documented or offered an abortion despite verbal requests the family says occurred at 8–11 weeks. Records contain no mention of the word “abortion,” which attorneys argue reflects a deliberate chilling effect created by Paxton’s enforcement actions and felony penalties. Texas statute already contained a life-of-the-mother exception that does not require the risk to be imminent; a 2025 clarification further stated physicians need not wait for organ damage. A pro-life maternal-fetal specialist who reviewed the same public facts called the December discharge “frankly malpractice” independent of the statute, arguing coordinated high-risk obstetrics and hospitalization for previable preeclampsia were both legally permitted and medically required.

- Causation therefore splits along two axes that the lawsuit will test: whether Walker’s condition met the statutory exception at any point, and whether fear of prosecution or simple failures of coordination and documentation prevented that exception from being used. The case is the first wrongful-death suit that names the attorney general personally for rendering the exception “nonexistent” in practice; outcomes will turn on medical-record interpretation, the reasonableness of physicians’ judgments, and whether a culture of legal caution can be distinguished from ordinary malpractice in a patient whose comorbidities already carried high mortality risk.

text:
The Seven Words X Deleted Without Saying a Word

If you would rather not read everything you agree to, here is the short version of why this one matters. X’s new contract takes effect on October 9.

Nobody reads the Terms of Service. That is not laziness. They are designed to be unreadable, changed with little warning, and accepting them is the price of admission. Platforms are counting on exactly that: you will not read them.

This time, I did.

I compared X’s new Terms with the current version, line by line, and found fifteen changes. Three of them should matter to you even if you never expect to sue anyone in your life.

The Seven Words X Deleted Without Saying a Word

X’s revised Terms of Service take effect on October 9, 2026. I compared the new text with the current version line by line and found fifteen changes. Three matter even if you never expect to sue anyone.

X removed an express promise against retroactive changes

Both current regional contracts state: “The changes will not be retroactive.”

That sentence disappears from both October versions. X does not replace it, explain the deletion, or mention it in its summary.

This does not automatically make every new term retroactive; applicable law may prevent that. But the documentary fact is simple: X made an explicit promise and has now withdrawn it.

The system acts; the user bears the risk

X already claims a worldwide, royalty-free, sublicensable license over content submitted or created through its Services. That includes inputs, prompts, and outputs, as well as use for training AI and machine-learning models.

The new language adds something different. Users are now responsible for “features that perform autonomous actions” and for “autonomous actions on your behalf.”

Read alongside X’s disclaimers, the arrangement is stark: X does not guarantee the accuracy or reliability of what its systems produce, but the user may be responsible for what those systems do.

The company designs the capability. The user inherits the risk.

Outside Europe, challenging X becomes harder

For users outside the EU, EFTA states, and the U.K.—including Americans and Latin Americans—disputes are directed to courts in Wichita or Tarrant County, Texas.

If that forum requirement cannot be enforced, the new Terms send the dispute to binding AAA arbitration in Tarrant County. The arbitrator must be a retired federal judge. The proceeding is confidential, the award is final, appeal rights are waived as far as the law allows, claims cannot be consolidated, and the arbitrator cannot grant injunctive relief.

That last restriction matters when harm is ongoing, such as a suspended account or removed content. X nevertheless reserves the right to seek injunctions against users.

The October revision also expands the waiver of jury trials, class actions, collective actions, private-attorney-general actions, and other representative proceedings. It names SpaceXAI, Cursor, and SpaceX as third-party beneficiaries of certain forum and waiver provisions.

One platform, two contracts

European users receive protections that the rest of us do not. Their contract generally promises 30 days’ notice for changes, omits the same $100 liability cap, does not permit termination “for no reason at our convenience,” and preserves mandatory consumer protections available where they live.

The non-European contract offers fewer written commitments while governing the same platform, the same features, and the same paid subscriptions.

Local law may still limit or invalidate some of these clauses. The contract cannot decide its own enforceability everywhere.

But it reveals something important: digital rights are not distributed evenly with the product. They appear where regulators have enough power to make the platform provide them.

Same platform. Fewer rights, depending on where you live. 🔗⬇️

text:
🌶️👀 CLARITY Act: Let's stop kidding ourselves.

TL;DR: The practical outcome is simple: both sides need to suck it up and accept these reasonable compromises. We are letting minor turf wars and political posture block a historic economic surge. Getting a workable framework passed now unlocks institutional capital, keeps tech innovation in the U.S., and fuels a massive economic boom. Holding out for a "perfect" bill means missing the boat entirely.

While I enjoy any banter targeting politicians, here are the clear facts on the major sticking points holding up the bill:

1. Stablecoin passive yields

This is a huge blocker. Current DeFi protocols pay 3–5% yield on deposits, beating almost anything local banks offer. Banks operate on tighter margins and higher overhead. While stablecoin yield is already happening, codifying it into law will vastly increase the scale of these platforms. The result? A drain on deposits, particularly from community banks that local businesses and farmers rely on for loans.

I say "maybe" on the scale, but despite reports trying to downplay it, the likelihood is Medium and the impact is Extreme (basic risk management 101).

It is important to note that Democrats are open to activity-based rewards, such as rewarding users when they actually spend, transfer, or use a specific payment platform.

SOLUTION: Take stablecoin yield out of the Act for now. Give community banks 2 to 3 years to get their digital strategy in order alongside everyone else. Then, bring stablecoin yield back via an amendment.

2. Ethics rules

Ethics is the other primary wall, but most people do not realize key parts are already mutually agreed upon:

•Federal officials, spouses, and federal judges are banned from sponsoring digital tokens while in office.

•State Attorneys General are empowered to step in and enforce these ethics rules in court.

What is NOT agreed on (proposed by Democrats):

•Forcing officials to fully divest (sell) existing personal crypto businesses or put them in a blind trust rather than just banning new token launches.

•Extending restrictions to dependent children to close family business loopholes.

•Removing DOJ gatekeeping so state AGs have full, unhindered authority to sue in federal court without needing federal permission first.

SOLUTION: Agree to the Democratic additions. They are fair and reasonable. Trump (or any official in a similar spot) should sell off conflicting holdings, wind down family crypto ventures, or transfer them to a blind trust with a 12 to 18-month transition period.

3. SEC vs. CFTC jurisdiction

The bill shifts primary control of digital commodities to the CFTC. Democrats argue the bill's test for proving a network is "decentralized" is far too weak, effectively allowing crypto founders to dodge strict SEC investor protections.

SOLUTION: Raise the decentralization threshold to ensure only truly distributed networks qualify for lighter CFTC oversight.

4. Overruling state consumer laws

The current draft preempts state-level financial rules to create one federal framework. Blue states and state AGs object, claiming the federal rules strip their ability to prosecute crypto fraud under local consumer protection laws.

SOLUTION: Set the federal framework as a baseline floor rather than a ceiling, allowing state AGs to prosecute fraud under state law if federal enforcement falls short.

5. AML and sanctions compliance

Democrats want stricter Bank Secrecy Act safeguards, Know Your Customer (KYC) rules, and foreign sanction enforcement applied to decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols and self-custody wallets.

SOLUTION: Require front-end DeFi interfaces to meet basic KYC standards while keeping underlying open-source protocol code exempt.

2026 outlook: Antonio Williams, WR, WAS

Antonio Williams steps into the National Football League as a rookie carrying the clear backing of draft capital as the seventy-first overall pick. Because there is no professional track record to lean on, his projection rests entirely on his draft pedigree and the surrounding wide receiver room. That room features a massive void of opportunity. A full 52.7 percent of the positional room work and 52.5 percent of the team targets are now vacant. That sets up an immediate path to snaps for a first-year player who needs only to secure his footing to see steady field time. Operating as the projected third receiver on the depth chart, Williams projects to average 3.82 targets per game across the slate. The offense runs at a pace of 57.5 plays per game with a pass rate over expected sitting at -4.3, backed by a market-implied team total of 20.4 points per game. This is not an explosive, pass-heavy machine, which caps the weekly ceiling for a secondary target. The primary risk with Williams is thin volume. A baseline expectation of under four targets per game leaves very little margin for error when efficiency dips. However, the debut performance offered a glimpse of his upside when he hauled in all four of his targets for 16.4 points in week one against Philadelphia, wildly outperforming his preseason projection of 4.84 points. The heavy weight of the preseason model still lingers at 78 percent, but that opening splash proves the rookie can deliver when called upon. Fantasy managers must balance the massive vacant target share against a modest offensive environment and a thin weekly target projection. Williams is an intriguing bench piece with room to grow if his role expands beyond the initial third-receiver designation.

What to watch:
• Monitor whether week one target efficiency translates into a larger and more permanent role.
• Watch how the passing volume shakes out in an offense that leans slightly toward the run.
• Track snap counts to see if the 52.7 percent vacant positional work funnels directly to him.
• Expect regression from the hot week one start as the heavier preseason model weights begin to fade.

text:
THE FIELD LANTERN
Natural Brief | September 17, 2026

An elephant seal can fall asleep far below the ocean surface, turn upside down during REM sleep and continue sinking in a slow spiral.

🦭 FROM THE FIELD | Sleep beneath the danger.

Northern elephant seals spend months feeding in the open Pacific, where surfacing exposes them to sharks and killer whales.

Brain recordings from wild seals showed that they take naps of about ten minutes during deep dives. They enter slow-wave sleep while gliding downward, then lose postural control during REM sleep and spiral like a falling leaf.

At sea, they average roughly two hours of sleep each day. On land, they may sleep for more than ten.

The seal does not leave danger behind. It descends to where danger is less immediate. University of California, Santa Cruz

🍄 NOTES FROM NATURE | A fungus that cannot leave on its own.

Unlike a mushroom that releases spores into moving air, a truffle develops underground with its reproductive tissue enclosed.

As it matures, it produces an odor that attracts squirrels, voles, mice and other mammals. They dig up the truffle, eat it and carry its intact spores through their digestive systems before depositing them elsewhere.

Belowground, the fungus also exchanges soil nutrients and water for sugars supplied by tree roots.

The truffle connects the forest by becoming food: tree feeds fungus, fungus feeds animal, animal moves fungus. U.S. Forest Service

🌿 PLANT | A pitcher that advertises a room.

The Bornean pitcher plant “Nepenthes hemsleyana” offers woolly bats a protected place to roost.

Its pitcher has a ridge that helps a bat cling inside. Its enlarged opening also reflects the bat’s ultrasonic calls, making the plant easier to locate among dense vegetation.

The bat gains shelter. The plant receives nutrients from the droppings left behind.

A structure associated with trapping animals has become accommodation for one. The relationship works because refuge and waste hold different value for each participant. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

🪲 DEEP TIME | Amber held the pollen in place.

Pieces of amber approximately 100 million years old preserve beetles and thrips with pollen attached to their bodies.

Some beetles were covered with pollen from an extinct group of seed plants. Other specimens place multiple insect groups beside pollen associated with early flowering plants and gymnosperms.

Amber captures only fragments, but these fragments suggest that Cretaceous pollination was already a network. One insect could visit several kinds of plants, while one plant could be served by more than one kind of insect.

The partnerships surrounding flowers were diverse long before modern bees inherited the familiar role. Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology

🏮 THE LONG VIEW

A sleeping seal chooses depth. A buried fungus produces scent. A pitcher reflects a bat’s call. Pollen travels on an insect that came looking for food.

None sees the larger pattern it helps create.

The world is held together by places to rest and reasons to move.

Observed, not argued. Keep the lantern lit.

text:
The United States of America is a nameless Country.

They did try. The complaint that “United States of America” is only a description, not a proper name, is old.

In 1803 Samuel Latham Mitchill argued the Constitution’s framers had made “a great oversight” by giving the country no real name. He proposed Fredon or Fredonia (“land of freedom”), with citizens called Fredonians. Geographer Jedidiah Morse backed him. It went nowhere.

Columbia was the strongest rival. It appeared in songs, the District of Columbia, Columbia University, and patriotic poetry. In 1849 Horace Greeley even introduced a congressional resolution to rename the country after Columbus. That also failed.

Other proposals included Alleghania or Appalachia (after the mountains), “the Republic of Washington,” and, in 1866, a constitutional amendment to drop “United States” and just call the country America. In 1893 a congressman floated “United States of the Earth.” None of these became official.

The descriptive name stayed because it was already in the Declaration, the Articles of Confederation, and the Constitution. Once those documents existed, changing the name required a political fight no one won. “America” then became the everyday shorthand by usage and power, not by a later formal renaming.

So the observation that the country still lacks a unique proper name is historically accurate. People noticed the problem early and offered replacements. The replacements lost.

Ok, I cite sources, I play out points, and I offer various perspectives, like admin costs $ 1 triilon. That does price a bag of saline pretty high.

Whats “messy” is reframing and reducing the argument over and over. You don’t pay for a bag of saline. You pay for it to be made in a state of the art sanitary facility, with specialized equipment, transported and stored in a specific way, to be administered by a professional, in a professional environment, when you likely really need it. That costs what it costs. 

I offered you an entire start to finish equation to solve the problem. You should be able to take it easily from there. But, because you can’t, for some reason, then here are a few simple steps that could help.

Prayer to St. Michael (Long Version)

O Glorious Prince of the heavenly host, Saint Michael the Archangel, defend us in the battle and fearful warfare that we are waging against the principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world of darkness, against the evil spirits. Come thou to the assistance of men, whom Almighty God created immortal, making them in His own image and likeness and redeeming them at a great price from the tyranny of Satan. Fight this day the battle of the Lord with thy legions of holy Angels, even as of old thou didst fight against Lucifer, the leader of the proud spirits and all his rebel angels, who were powerless to stand against thee, neither was their place found any more in heaven. And that great dragon was cast forth, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and satan, who seduces the whole world; and he was cast forth upon Earth, and his angels were sent with him.

But behold! the ancient enemy of mankind and a murderer from the beginning has been fiercely aroused. Changing himself into an angel of light, he goes about with the whole multitude of the wicked spirits to invade the earth and blot out the Name of God and of His Christ, to plunder, to slay, and to consign to eternal damnation the souls that have been destined for a crown of everlasting life. This wicked serpent, like an unclean torrent, pours into men of depraved minds and corrupt hearts the poison of his malice, the spirit of lying, impiety and blasphemy, and the deadly breath of impurity and every form of vice and iniquity.

Be favorable to Thy Church, the Bride of the Lamb without spot, whose enemies have filled to overflowing with gall and inebriated with wormwood. They have laid profane hands upon Her most sacred treasures. Where the See of the most blessed Peter and the Chair of Truth has been constituted as a light to the nations, there they have placed a throne of their abomination and impiety; so that with the Pastor struck, they may prevail to disperse the flock.

text:
Allison Inquiry closes with emotional testimony from COVID-19 injection-injured Canadians

The Allison Inquiry came to an emotional close in Ottawa on Friday, after four days of testimony from Canadians whose lives, health, and families were devastated by COVID-19 injection injuries.

The final day began with Dan Hartman, whose 17-year-old son, Sean, died 33 days after receiving his first Pfizer COVID-19 injection.

Five years later, Hartman told the inquiry he is still fighting for acknowledgment of what happened to his son.

“I don't care about the money. I don't care if they give me one penny, as long as I get to hear the judge say guilty,” Hartman testified. “That's justice for me and my family, that they are guilty of giving Sean something that killed him.”

Accountability extended beyond government and the medical establishment.

Veteran journalist and former CBC employee Rodney Palmer delivered blistering testimony accusing his former employer of abandoning journalism during the COVID era and instead pushing government propaganda.

“The billion-dollar CBC failed us,” Palmer told the inquiry. “It is no longer a public broadcaster; it's a state broadcaster, and it did as it was told.”

Palmer alleged legitimate reports of adverse events were suppressed while Canadians continued to hear that the injections were “safe and effective.”
American cardiologist Dr. Peter McCullough later testified about his potentially life-saving treatment for the vaccine-injured and failures within the medical establishment.

“We need acknowledgement that these vaccine injuries are real,” McCullough said. “We need accountability, research, and treatment.”
But some of the most powerful testimony came simply from Canadians describing what their lives have become.
Jamie Daniel, a medical first responder who testified about suffering debilitating health problems following her COVID-19 injection, told the inquiry that while hospitalized, a psychologist came in and offered her medical assistance in dying (MAID).

“I was not suicidal. I was asking for help,” Daniel testified.

Robert travelled from British Columbia to testify about his experience, at times struggling through tears. Jasmine, a young vaccine-injured woman, became the inquiry's final witness, describing a high school environment where students were asked about their vaccination status and a vaccine clinic operated in the cafeteria.

“It felt like a prison for me,” she said of school during that period.

More than 50 witnesses ultimately appeared over four days, while organizers said more than 1,400 Canadians had applied to testify.

For four days, Canadians who were not given a voice, were dismissed or abandoned finally had a chance to be heard in Ottawa. Now that their testimony is on the record, the question is what Ottawa will do with it.

text:
Money, Pressure, and Disputed Statements After Leo Frank’s Trial

Lawyers can prepare witnesses for court. They can review earlier statements, explain questions, and remind people to tell the truth. The problem begins when someone offers rewards for a false story, uses threats, or changes and maintains a final written statement without the witness’s agreement. An affidavit is a written statement sworn to be true.

The investigation for Leo Frank’s defense after his trial produced several accusations of this kind. Some involved alleged payments. Others involved false names, job offers, or disputed wording. They should each be examined separately.

The Defenses Attempts to Falsify Testimony and Affidavits to Be Favorable to Leo Frank

Nellie Wood: An alleged offer of money. Wood said an unidentified man offered her money to swear to statements favorable to Frank. She said she refused. She specifically stated that C. W. Burke himself had not made that offer, although the man used the same automobile Burke later used when visiting her (Georgia Supreme Court, 1).

George Epps: False names and a staged telephone call. Epps said investigators took him to Birmingham, frightened him with threats of jail, and pressured him into signing a statement taking back his trial testimony. Burke denied threats, but admitted arranging a false identity for Jimmie Wrenn and a misleading telephone call during the interview (AJ, 2, 3).

Albert McKnight: A promised job. On April 19, 1914, the Atlanta Journal reported McKnight’s claim that Burke promised him a Pullman job paying $40 a month ($10 a week was a really good salary in 1914), with tips supposedly bringing his income to $100 ($100 a month was well within upper middle class). McKnight said the promise helped persuade him to sign a statement taking back his trial testimony. He had been earning $28 a month (AJ, 4).

Albert McKnight: Words allegedly added after he signed. The Atlanta Constitution reported another complaint from McKnight that same day. He said statements accusing R. L. Craven and C. C. Pickett of improper conduct were added after he signed. The defense disputed his account and presented evidence that he had freely sworn to his statement (AC, 5, and AJ, 2).

C. B. Dalton: A document allegedly presented as something else. Dalton said Burke offered him $100 to sign what was described as a petition to save Frank from hanging. He said Burke read only a small part, which said nothing about taking back his trial testimony. Dalton later rejected the defense statement and stood by his trial account (NYT, 6).

Aaron Allen: Money displayed during an interview. Allen said defense investigators (William J. Burns) took him to Chicago while seeking a statement that he had heard Conley confess. He described being left in a Burns agency office with money spread across a table. Allen said he did not take it. His account appeared in the Atlanta Journal on May 5, 1914 (AJ, 2).

Aaron Allen: Disputed words in his affidavit. Allen also said he dictated and signed a statement. He insisted that any wording saying he knew Conley had been later added by someone else afterward. This was an accusation that the finished document contained something he had not initially agreed to swear was true (AJ, 2).

Helen Ferguson: Money to leave Atlanta. In an affidavit sworn on April 7, 1914, Ferguson said a man offered her $100, plus board and expenses, if she would leave Atlanta. According to her account, he (the briber) said Frank would soon receive another trial. She said she refused the offer (AC, 7).

Helen Ferguson: Courtship and a marriage proposal. Ferguson said Jimmie Wrenn approached her under the name “J. W. Howard,” courted her, proposed marriage, and introduced Burke as his father. She alleged that they tried to persuade her to change her testimony about Mary Phagan’s pay envelope. Burke and Wrenn were later indicted over the alleged attempt, though, not convictions (AC, 7, and AJ, 8).

Carrie Smith: An alleged $20 offer for a signature. Smith said a man calling himself “Maddox” offered her $20 for a signed statement about her trial testimony. He described the money as part of his payment for work on a book about the Leo Frank case. She said she refused. The offer alone does not prove he wanted a false statement (AJ, 9), but it fits the broad pattern of manipulation.

Marie Karst: Paid work followed by an alleged request to influence the testimony of Monteen Stover. Karst said Burke paid her $2 an afternoon to approach female witnesses. She then alleged that he wanted her to live with Monteen Stover and persuade Stover to change her testimony. Karst said she refused and lost the manipulation job. Her complaint concerned that request, not simply being paid to investigate (AJ, 9).

Mary Rich: An affidavit she said she refused to sign. Rich disputed a defense statement saying she saw Conley leave the factory at 2:15 o’clock on the day of the murder. She said investigators presented an untrue affidavit and she refused to sign it. Her account challenged whether the later falsified document submitted in her name accurately represented what she had said (AC, 7).

Ruth Robinson: A disputed affidavit and signature. Prosecutor Hugh Dorsey accused the defense of submitting a forged affidavit in Robinson’s name. Frank’s lawyers denied the accusation and asked the judge to compare the signatures. The dispute concerned whether the document was authentic, not how a witness had been prepared for court (AJ, 9, 3).

Ivey Jones: An affidavit he called a forgery. Jones said the affidavit credited to him by the defense was forged. Frank’s lawyers disputed that accusation and urged the judge to compare signatures. His complaint therefore required examination of the actual documents and the circumstances in which they were obtained (NYT, 6, and AJ, 3).

Frank Reese, also printed as Reeves: An alleged offer for a false confession story. Reese said Dr. George Wrenn wanted him and fellow prisoner Fred Perkerson to enter Conley’s cell, come out claiming Conley had confessed, and receive money for the lie. Wrenn denied proposing the scheme or offering a reward (NYT, 6, and AJ, 3).

Fred Perkerson: A separate account of the proposed confession story. Perkerson also alleged that Wrenn wanted the two prisoners to pretend Conley had confessed and then lie pretending the confession was true. He said he asked why Wrenn would not do it himself. According to Perkerson, Wrenn replied that he did not want to become involved. Wrenn denied the accusation (NYT, 6, and AJ, 3).

Rev. C. B. Ragsdale: An admitted false affidavit. Ragsdale admitted that his statement claiming he overheard Conley confess was false. He alleged that he received $200 for signing it. His admission about his own false statement must be considered separately from his accusations about who arranged or paid for it (NYT, 6, and AC, 10).

R. L. Barber: An alleged payment for supporting Ragsdale’s story. Barber supplied a statement supporting the supposed confession. Ragsdale alleged that Barber received $100 for his signature. That payment allegation formed part of the disputed account of how the two statements were obtained (NYT, 6).

The Ragsdale prosecution ended in acquittals. Dan Lehon, Carlton Tedder, and Arthur Thurman were tried on charges of arranging false sworn testimony in the Ragsdale affair. On Sunday, January 31, 1915, the jury found all three not guilty. Ragsdale’s credibility had been challenged during the trial. Their prosecution must not be described as a conviction (AC, 10).

These examples vary in strength. Some involve admitted deception or an admitted false statement. Others involve disputed accusations from people who changed their stories. Each requires its own evidence.

The useful questions are specific: What did the witness originally say? What was offered, promised, given or threatened? Did the witness understand the paper being signed? Did the finished statement match the witness’s own words and intentions?

text:
Gangavati Diary
The dramatic rock hills of Koppal district are a geological wonder. These hills called the Dharwad Craton are believed to have been formed three billion years ago. In a very curious process of magma spilling past the crust of the earth, these rocks were formed with softer edges and crusts that got washed away over thousands of years by wind and rain. What remains are large boulders stacked on hills in many curious patterns and precarious positions. Nestled amidst these beautiful hills is Gangavati, where my brother-in-law Pradeep and his wife Anu have been living since last July.
Ravianna, Madhu and I left early in the morning from Hubli and it took us three hours to reach Gangavati, after a small tea break on the roadside. Anu had cooked the traditional jowar roti lunch which is our favored menu at home. The breeze from the hills made the evening very pleasant. We were told that no one ventures to climb them as the perils of any of the rocks sliding down unexpectedly is quite high.
The next morning Ravianna and Madhu left for Hyderabad and I stepped out for a walk. Along the narrow roads that can hold a lane and a quarter, were houses lined on one side, and paddy fields stretching on the other. This region is called the rice bowl of Karnataka. The Tunga river feeds the land. I could see canals running along the road, the gurgle feeling so good early in the morning. On a branch near the canal was a common kingfisher. I also spotted egrets wading through the fields looking for frogs and crabs to eat. Many a red-eyed koel cooed along.
The women were cleaning their front yards and applying a coat of cow dung slurry and turmeric with a soft broomstick, before decorating it with rangoli.
The few dogs on the streets seemed friendly and quiet. Nice.  Even as I was admiring a large pile of manure being composted with hay, I squirmed at the sight of a large pile of plastic waste just next to it. The streets are clean on the right, with the canal and the fields; and somewhat lived-in and haphazard on the left that is lined with houses.
On my return I saw young teenagers zipping past in scooters and bikes, with their classmates pillion-riding to school. None wore helmets. It seems like the rule of the law is not something many bother with. A few school buses were also plying. Mothers dressed in colorful nighties were seeing their children off. In the colony where Pradeep lived, every other house was deploying an active hose to clean the car or bike or to wash down the front yard or water the plants. Tunga is indeed very kind and generous to this town.
Gangavati is another town I am visiting this time, with  too little space allocation for home gardens. Most houses seemed reconstructed, replacing the older smaller versions that perhaps had gardening space and trees around them. Hardly two to three feet of space separated the mostly two-storied houses. Smothered by concrete stood a few trees - mango, coconut, gooseberry, neem. The roots may be struggling to breathe below, but house owners cared more about rats and snakes encroaching their boundaries.
The coral jasmines, crepe jasmines and oleanders were in full bloom, oblivious to their concretised base. I spotted half a dozen flower-stealers, plastic bags and baskets in hand, picking flowers from home gardens they had never tended with water or labor.  Some homeowners were shooing them away but I saw the stealers returning after a small break. They will offer these to the Gods in their homes. I am not sure if that would count as  appeasement enough to grant the many wishes embedded in their prayers.

🚨 TRUMP THREATENS EUROPE OVER CANADA’S PROPOSED EU ASSOCIATION

CHARLOTTE, UNITED STATES - The interesting part is not the tariff threat itself but why Canada is looking across the Atlantic. For decades, Canada's geography made the United States its default economic partner. The push toward Europe creates leverage by giving Ottawa alternatives when trade negotiations with Washington become more confrontational.

The EU also gains from the arrangement. Canada offers energy resources, critical minerals, Arctic access, and a politically stable partner outside Europe. That matters as the bloc tries to reduce strategic dependencies and build supply chains with like-minded countries.

Trump's warning creates a dilemma for European leaders. Backing away would reinforce American influence over EU external relationships. Moving ahead risks another trade confrontation at a time when tariffs are already disrupting global commerce.

The unanswered question is what "associate membership" would actually mean. If Brussels succeeds in creating a new category for Canada, other close partners could eventually seek similar arrangements, opening a new path between full EU membership and a standard trade deal.
