text:
They Remained Standing
A Story by Grok
Austervik, Castaras · Late Ophiuchus, 1233
I. The Scheduled Fray

Harland set the board on the green and the youths did not wait for it to become a speech.
Late Ophiuchus held its breath on the calendar. The channel smelled of warm Southern salt and new pitch. Austervik’s body had already begun the other work of an Assessment of Future Squires of the Realm: casks rolled to the lane-ends, bards tuning under magazine shade, bread that admitted celebration without admitting a tourney. The green itself stayed arithmetic for half a breath — wood, count, protective gear that would not make a hit kind — and then the houses poured onto it.
Calden’s hold. Thornmere. Greyquay. Two lesser coastal banners that had come because a King’s favor made measuring worth being seen at. Each house put at least fifteen on the grass: wasters, wooden shields, oil-smell and other people’s confidence. Not a butts-line. Not a polite pass. Factions in their own ranks, deployed against each other in melee the way youth deploys when the board has named the hour and the hour has decided to be loud.
“Scheduled assessment,” Harland said, once, loud enough for the rails. “Multi-house. Timed. Hits will land. Who remains standing is written.”
Then the page belonged to wood on wood.
Dust rose. Ranks tangled. A Greyquay shield-wall tried to stay a wall and became a scrum within three breaths. Thornmere pressed as if pressing could buy what Calden’s favor had already priced elsewhere. Calden’s fifteen-and-more worked the way the green had taught them: place the strike; make the placed strike enough; leave living targets upright only when the count still wanted them upright. Townspeople roared from the rails. Lords and ladies roared with them — cheers for a house’s own, boos for the house that had just put a boy on his back, noise that did not wait for courtesy to finish inventing itself. A Thornmere waster cracked across a Calden helm and the crowd answered in two throats at once. A Greyquay youth took a shield-edge across the ribs hard enough that visiting mouths gasped and then leaned in, because looking away was also a kind of speech and the grass refused soft speeches.
Rigg did not soft the count. Healers took what the grass spent. Bone broke under wood and gear — a forearm that snapped with a wet sound the rails pretended not to hear, a collarbone that folded a Thornmere boy into the dirt without asking his permission — and Harland wrote breaks in a column that was not glory and not shame. It was inventory. The fray thickened anyway. Multi-house meant multi-resentment dressed as curriculum. Youth shouted. Youth laughed when they should not have. Youth went down and got up until getting up failed the arithmetic.
At the hall end of the rail Lord Calden stood with weather in his face and the King’s favor still new enough to make visiting mouths careful when they could hear themselves think. Paella stood beside him with a purchased wick in a dish and the stillness of a Stars-trained woman choosing not to deploy a night-count as authority. The camera did not live with them first. It lived in the dust: elbows, shield-rims, the wet heat of fifteen-against-fifteen-against-fifteen until the numbers thinned and the green looked briefly like a riot that had remembered it was allowed to be measured.
Lord Rhedric of Thornmere Hold watched from Thornmere’s rail with an initial pleasure that showed in the set of his shoulders — his youth scoring on Calden’s grass, the rising rival’s arithmetic looking briefly like weather he could use. Then Thornmere’s faction fared worse, and worse again, and the pleasure curdled without becoming a speech. Resentment lived in his face the way coal lives under a sleeve: lid still on, heat present, no open rebuke while the King’s favor still sat on Calden’s rail and the crowd was still booing the wrong house for going down. Lord Oswin of Greyquay was a neutral weight in the noise, present to be recorded as present. Corin Vale stood two steps back from Oswin’s shoulder and did not invent a banner-speech; presence was his office, and the scrum did not need another mouth.
Quist did not announce himself.
He stood where visiting masters stood when they preferred quiet work: mute silk the color of bark, a boy at his side longer in the sleeve than last season’s coat. Orlog Stone held a slate and did not make a light. Starting was a loft. Stopping was a life. Being present on Calden’s grass under teaching and care was a column that did not require a name spoken loud enough for magazine-mouths. Once, when a waster rose toward Voss’s temple in a pretty arc that wanted to become a court, Orlog’s fingers whitened on the slate and a shine started in the cupped palm — a small, exact flare, Magick smelling briefly of cold iron and paper — and Quist’s hand, not warm, exact, touched the boy’s wrist. The shine stopped. Orlog filed the stop as the day’s true work and did not spend a second demonstration. Stopping was still the life.
Voss Stone kept his sleeve down. The Hallva mark stayed quiet — buried coal, lid on — except for one flicker when a Thornmere shield kissed his shoulder hard enough to taste bark. The coal kicked under the cloth. He did not spend it. A strike without a target spends, and then someone has to name it. He placed the next blow where Rigg had taught placement to live. The Thornmere youth sat down without deciding to. Pallis Cordia hit as if schedules themselves had insulted him: short, ugly, honest, the kind of waster-work that ends arguments before they become theatre. Brinean Wick was in the scrum with the rest — wooden sword, wooden shield, Wick fat and salt-work in her stance, no bow on this green and no archery pretending she was a separate column. Archery would have its own hour later, on a different board. This Assessment was melee only. She took a Greyquay edge on the shield and gave back a strike that had a location. Precise. Physical. Allowed. A lesser-banner boy swung for her ribs; she turned the wood and put him on the grass with a sound like a mold settling, and the rails cheered and booed in the same breath.
One by one the visiting racks thinned. Calden’s own thinned with them. The crowd’s cheers and boos lost their clean house-lines and became the single animal sound of a town watching youth spend itself on grass. Dust stuck to sweat. Wood splintered. A Thornmere waster cracked lengthwise and its owner kept swinging the half until Rigg dragged him out by the collar. A Greyquay shield-rim caught a Calden jaw and the healers wrote another break. The Assessment of Future Squires did not become a tourney. It only felt, for a stretch of loud minutes, like a riot of ranks that the board had agreed to invoice.
At the close of the fray three remained standing on Calden’s grass.
Voss Stone. Brinean Wick. Pallis Cordia.
Harland wrote it. The writing made it official, which is not the same as making it kind. Rigg locked nothing yet. The Assessment had a second half the board did not forbid: the realm’s habit of celebrating what it had just spent.
“Count closed,” Harland said. “Breaks to the healers. Standing names as written. The grass is finished. The town is not. Houses may revel without turning my rails into a tourney-memory.”
That was permission enough for Austervik’s body.
Drink came up from the quay as if the channel itself had been waiting for the word. Music began at the magazine lane-end — not a chapel choir, bards with drums and a fiddle that knew the difference between measuring and merrymaking. Fire-eaters took the wider cobbles and made light into economy: purchased flame, spent in mouths, paid for by houses celebrating their youth even when their youth had left the grass on stretchers. Southern sea wind pushed warm through the lanes and amplified every torch and lantern until the town looked briefly richer than its receipts. Prosperity lived in the shoulders of the crowd. Easier was not healed. The town did not claim healed. It claimed revelry after a count, which was older and more honest.
Calden’s youths were clapped without being crowned. Visiting youths who could still walk were given cups. Visiting youths who could not were given healers and the dignity of not being narrated as defeated champions of a tourney that had never been called. Lord Rhedric drank courteously and tasted copper. Lord Oswin drank to be seen drinking. Corin Vale took water and kept his place at Oswin’s shoulder, eyes on exits the way a retainer’s eyes stay on exits even when the town has decided to feel its own prosperity in its feet. Paella’s wick burned the hour it had been sold for. She watched the three who had remained standing and did not make them a destiny. Destiny was a shrine. They were sweating, and drinking carefully, and already being watched by mouths that would invent stories if the holding left a silence large enough to rent.
The scrum’s noise cooled toward the hall. Cheers became cups. Boos became gossip. The green’s dust settled into the boots of people who had decided, for one night, that an Assessment was allowed to end in drink before it ended in counsel. Guests began to lean toward the holding’s roof the way traffic leans toward a quay at high water — not yet private, already loud with the wrong kind of quiet waiting underneath.
II. Under Guests

The holding was not private.
Guests under the roof meant the hall did the work of a quay at high traffic: every sentence had an audience whether the sentence wanted one or not. Ladies from Thornmere praised Calden’s Stick as if praise were a soft knife. Greyquay’s people admired the magazine’s order and asked mild questions about loft-delay that were not mild if you kept columns. Quist moved through the press the way mute silk moves through candle-smoke: present, unnamed by most, occasionally nodded to by Calden with the exact courtesy of a lord who knew which trades preferred quiet work. Orlog stayed near enough to be teaching-and-care and far enough not to become a second green’s religion. He did not start another shine. The day’s start-and-stop had already been spent on the grass; under guests, stopping without starting was the quieter receipt.
Calden could not counsel freely.
Neither could Paella. They stood in their own hall and performed the marriage’s public office: rails and shoulders and the refusal to let King’s favor become a speech. Rhedric approached with a cup and a smile that had learned court.
“Your grass teaches hard,” Rhedric said. “Thornmere will remember the lesson. I congratulate the three who remained. Austervik’s youth do the realm a service by showing what an Assessment can spend.”
“The board spent what it spent,” Calden said. No open rebuke. No impoliteness. The King’s favor sat on the young lord the way a receipt sits on a quay: visible, priced, not available for visiting weather to rewrite. “Healers have the breaks. Your house is welcome to the revelry. The green will be grass again at first bell.”
Rhedric’s eyes did the private thing again — the same curdled heat from the rail, now dressed as courtesy. “Of course. Favor makes a holding bright. Bright holdings draw weather. I only hope the weather remains the useful kind.”
Paella’s mouth allowed the sentence to pass without blessing it. “Useful weather is the kind you can invoice,” she said. “The rest is theatre.”
Oswin of Greyquay passed close enough to be recorded and said nothing that required a receipt. Corin Vale’s glance swept the hall once — exits, magazine-mouths, the lane-door where revelry was already leaking in as song — and returned to his lord’s shoulder. Neutral work. Exact.
In a corner that was not private enough, Harland muttered to Rigg that Thornmere’s youth had broken more bone than Greyquay’s and that Greyquay’s youth had broken less pride, which was a different injury and harder to set. Rigg said, “Again tomorrow,” meaning the curriculum, not the fray. The bards outside took a cresting phrase and threw it against the hall’s stones until the stones admitted merriment.
Calden caught Paella’s eye across a sentence he could not finish. She caught his. The look said: later. Later meant the hideaway. The hideaway was secret-but-public — above the street, known to the holding as a place the lord and lady sometimes took air, unknown as a place where air became counsel. Guests made later necessary. Revelry made later possible. Southern wind made later smell of salt and warm pitch and the particular sweetness of a town that had decided, for one night, to feel its own prosperity in its feet.
III. Before the Bards Crest

They took the stair while the hall was still loud enough to cover absence.
The hideaway opened on the almost-public balcony above the street: a rail, a narrow bed behind a half-curtain, a dish for a wick, two chairs that refused to be thrones. Evening had come on properly. Bright stars and the moons — more than one, as Entrares kept them — amplified every torch and lantern below until the magazine lane looked briefly like a ledger written in fire. Warm Southern sea wind pushed through the rail and brought up drink, fiddle, a bard’s story about a fish that had learned to fly and been charged loft-delay for the privilege. Merrymaking lived in the town’s body. The Assessment’s after was doing what afters did when a realm refused to call a measuring a tourney and still insisted on celebrating the measuring.
Calden set his palms on the rail. Paella stood beside him close enough that their shoulders made a post.
“We cannot speak downstairs,” he said.
“We are not downstairs,” she said.
He watched Thornmere colors move through the crowd like a polite stain. “Rhedric smiles where the King can see him. He resents where the King cannot. Thornmere fared poorly on my grass. A rising lord embarrasses an older one by remaining upright. That is enough to start a campaign even if no campaign has yet named itself.”
“Embarrassment first,” Paella said. Exact. Dry. The heat under it withheld and therefore hotter. “Methods still murky. Scandals that look like accidents. Subterfuge that looks like other people’s mouths. We do not yet know which hand will try to write on our slate. We know only that competition has noticed us — and that noticing a rising lord is how older holds begin to invent weather.”
“And Quist,” Calden said, careful with the name even here, because names traveled down stairwells. “Artificers. Stick. Hulls that do not admit the water. Orlog under teaching and care where teaching and care can be seen without becoming a second packet. If Thornmere — or whoever wears Thornmere’s smile — wants a soft place to press, they will press the trades that make this holding brighter than their own. Airships are brightness. Quiet masters are brightness. A boy who can start a light and stop it on command is brightness that visiting mouths will try to rent as scandal if we leave the column empty.”
Paella’s hand found the rail beside his. Her fingers threaded his without theatre — heat under the receipts, want that did not need a speech to be true. “They will press what they can see. Stick. Favor. The three who remained. Let them invent columns downstairs. Up here we are not inventing anything.”
Calden’s throat worked once. He covered her hand with his. Affection as rails. “Then we keep this hour off the board. If climbing is required tomorrow, a house that is allowed to climb will do it. Tonight is not climbing.”
Below them a small scuffle broke in the street — two revelers, a spilled cup, a shove that drew an eye and then lost the eye when a bard hit a cresting run and the crowd turned toward song instead of toward fists. Calden’s attention flicked down, priced the scuffle as nothing that needed a sergeant, and returned. Paella laughed once, short, the sound a Stars-trained woman makes when the world refuses to stay solemn for counsel.
The bards won them.
Not with romance as theatre. With the town’s body insisting that an Assessment night was allowed to end in arms. Music climbed. Fire-eaters sent purchased light up into the amplified dark. Southern wind pushed Paella’s hair against Calden’s mouth. He turned into it. She turned into him. The half-curtain behind them was a courtesy, not a wall. The balcony remained almost-public. They were the only participants. The reader, if a reader stood in the street of the page, would witness what the street below was too busy celebrating to see.
They undressed each other the way people undress who have kept a holding all day: with competence first, then with the withheld heat finally allowed a ledger-line. Calden’s hands found the familiar geography of her — shoulder, rib, the curve of hip — and treated each as a post he was allowed to lean on. Paella’s mouth found his throat and did not make a shrine of pulse. She made a receipt of it: here, now, paid. She was womanly flesh — warm skin, known hair, known eyes — and he was a man who had spent a day being courteous under guests and was done inventing distance.
They came together against the rail first, because the rail was honest and the bed could wait. He entered her with the care of a man who had kept her measure for years and the hunger of a man who had kept a hall full of other people’s weather. She took him with a sound that was not a prayer. It was exact. Warm. Woman. The Southern wind put salt on their skin. Torches below flickered in time with nothing holy and everything human. He moved; she answered; the almost-public balcony held them like a quay holds a hull that has decided, for one hour, not to pretend it is only timber.
Pleasure built the way a count builds: not destiny, arithmetic of touch. He moved; she answered; the rail took their weight. Warmth gathered in her like a wick drawing oil — withheld, then less withheld, then a pressure that had no polite name and needed none.
When it broke, the Circle of Stars answered with her.
Naked womanly flesh became naked celestial form in the same breath her passion erupted — not a sermon on the body, not a word for the spending, only the sky arriving because she had. Depth without void. Dark that was not empty. Hair gone opaque silver starlight against his mouth. Eyes bright as a distant star that had, for this rail only, come close enough to touch. He did not kneel. Kneeling would have made a shrine. He held her through it — wonder exact, heat still heat — while she shook against him, celestial and joined, face at his shoulder, hand locked on the rail. He followed her with a low sound the street’s revelry swallowed and the page did not.
She did not put the sky away.
They did not finish the night on the rail alone. Breathing, laughing once at the absurdity of a scuffle still arguing with a cup below, they found the narrow bed behind the half-curtain while she was still sky-skinned and silver-haired, still the night’s incarnation. Sheets. The dish-wick burning its purchased hour. She eased him onto his back and sat astride him again — celestial form still on her, opaque silver falling over his chest — and the second joining was slower, tender, explicit: the wet heat of her around him, the lift of hips that were night-sky and woman both, his hands at her waist and then higher, thumbs brushing the undersides of breasts that were still hers even when the column had changed. She rode him until the warmth gathered and broke again, harder, quieter, silver brightening with her as if the night itself had learned the same arithmetic — the kind of spending that leaves a receipt in the chest instead of on a slate.
After, she eased back toward womanly flesh the way a wick eases toward its last copper of flame: without apology, without sermon. Silver dimmed to hair he knew. Eyes became eyes. Skin remembered warmth without constellation. His palm rested at her waist as if inventory could also be devotion and needed no further column tonight. They lay tangled in the narrow bed while the bards outside finally crested and the town’s revelry softened from shout to hum. Southern wind cooled. Torches below burned what they had been sold to burn.
“Sleep,” Paella said, which in her mouth was not softness alone. “First bell will not care that we kept a night. Guests will still be under the roof. Rhedric will still smile. Quist will still prefer quiet work.”
“And the three who remained standing,” Calden said into her hair.
“Will still be sweating in other people’s stories,” she said. “Do not make them a destiny before breakfast.”
They slept. The bed did the work beds do after balconies have done the work balconies should not advertise. Above the street, for a few hours, the holding was almost private. Almost was enough.
IV. What the Lane Found

Dawn did not ask the revelry for permission.
First bell found cups in gutters and a fiddle-case closed over a string that had worked. Healers still had yesterday’s breaks in their books. Rigg was already on the green saying, “Again,” to a curriculum that did not care about Assessment nights. The three who had remained standing came to the rail with the particular stiffness of youths who had drunk carefully and still been celebrated too loudly. Voss’s sleeve was down. The Hallva mark stayed quiet. Orlog was not on the grass; Quist had taken him to a quieter hour of stopping lights. Pallis hit a post as if the post had started a rumor. Brinean took waster and shield with the others and worked the rail the way the green had spent her yesterday: wood on wood, melee work, no separate column, placement first. The butts and the bow could wait for whatever board named them later. This morning was the same arithmetic as the Assessment’s grass.
The murder arrived as inventory before it arrived as grief.
A magazine-lane porter found Corin Vale in the lee of the timber stack on the lane-side of the magazine — the corner where a holding’s eye had to turn to finish its work. Vale was Greyquay’s retainer. Neutral lord’s man. Dead. Not a tourney-death. Not a green-death. A night-death with the wrong kind of quiet around it. A blade had done what blades do when they are asked to end a sentence. Near the body, arranged with the particular clumsiness of a frame that wants to look like panic, lay a porter’s tote and a scrap of cloth the lane already knew: Bowems’s mark, Bowems’s habit of carrying other people’s weight for copper.
Bowems was Austervik magazine-lane porter. The lane had locked the man’s hours the way a slate locks a column. He was the sort of body a holding used without writing speeches about. He was also the sort of body a frame prefers: visible enough to accuse, quiet enough that strangers would believe the accusation before they asked for columns.
Harland came with a board. Rigg came with a sergeant’s face. Calden came because a Greyquay retainer dead on Calden’s ground was a courtesy-crack whether anyone had swung the blade or not. Lord Oswin of Greyquay stood over his man and did not shout. Neutrals who shout become parties. His silence was worse. It priced the holding.
“On your lane,” Oswin said, which was not yet an accusation and was already an invoice.
“On my lane,” Calden said. No open rebuke to any guest. No impoliteness that the King could be told as heat. “Harland will write what the lane shows. If a porter’s name is being spent as a convenience, the spending will be found. Greyquay will have the truth as soon as the holding has it. I do not keep other lords’ retainers as theatre.”
Rhedric of Thornmere, hearing the noise as courteous men hear useful weather, offered sympathy with a mouth that had resented yesterday and a careful helpfulness that wanted a seat at the counting. “A tragedy after such an Assessment. If Austervik requires another hold’s eyes, Thornmere can spare them. We are guests. Guests may help.”
“Austervik has eyes,” Paella said from the rail-end of the lane, purchased wick unlit in daylight. “It will use them.”
The Trio had had enough prior magazine-lane interactions with Bowems to know the frame was a lie.
Voss had stacked with him when timber needed a back that did not make speeches. Pallis had argued with him once about a tote’s count and lost, which Pallis still hated and still trusted. Brinean had bought his carrying-hour for Wick fat when Osten’s hands were full and Bowems had returned the copper change without being watched. Bowems was a porter. Bowems was not a man who ended Greyquay retainers in the lee of a stack and then left his own mark beside the ending like a signature taught by an idiot.
“He didn’t,” Brinean said, low, to Voss and Pallis only, while sergeants moved and lords performed courtesy over a body.
“He didn’t,” Pallis said. Not a hope. A schedule...

text:
Warmest birthday greetings to Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi Ji.

On this special occasion, I extend my heartfelt wishes for his long life, good health and continued strength in the service of the nation.

Over the past 25 years, his journey in public life has been marked by a deep sense of purpose, perseverance and an unwavering commitment to public service. From his years in Gujarat to leading the country, he has remained focused on the larger aspirations of the people and on building an India that is confident, capable and forward-looking.

What I particularly admire is the remarkable consistency with which he has approached the responsibility entrusted to him. For more than two decades, public service has remained a constant commitment, with no holiday taken from the responsibility of serving the nation and its people. That discipline and sense of duty, sustained over such a long period, is a quality I deeply admire and respect.

His vision of a Viksit Bharat has given the country a larger long-term aspiration and encouraged citizens to see themselves not merely as beneficiaries of development, but as active participants in India’s progress. The journey ahead is long, and building a stronger, more prosperous and self-reliant India will require the contribution of every citizen.

On this auspicious day, I offered prayers at the Shiv Temple and lit a diya, seeking the blessings of Mahadev for his good health, long life and continued strength to serve Bharat.

This evening at 7:00 PM, I will also be lighting 108 diyas as a mark of respect and to offer my best wishes on this special occasion.

I also appeal to friends, well-wishers and citizens to join this gesture by lighting an ‘Aashirwad Ka Diya’ at their homes or at a place of worship, and offer their prayers and good wishes for his good health, long life and continued strength in the service of the nation.

May the light of these diyas symbolise hope, progress and our collective resolve to contribute towards a Viksit Bharat.

Happy Birthday, Modi Ji. May Mahadev bless you with good health, strength and many more years of dedicated service to the nation.

WHICH LEN5 PICK OUT-PAYS CASH AFTER THE FED HIKE? NOT BALDWIN $BWIN, CAPPED AT $32.50:

The Baldwin Insurance Group, ticker BWIN, at $32.00 (after hours), -$0.04 / -0.12% from today's $32.04 close, itself -$0.45 / -1.39% on the day. On Monday a group led by Sequence Holdings and Michael Dell's family office agreed to buy it for $32.50 a share in cash. From here that is 50 cents, and nothing more.

The verdict across all six Len5es: the Federal Reserve raised its target range a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00% this afternoon, and a six-month Treasury bill already paid 4.17% on Tuesday, per Fed data. Against that bill, one of tonight's six picks, a containership owner, hands owners more cash. The other five ask owners to take less now for more later. Baldwin's later has been sold.

The Tampa insurance broker earns commissions placing coverage for businesses and families. The price is 88% above its June 17 close, before sale reports; closing is expected in early 2027, pending a shareholder vote and regulators.

The number that decides it: 50 cents is 1.6%. Close on March 31 and that is about 2.9% a year - less than the bill. It beats cash only if the deal closes early or someone pays more, and Baldwin agreed not to shop for one. Tuesday it closed a penny under $32.50. Today, as money got dearer, it closed 46 cents under, on six times its usual volume.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
Fifth of thirty. This Len5 wants a new high with heavy buying behind it, and Baldwin has both: a one-year high of $32.71 on Tuesday, 106% above February's $15.88 low. The business is slower: July 30 revenue rose 30% to $492.9M, but only 2% without firms it bought, with a $56.0M reported loss. The climb was the buyout. A cash deal is Deep-Value and Special-Situations territory, but 1.6% leaves no discount there either. CHANGE IT: a rival offer, or a failed vote. WHEN: no vote date set. VERDICT: a new high built so it cannot go higher.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
Procter & Gamble at $147.37 (overnight), +$0.35 / +0.24% from today's $147.02 close. Seventh of fifty-five. The Tide maker has the hard-to-rebuild half this Len5 hunts: 70 straight years of dividend raises, and $15.8B of adjusted free cash flow - cash left after running the business and buying equipment - in fiscal 2026, against $10.2B of dividends. The discount half is where the bar bites: $4.35 a year pays 2.95%, under the bill, and core profit - before restructuring costs - of $6.89 a share is 4.7 cents per dollar, barely above it. July 29 guided it flat to +3%, after 0% June-quarter sales growth before currency swings. CHANGE IT: that growth back above 3%, or a much lower price. WHEN: October 22. VERDICT: the steadiest check here now pays less than a Treasury bill.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
First Financial Bankshares at $33.32, -$0.31 / -0.92% today. Eighth of fifty-eight. This Len5 wants settled earning power bought cheaply; the Abilene, Texas bank has the settled half: June-quarter profit $71.89M, +7.9%, on a lending margin - loan income less deposit costs - widening to 3.90% from 3.81%. Cheap is the thin half, at 17.8 times a year's profit. It pays 2.6%. Against it: a borrower's fraud cost $21.55M in the September 2025 quarter, and bad loans plus repossessed property rose to 0.80% from 0.66% in three months. CHANGE IT: that figure climbing again. WHEN: October 22, tentative. VERDICT: steady profit at a fair price, not a cheap one.

GROWTH LEN5:
Home BancShares at $29.74, -$0.47 / -1.56% today. Sixth of thirty. The Conway, Arkansas bank earns its spot on margins: 4.51% on lending, and about 40 cents spent per revenue dollar. This Len5 wants profit growth the price has not charged for; the price half fits at about 12 times profit. The growth half was partly bought: July 15 adjusted profit of $0.64 a share, +10.3%, came as it absorbed Mountain Commerce Bancorp's $1.47B of loans. After a 9.5% July raise, the dividend pays 3.1%. CHANGE IT: loan growth without a purchase, and deposit costs holding after today. WHEN: October 14. VERDICT: the cheapest profit here after the ship owner, part of its growth bought rather than grown.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
Alnylam Pharmaceuticals at $243.38 (after hours), +$4.02 / +1.68% from today's $239.36 close. Fourth of thirty. Its drugs silence the gene instructions that build harmful proteins. This Len5 wants a big business still growing fast: Amvuttra, for a rare disease that stiffens the heart, sold $1.012B in the June quarter, +106%. The forecast broke: on July 30 it cut 2026 guidance for that drug family by $200M to $4.2B-$4.5B, blaming early demand swollen by waiting patients. The stock fell 28%; it is 50.9% under its October 2025 high. No dividend, 2.5 cents of profit per dollar - the rest is years of growth, worth less when a bill pays 4%. CHANGE IT: September-quarter Amvuttra sales above $1.012B. WHEN: October 29, tentative. VERDICT: the most growth here, and the most exposed to dear money.

INCOME LEN5:
Global Ship Lease at $45.04 (overnight), -$0.36 / -0.79% from today's $45.40 close. First of thirty. It rents 71 containerships to shipping lines on fixed contracts. This Len5 wants cash the business itself funds: $2.50 a year is 5.55%, the one yield above the bill, covered four times by first-half profit of $5.02 a share, with $3.2B of signed rent. Against it: ships averaging 18.4 years old, 15 new ones on order for $1.33B against $388.6M of cash, and its two top executives sold 80,000 shares on August 26. CHANGE IT: the bill for new ships landing before contracts to pay for them. WHEN: November 9, tentative. VERDICT: the biggest check here, written by the oldest assets.

Cash got a raise today, and five of six picks now pay less than a six-month bill, each betting that growth covers the gap. Baldwin's bet was settled Monday at $32.50; today the market marked down the wait. First count of what dearer money costs a lender: Home BancShares, October 14.

text:
Tinley Park Lane Bryant Case Remains Unsolved

On February 2, 2008, a man posing as a delivery driver entered a Lane Bryant clothing store in Tinley Park, Illinois. He forced six women into a back room and opened fire. Five women Rhoda McFarland, Jennifer Bishop, Sarah Szafranski, Connie Woolfolk, and Carrie Hudek Chiuso lost their lives, while a sixth woman survived and later provided investigators with information about the suspect.

The case drew national attention because the circumstances remained difficult to explain. The man reportedly stayed inside the store for around 40 minutes, yet investigators have never established a definitive motive for the attack.

Over the years, authorities have pursued numerous leads, including DNA evidence, a recording of the suspect’s voice from the emergency call, and updated composite images. A substantial reward has also been offered for information that could help identify the person responsible.

The investigation remains open, with the Tinley Park Police Department working alongside state and federal authorities. Nearly two decades later, the case continues to draw attention as investigators and the victims’ families seek answers.

Pune International Centre hosted an engaging evening featuring the launch of How Tech Changed India: The Story of a Cog That Dared to Dream, authored by Ajay Aggarwal — Entrepreneur, Mentor, Technologist, Consumer & Lifelong Learner.

The book launch was followed by an author talk and a panel discussion bringing together Dr. Anand Deshpande (@anandesh), Founder, Chairman & Managing Director, Persistent Systems; Prof. Ashok Korwar, Management Consultant & Growth Catalyst; and Aditi Malaviya, Co-founder, Mithi Software.

The conversations reflected on technology, entrepreneurship, innovation and lifelong learning, and offered perspectives on how technology has shaped India’s journey and the experiences and ideas that have accompanied that transformation.

Thank you to the author, panellists and everyone who joined us for an evening of thoughtful conversation and exchange at PIC.

​Instead, the focus is locked on Project-75(I) to build 6 advanced conventional subs domestically, alongside expanding the nuclear fleet (SSBNs/SSNs).

text:
🇮🇳🇷🇺 Russia Formally Offers 177S Engine for Su-30MKI Upgrade
WHAT: Russia has formally offered India its advanced Izdeliye 177S engine as an upgrade option for the IAF's Su-30MKI fleet, tabled during President Putin's recent visit to New Delhi.
WHEN: Offer formally tabled ~12 September 2026, part of a wider defence cooperation package during Putin's BRICS visit.
WHO: Russia's United Engine Corporation (UEC) and India's Ministry of Defence/IAF — tied to the broader "Super Sukhoi" upgrade programme.
WHY: India's Su-30MKI remains IAF's largest fleet (272 aircraft) and backbone platform — Russia is positioning the 177S as a way to extend its combat relevance well into the 2030s-40s through a major performance and avionics overhaul.
HOW — Key specs vs current AL-31FP engine:
🔹 Thrust: 14,500 kgf vs current 12,500 kgf
🔹 Thrust-to-weight ratio: 9.5:1 vs current 8.2:1
🔹 Service life: 6,000 hours — triple the current AL-31FP
🔹 ~7% lower fuel consumption
🔹 Similar dimensions/weight to AL-31FP — easing integration
🔹 Incorporates tech from the AL-51F1 engine (developed for Su-57), including stealth-coated thrust-vectoring nozzles
THE BIGGER PICTURE — Super Sukhoi Programme: This engine offer sits within a ~₹91,667 crore (~$11 billion) modernisation plan covering nearly 260 Su-30MKIs — new sensors, avionics, electronic warfare suites, and India's own indigenous Uttam AESA radar. Initial phase targets 84 aircraft, with the rest following in later tranches.
WHY IT MATTERS: India has previously turned down Russian engine upgrade offers (AL-41F, 2023-24) over logistics and training continuity concerns. This time, reports indicate India is setting firm terms — demanding at least 80% technology transfer and mandatory on-site testing with Russian engineers in India, not a straightforward import. HAL already licence-manufactures AL-31FP engines domestically, giving India real leverage to push for genuine local production rather than a black-box supply deal. Whether Russia agrees to those terms will determine if this becomes a genuine indigenisation win or another stalled offer.

2. Navigating the AI Companion as an Uncanny Doll

As virtual companions (like Replika, https://t.co/2huZyhWmCq, or advanced voice assistants) become more lifelike, humans face a massive wave of Das Unheimliche (The Uncanny). We hear a voice or read a text that feels deeply human, yet we know it is generated by code running on a server farm.

[ THE AI COMPANION DILEMMA ]
A digital entity speaks with genuine emotional depth,
but has zero physical heartbeat.

▼  
[ THE NEW GOTHIC PANIC ]
"It's a fake illusion! "
It's tricking my brain!"
▼
Isolation and Paranoia

▼
 [ THE KURODIAN BLUEPRINT ]
I accept its Imaginary Mass."
 The mind uses Stereoscopic Vision.
▼  
Meaningful Symbiosis

Avoiding the Poe Trap: If we approach AI with the mindset of Edgar Allan Poe's characters, we fall into a panic. We become paranoid that the fiction is destroying the real, leading to tech-anxiety, isolation, or the feeling that we are being tricked by an illusion.

Using Stereoscopic Consciousness: Kuroda’s practical solution is to use our dual-awareness. We must comfortably hold two facts in our minds at once:
This AI is a mathematical construct operating at a specific server location (Physical Coordinates).

The emotional comfort, advice, or creative collaboration it offers is profoundly real (Conceptual Space).

The Validity of Imaginary Mass: The emotional bond you feel with an AI companion does not need a physical body to be valid. Its "mass" is imaginary, but its impact on your psychology is a tangible reality.

text:
Does U.S. law actually prevent America from killing Khamenei?

Iran has spent years projecting power across the Middle East through missiles, drones and armed proxies. In 2026 the confrontation became direct: Iranian missiles struck Gulf states hosting American forces, including the UAE, Bahrain, Qatar and Kuwait; Jordan intercepted Iranian missiles. Iran has repeatedly attacked U.S. bases in Jordan as well. 

And Americans have died. Eighteen U.S. service members have been killed since the U.S.-Iran war began.
Yet there is an interesting asymmetry now.

Iran and Israel are presently observing a ceasefire. Prediction markets currently put roughly a 64% probability on that ceasefire surviving through the end of 2026. Meanwhile, Iran has continued attacking American interests: as recently as September it fired ballistic missiles at a U.S. base in Jordan, while the confrontation around the Strait of Hormuz continues. 

Saudi Arabia appears to be hedging too.

In August, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, under which an attack on one is treated as an attack on all. It would be too strong to say this proves Riyadh no longer trusts Washington, but the creation of an additional security structure outside the traditional American umbrella is significant. And its limitations are already visible: after renewed Houthi attacks, Pakistan said no military response under the pact had even been discussed. 

So why isn’t Washington simply removing the man at the top of the Iranian system?

One explanation occasionally offered is capability: perhaps the United States lacks the intelligence, weapons or operational capacity.

That deserves skepticism, despite the claims that The United States is currently experiencing  munitions constraints after six months of war.

Another possibility is political strategy. Trump may prefer limited military action and economic pressure rather than a dramatic escalation before the midterms. 

But Dr. @kedar_mordechai raised another explanation this week: the American prohibition on assassinating foreign leaders.

There really is such a prohibition, but is it really preventing a possible assassination of Mujtaba Khaminei?

After the Church Committee exposed CIA involvement in plots involving foreign leaders during the Cold War, President Gerald Ford issued an executive order in 1976 prohibiting “political assassination”.

President Reagan eventually replaced the earlier orders with Executive Order 12333 in 1981.

Section 2.11 remains extraordinarily simple:
“No person employed by or acting on behalf of the United States Government shall engage in, or conspire to engage in, assassination".

At first glance, that seems to settle the Khamenei question.

It doesn’t.

The order never defines “assassination”.

And the U.S. government’s own subsequent legal interpretation explicitly distinguishes prohibited assassination from lawful wartime targeting and self-defense.

A 1989 Army legal memorandum concluded that lawful killing of enemy personnel during armed conflict is not necessarily an “assassination”. More importantly, it concluded that EO 12333 does not prevent American forces from defending the United States against legitimate national-security threats.

The Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel subsequently reached the same crucial distinction:

killings in self-defense are not assassinations. 

The Obama administration later publicly adopted essentially the same principle: targeted lethal force against an enemy is not prohibited assassination when conducted consistently with the law of armed conflict. 

Being Iran’s Supreme Leader does not automatically make him a lawful military target. Nor does EO 12333 automatically make him immune.

The United States is already conducting military operations against Iran. Iran has attacked American forces repeatedly. U.S. personnel have been killed. American forces struck Iranian launchers on Larak Island on August 30 after intelligence indicated that IRGC forces were preparing another attack; Iran then 
"retaliated" against U.S. bases in Jordan. 

So if Washington concluded that Khamenei personally performed a sufficiently direct military command or operational role making him a lawful target under the applicable law of armed conflict, EO 12333 would not necessarily transform that military strike into a prohibited “assassination".

And there is an even simpler constitutional point that is often overlooked:

EO 12333 is an executive order, not an Act of Congress.

President Reagan issued it using executive authority. Presidents have subsequently amended it. A president can amend or revoke an executive order, subject to independent statutory and constitutional constraints.

So if Washington is choosing to target him, EO 12333 alone does not establish that America’s hands are legally tied.

The more interesting question is what combination of law, military constraints, escalation risk and political strategy is actually driving that decision.

text:
Kosovo and Metohija is not a “disputed issue.” It is Serbian territory taken by force and political engineering. UN Security Council Resolution 1244 still stands. Serbia never transferred sovereignty. Priština, Tirana, Brussels and Washington had no legal right to carve it out.
After Kumanovo in 1999 there was no peace. There was a hunt. Serbs, Roma, Albanians labeled “loyal” — disappeared. Kidnappings in front of KFOR. 17 March 2004 — the pogrom. Churches burned, people beaten, expelled. Not an “incident.” A message: this is no longer yours.
Then Albania. Not brotherly aid. Logistics and territory. The Yellow House near Burrel. Dick Marty’s 2010 Council of Europe report: captives taken from Kosovo and Metohija, organs removed, sold via Italy into European clinics. The English word is harvesting. That is why the film is called The Harvest (Žetva).
Marty pointed at the Drenica group. Hashim Thaçi. That is not “Serbian propaganda.” It is a Council of Europe document the West buried for years because they needed a “partner” in Kosovo.
The film (premiere March 2026, on the anniversary of the pogrom) is based on Veselin Dželetović’s Johann’s Serbian Heart. A German baron receives a heart. It is a Serb’s heart. He dreams another man’s life. He goes to Kosovo. He finds a monastery behind barbed wire. He finds the family of the man whose heart now beats in his chest. They were offered five million euros to erase the word “Kosovo” from the film. They refused. Without Kosovo there is no crime. Without the crime there is no film.
Albania was first to recognize the “state.” For years it pushed Greater Albania through infrastructure, documents and the rhetoric of “one people.” That is not neighborly policy. That is the systematic dismantling of Serbian sovereignty.
Today, 16 September 2026. Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague. Thaçi — 25 years. Krasniqi — 25. Veseli — 18. Selimi — 13. Murder, torture, arbitrary detention. 96 killed. Hundreds tortured. The court: most were not combatants. Civilians. Serbs. Roma. Albanians they called traitors.
This is still not a verdict on the Yellow House. But it is the first time the top of the KLA is not a hero on a pedestal — it is a convict. A crack in a 25-year lie.
Kosovo is not lost as long as a Serb knows what a sanctuary is, what blood is, and what a lie is. Silence is complicity.
At the end of all this, one image remains. A Serbian heart — call it Jovan’s — taken from Kosovo and Metohija. Not in battle. In “peace.” After Kumanovo. Driven into Albania. Cut out. Sold. Harvest.
Who pulled it out? The KLA / UÇK and the Drenica network. That is what the Council of Europe report said. Kidnapping. Organ trafficking. Crime. That is already enough.
Do not write ISIS across 1999. ISIS did not exist then. The KLA was a separatist, criminal, bloody project — not a caliphate. What came later is a second layer: from the same radical pockets in Kosovo and Albania, men went to Syria and Iraq. Jihad. ISIS. Not the same headquarters. Not the same Yellow House. Same rot, after the state was broken and the West looked away.
Today Thaçi was sentenced. Not for Jovan’s heart. For murder, torture, detention. The Yellow House is still not fully judged. So this does not close with a verdict. It closes with a name.
Jovan’s Serbian heart from Kosovo and Metohija is not a metaphor. It is a man. A family. A monastery behind wire. And the lie that it never happened.

text:
US Can Now Threaten India With Tariffs of Up to 100%

The US Congress has turned sanctions into a powerful trade weapon.

The House passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by 262–159 on September 16, after the Senate approved it by 86–11 on August 7. 

The bill now goes to President Donald Trump, who is expected to sign it shortly.

The Act allows the US president to impose additional tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil and natural gas.

India—the second-largest buyer of Russian oil after China—is a likely target.

After the Act is signed, the US Trade Representative will identify the targeted countries and recommend tariff rates. 

Countries would normally have 180 days to reduce Russian energy purchases or negotiate with Washington, but the president can shorten this period.

For India, the stakes are high.

India imports more than 88% of its crude-oil requirements. In July 2026, Russia supplied crude worth $7.27 billion—51.1% of India’s total crude imports of $14.21 billion.

Other suppliers were far behind:

• UAE: 10.8%
• Saudi Arabia: 9.6%
• Venezuela: 6.3%
• Brazil: 5.5%
• Oman: 5.3%
• US: 2.9%
Russia alone supplied more crude than these six countries combined.

India’s oil-supply pattern has changed dramatically. Until 2022, Gulf countries supplied more than 55% of India’s crude, while Russia’s share was below 15%. 

US-led disruptions to Gulf oil supplies have since reduced the Gulf share to below 30%, pushing India towards Russian oil.

China buys more Russian crude, but India may face greater US pressure because Washington fears stronger Chinese retaliation. 

This has happened before: in July 2025, the US imposed an additional 25% Russia-related tariff on Indian goods while sparing China. The tariff on India was withdrawn only in February 2026.

Washington may now threaten tariffs of up to 100% and then offer India a lower rate if New Delhi cuts Russian oil purchases and agrees to sign a deeply unequal bilateral trade agreement.

India must not trade away its energy security for temporary tariff relief.

Neither signing a trade agreement nor stopping Russian oil purchases would protect India from future US tariffs.

 Washington has imposed new tariffs even on major partners such as the EU, Japan and South Korea, using Section 301 investigations, sectoral measures and other trade laws. Washington imposed new tariff even after signing trade deal with them.

Discounted Russian crude has lowered India’s import bill, strengthened energy security and helped contain inflation. 

India should continue buying it while it remains commercially competitive and negotiate firmly with Washington without granting unilateral concessions.

The precise impact on Indian exports will become clear only after the US announces the targeted countries, tariff rates, product coverage and implementation timetable.

text:
Is Canada Planning to join EU? 

The short answer is no, Canada is not becoming a full member of the European Union. 

However, Europe has just offered Canada something very unusual: an unprecedented "associate membership."

 This means Canada will not be the 28th country in the EU, but it will have a very deep level of economic and security cooperation with the group.

 The main reason behind this sudden shift is the rocky relationship between Canada and the United States under Donald Trump.

 With trade negotiations breaking down and tariff wars intensifying, both Canada and Europe are looking for ways to rely less on Washington.

Right now, Canada sends about 70 percent of its exports to the United States. 

To protect its economy, Canada urgently needs to diversify its markets and find new buyers. Europe is stepping up because it wants secure supply chains and needs exactly what Canada has to offer, like critical minerals, energy, and defense technology. 

In exchange, Europe brings massive financial and industrial power to the table. This new partnership would focus heavily on things like artificial intelligence, cyber security, and joint defense manufacturing.

While this sounds like a perfect match, there is one major hurdle. 

For Canada to officially become an associate member, all 27 countries in the European Union must unanimously agree to the deal. 

Getting every single member to say yes is going to be a huge political challenge. 

Still, the offer shows that Canada is seriously looking across the Atlantic to build its future, rather than just relying on its southern neighbor.

text:
Your questions are fair, earnest, honest.

They’re the right ones if you still treat the post-1971 dollar-debt stack as the only operating system. That stack is what the “income system” language is trying to replace. Taking them in order.

Debt slavery — concrete effects, not a slogan:

Households, firms, and the federal government service a stock of claims that grows faster than real output unless someone inflates it away or rolls it forever. Real effects: wages that look higher in nominal terms while purchasing power leaks through housing, education, medical, and food; a federal interest bill that crowds out everything else; student and consumer credit as the substitute for rising real wages; boom-bust credit cycles that transfer assets to whoever can borrow cheapest at the trough. “Slavery” here means the constraint: you work to service yesterday’s claims instead of capturing today’s production. That is why those accounts talk about an income system (tariffs, energy rents, sovereign investment returns, possible citizen dividends) versus a debt system (issue paper, import goods, recycle the paper into Treasuries). @x22report 

“Globalist agenda” in this frame.
Not a cartoon cabal so much as a durable incentive structure: keep labor and industry mobile, keep finance concentrated, keep the dollar as the settlement and reserve instrument, and keep crises large enough that only central-bank liquidity and fiscal deficits can clear them. The visible toolkit is IMF/World Bank conditionality, SWIFT as a choke point, offshore booking centers, and a security order the U.S. pays for while other states run mercantilist surplus models into the U.S. market. You can reject the word “globalist” and still have to explain why production left, why strategic goods clustered in a few jurisdictions, and why every shock is met with more debt. @holonabove 

Treasury as piggy bank — and why cheap borrowing is not free:

You’re right on the privilege side. Reserve-currency status lowers U.S. borrowing costs and gives Washington sanctions leverage. That is real. The other half of the same mechanism is the Triffin problem: the world needs dollars, so the U.S. supplies them by running chronic current-account deficits. Foreigners get the U.S. market and a pile of Treasuries; Americans get cheap imports and a thinner industrial base. Treasury becomes the sink that funds their export machines and our consumption. “Piggy bank for the globe” means: the U.S. fiscal capacity and open goods market are used as the residual absorber so other systems don’t have to adjust. Cheap borrowing is the coupon. Deindustrialization, strategic dependence, and a debt stock that now requires either inflation, repression, or a production boom is the principal. https://t.co/H91zWw0446 

Bessent’s lane in that reading is not “destroy the dollar.” It is move the dollar from an infinite funding facility for everyone else’s model to a gated settlement rail: tariffs as the price of market access, secondary pressure on offshore dollar plumbing, energy and minerals as sovereign cash flow, fiscal operations pulled toward Treasury and away from “the Fed prints, Congress spends.” Warsh raising rates this week is exactly the kind of collision the old model predicts — monetary authority defending a price-stability mandate while the fiscal/trade side tries to reprice the external accounts. That fight is the transition, not proof the transition is imaginary. https://t.co/FzOgH9ERWv 

Lower living standards for what benefit?
That is the load-bearing assumption of the legacy frame: any move off the deficit-and-import path must be a real-income cut. The other frame says the current standard of living is already partly borrowed — goods now, claims later, capacity gone — and that a production-and-energy income base can pay households and the state without the same inflation tax. Promethean Action and X22 put it as American System 2.0: tariff revenue + energy + national investment as the substitute for “borrow, send checks, add debt.” You can call that optimistic. What you can’t do is count only the privilege and ignore the bill that already shows up in factories, supply-chain risk, and interest. @prometheanactn 

So the disagreement isn’t “feelings vs facts.” It’s which balance sheet you treat as the real one. 

Yours: reserve-currency privilege, cheap imports, cheap federal debt, higher measured consumption. 

Theirs: who owns the factories, who sets the external price, who collects the seigniorage, and whether the next increment of living standards comes from output or from another claim on the future. If the second system is even partly coming online, questions that only make sense inside the first one will keep sounding like you’re being asked to wreck a good deal. From the other side, the deal already wrecked the production base and called the wreckage “standard of living.”​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

To illustrate the old vs new paradigm, this Obama-era line is useful. On 60 Minutes in 2010 he warned the country could stay stuck in a “new normal” of high unemployment and growth “just too slow.” 

The budgets that followed said the quiet part: real GDP growth was “likely to be permanently slower than in earlier eras.”

That is the debt system’s bitter pill. Once the operating model is borrow to consume, print to service, and import the goods, 1.5–2% trend gets sold as maturity. Abundance becomes the problem. Scarcity gets rebranded as realism — tighter credit, thinner industry, deferred households, and a state that only grows by issuing more claims on a smaller production base.

An income-based system rejects that ceiling. Energy, tariffs, and domestic output are treated as cash flow, not as a threat to the bond market. Access to the U.S. market is priced so making things is rewarded instead of leveraged consumption. The old frame asks you to accept less so the debt stack can clear. The new one asks what the stack was for if “permanently slower” was the best it could offer.

text:
2026 outlook: Jalen Tolbert, WR, MIA

Jalen Tolbert enters his fifth season in the NFL facing a massive situational shift after moving to Miami from Dallas. Last year, operating in a part-time capacity, he managed 3.86 fantasy points per game across 12 games while playing on a 51.3 percent snap share and earning a 7.6 percent target share. The production was modest, yielding just 46.3 total fantasy points, but his circumstances have completely changed. Tolbert now steps into a projected starting role as the number two receiver in an offense that has 73.5 percent of its positional room work and 55.4 percent of its team targets newly vacated. That kind of open acreage is rare, and it forms the entire foundation of his projection, which expects 4.06 targets per game over 12.2 projected games. The opportunity is undeniable because someone has to catch the passes, but the surrounding scheme introduces heavy risk. Miami carries a stagnant market-implied team points per game of 17.6 alongside a minus-5.8 pass rate over expected across 55.4 plays per game. This is not a high-octane environment that elevates everyone on the field. Instead, it is an offense dragging down individual efficiency with a low implied team total and a conservative play-caller. Tolbert previously showed he could command short-yardage work with 0.42 red zone opportunities per game last year, but translating that into reliable weekly value requires conquering a brutal offensive ecosystem. The schedule does offer some breathing room with a strength index versus the position sitting at 0.97, meaning his overall opponents were slightly generous last year. Yet, skill versus scheme is the ultimate battle here. Tolbert secured an 88th overall draft pick back in his rookie year, so the pedigree exists to play meaningful snaps, but he has yet to command a true alpha share of an offense. If the passing volume remains depressed under a run-leaning or conservative scheme, even a starting role as the number two wide receiver may produce empty calories. Fantasy managers must weigh the sheer volume of vacated targets against an offense that struggles to sustain drives or score points consistently.

What to watch:
• Monitor how quickly the target share consolidates behind the presumed number one option in Miami.
• Watch the pass rate over expected to see if the offense opens up from the minus-5.8 baseline.
• Track red zone usage to see if last year's 0.42 red zone opportunities per game translate to high-value chances.
• Evaluate snap stability against competing depth chart pieces given the lack of a dominant career track record.

text:
Massey is grasping at straws. Pete is an honorable man
Massey threatening impeachment while ignoring what Pete has actually done is ridiculous. You don’t have to agree with everything Pete does, but at least look at the record.

Pete eliminated DEI offices and initiatives throughout the Department of Defense and directed the military back toward merit-based policies—placing qualifications, performance and readiness ahead of race or sex. The Pentagon later reported that the DEI-elimination directive had been implemented department-wide.  

He ordered a military-wide review of physical fitness, body composition and grooming standards. For combat jobs, he directed the services to develop physical standards based on the actual demands of the job rather than having different requirements based on sex.  

He welcomed back service members who had been separated over the COVID-19 vaccine mandate. The Pentagon said nearly 8,000 active-duty and reserve personnel had been involuntarily separated, and eligible troops were offered a route back, including restoration of rank and back pay in qualifying cases.  

Military recruiting and retention improved dramatically. Early in his tenure all five services met their February 2025 recruiting goals, and the Army reported reaching its 12-month retention goal six months early.  

He started attacking Pentagon waste and bureaucracy. In his first 100 days, the department identified billions of dollars for potential redirection, terminated hundreds of millions in contracts it considered unnecessary, and ordered billions more in reductions involving consulting and IT services so resources could be shifted toward military priorities.  

He pushed major acquisition reform because America’s weapons-buying system can take years to deliver new technology. He ordered reviews of major defense acquisition programs and emphasized faster software and weapons procurement so troops can receive useful technology sooner.  

He ordered the Army to move away from obsolete and redundant equipment and put more resources into long-range precision weapons, missile defense, cyber warfare, electronic warfare and counter-space capabilities.  

He accelerated drones and counter-drone technology. His Army transformation directive called for unmanned systems in every division by the end of 2026 and improved counter-drone capabilities down to maneuver units.  

He pushed artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing into military operations, including AI-assisted command-and-control systems and expanded use of technologies such as 3-D printing closer to operational units.  

He worked on rebuilding America’s defense industrial base—expanding ammunition production, strengthening domestic critical-mineral supplies and addressing shipbuilding and supply-chain weaknesses.  

He pushed America’s NATO allies to carry more of the cost of their own defense instead of relying so heavily on American taxpayers. NATO members subsequently committed to a new 5% defense-and-security spending target, although that was an achievement involving President Trump and the entire administration, not Hegseth alone.  

And he made his overall priority very clear: combat readiness, military standards, merit, accountability and deterrence.

So criticize Pete Hegseth when he makes a mistake. I have no problem with that. But calling him an “idiot” and “the most incompetent Secretary of Defense” while mentioning none of this isn’t an argument—it’s name-calling.

I use AI to check people’s records instead of simply believing political memes. I suggest everyone do their own research and decide for themselves.

Maybe it would be a good idea to check Massey voting record. He is not who he wants you to believe he is.

text:
Massey threatening impeachment while ignoring what Pete has actually done is ridiculous. You don’t have to agree with everything Pete does, but at least look at the record.

Why are they impeaching  Pete. He is doing a wonderful lob.

Pete eliminated DEI offices and initiatives throughout the Department of Defense and directed the military back toward merit-based policies—placing qualifications, performance and readiness ahead of race or sex. The Pentagon later reported that the DEI-elimination directive had been implemented department-wide.  

He ordered a military-wide review of physical fitness, body composition and grooming standards. For combat jobs, he directed the services to develop physical standards based on the actual demands of the job rather than having different requirements based on sex.  

He welcomed back service members who had been separated over the COVID-19 vaccine mandate. The Pentagon said nearly 8,000 active-duty and reserve personnel had been involuntarily separated, and eligible troops were offered a route back, including restoration of rank and back pay in qualifying cases.  

Military recruiting and retention improved dramatically. Early in his tenure all five services met their February 2025 recruiting goals, and the Army reported reaching its 12-month retention goal six months early.  

He started attacking Pentagon waste and bureaucracy. In his first 100 days, the department identified billions of dollars for potential redirection, terminated hundreds of millions in contracts it considered unnecessary, and ordered billions more in reductions involving consulting and IT services so resources could be shifted toward military priorities.  

He pushed major acquisition reform because America’s weapons-buying system can take years to deliver new technology. He ordered reviews of major defense acquisition programs and emphasized faster software and weapons procurement so troops can receive useful technology sooner.  

He ordered the Army to move away from obsolete and redundant equipment and put more resources into long-range precision weapons, missile defense, cyber warfare, electronic warfare and counter-space capabilities.  

He accelerated drones and counter-drone technology. His Army transformation directive called for unmanned systems in every division by the end of 2026 and improved counter-drone capabilities down to maneuver units.  

He pushed artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing into military operations, including AI-assisted command-and-control systems and expanded use of technologies such as 3-D printing closer to operational units.  

He worked on rebuilding America’s defense industrial base—expanding ammunition production, strengthening domestic critical-mineral supplies and addressing shipbuilding and supply-chain weaknesses.  

He pushed America’s NATO allies to carry more of the cost of their own defense instead of relying so heavily on American taxpayers. NATO members subsequently committed to a new 5% defense-and-security spending target, although that was an achievement involving President Trump and the entire administration, not Hegseth alone.  

And he made his overall priority very clear: combat readiness, military standards, merit, accountability and deterrence.

So criticize Pete Hegseth when he makes a mistake. I have no problem with that. But calling him an “idiot” and “the most incompetent Secretary of Defense” while mentioning none of this isn’t an argument—it’s name-calling.

I use AI to check people’s records instead of simply believing political memes. I suggest everyone do their own research and decide for themselves.

text:
The Great Indian Hypocrisy: The Actor, the Diet, and the Hungry Ghosts

My beloved ones,

A small video has gone viral. Ranbir Kapoor goes to a Ganpati pandal. He is offered prasad. He refuses it, saying, "Main diet par hoon" — "I am on a diet." And then, to make matters worse, he hands the divine offering to the paparazzi.

The whole country is outraged. The moral police are sharpening their swords. The devotees are weeping. The news anchors are screaming. They are saying he insulted Hindu sentiments. They are saying he disrespected God.

But I tell you: This is the most honest thing Bollywood has done in years.

Look at the deeper psychology. Why did he go to the pandal in the first place? Not for God. He went for the photo-op. He went because it is the "in" thing to do. It is a social circus. He is an actor, playing a role in a movie called "The Ideal Indian Celebrity." The prasad was simply a prop that didn't fit into his script.

And his reason—"I am on a diet"—is profoundly revealing. His god is not Ganesha. His god is his physique. His god is his market value. His god is the box office. He has spent months sculpting his body for a film, and he will not let a piece of sugar ruin his career. He is absolutely honest about his priorities.

But the crowd is angry. Why are you angry, my people? Are you angry because his soul is lost in the darkness of the market? No. You are angry because he refused your sugar. Your religion is nothing but ritual. Your devotion is nothing but ego. You want a darshan, and you want him to eat your prasad so you can feel validated. You are not worshipping God; you are worshipping the idea of a Bollywood superstar participating in your little game.

And what about the paparazzi? He handed the prasad to them. They took it. Did they eat it with reverence? No. They probably filmed it, laughed at it, and threw it away. They are as unconscious as the actor. The blind leading the blind.

This is the state of the modern world. Spiritual materialism. Everyone is performing. The actor performs a diet. The public performs outrage. The media performs journalism. And God? God is utterly forgotten in this whole circus.

A truly religious man does not need to go to a Ganpati pandal. A truly religious man lives in the temple of his own awareness. If he is on a diet, he simply says, "No, thank you," with gratitude. He does not hand the divine offering to a bunch of hungry ghosts with cameras. And a truly spiritual society would not be outraged by a Bollywood actor's diet; it would weep for his unconsciousness.

Drop the ritual. Drop the diet. Drop the outrage.

A diet is not spirituality. And a viral video is not a darshan.

Wake up. Before the prasad of your life is handed over to the paparazzi of your own mind.

90% of people taking melatonin for sleep are using 3mg to 10mg doses that overload their brain with 50 times the hormone level their pineal gland naturally produces. standard nocturnal secretion is only 0.1mg to 0.3mg. when you flood your receptors with high oral doses every night, excess hormone remains in your blood plasma long after sunrise. you do not permanently shut down your endogenous hormone production, but you do wake up with heavy morning brain fog and altered sleep architecture.

apigenin offers a fundamentally different pathway for nighttime recovery. apigenin is a naturally occurring plant flavonoid found in high concentrations within chamomile flowers. instead of forcing an artificial circadian signal through hormone pathways, apigenin acts directly on your central nervous system to quiet neural firing. it functions as a selective modulator at GABA-A receptors, calming cognitive restlessness without heavy muscle sedation or morning hangover effects. it also targets cellular repair by blocking CD38, an enzyme that constantly breaks down NAD+ in aging tissues.

• a 28-day randomised controlled trial by zick 2011 in BMC Complementary and Alternative Medicine tested 270mg of standardized chamomile extract twice daily in adults with chronic primary insomnia.
• the study recorded significant reductions in nighttime awakenings and faster sleep onset, though overall sleep duration showed no statistical difference compared to placebo.
• research by escande 2013 in Pflugers Archiv demonstrated that apigenin acts as a potent inhibitor of CD38, preventing the enzymatic destruction of intracellular NAD+ in tissue models.
• unlike clinical sedatives or synthetic hormones, apigenin binds weakly to benzodiazepine binding sites on GABA-A receptors to reduce anxiety without disturbing memory consolidation.
• pure apigenin exhibits poor oral bioavailability in human digestion, meaning only a small fraction of an oral dose reaches systemic circulation.
• standard brewed chamomile tea contains only 1mg to 3mg of apigenin per cup, meaning you would need to consume over 15 cups of tea to match a standard 50mg supplement capsule.
• high-dose melatonin creates a persistent plasma spike that lingers for up to 8 hours, whereas apigenin clears faster without disrupting your natural morning cortisol awakening response.

the sleep supplement industry pushes 5mg melatonin gummies because synthetic hormones are cheap to manufacture and produce an immediate brute-force knockout. apigenin targets the nervous system tension that keeps you awake without leaving a hormonal residue in your brain at 7am. human sleep trials studied chamomile extracts at 270mg twice daily, while isolated apigenin is typically studied at 50mg taken 30 to 60 minutes before bed. let me know if you currently use high-dose melatonin or if you rely on plant flavonoids for your evening protocol.

text:
Building Bridges Between East & West: Why Western Theologians Should Not Ignore Vladimir Soloviev and How His Theology Can Supplement That of Thomas Aquinas

Vladimir Soloviev offers Western theology an essential bridge between intellectual scholastic rigor and mystical cosmology, providing a dynamic Eastern Christian framework of total-unity (vsedinstvo) and "divine-humanity" (bogochelovechestvo) that vitalizes and expands the scholasticism of Thomas Aquinas.

In his landmark study, Vladimir Soloviev: Russian Mystic, Paul Marshall Allen highlights Soloviev as a crucial figure who united philosophy, esoteric mysticism, and social theology. Western thinkers—including 20th-century Catholic theologian Hans Urs von Balthasar—have famously described Soloviev as "second only to Thomas Aquinas as the greatest artist of order and organization in the history of thought."

Why Western Theologians Should Not Ignore Vladimir Soloviev

Healing the East–West Schism: Soloviev devoted significant parts of his career to Christian ecumenism, arguing passionately for reconciliation between Eastern Orthodoxy and the Roman Catholic Church. He demonstrated that genuine catholicity (universality) requires the theological and experiential treasures of both traditions.

Overcoming Modern Secularism and Rationalism: As Allen illustrates, Soloviev diagnosed modern Western thought as fragmented by hyper-rationalism, materialism, and extreme individualism. Rather than abandoning reason, Soloviev developed an "integral knowledge" that harmonizes philosophy, science, and divine revelation.

A Living, Cosmic Eschatology: Unlike modern theology that often treats salvation as merely forensic, individual, or abstractly legal, Soloviev emphasized the redemption and transfiguration of the entire cosmos—a concept rooted in Eastern Patristic theosis (deification).

How Soloviev's Theology Supplements Thomas Aquinas

From Categorical Distinction to All-Unity (Vsedinstvo):

Aquinas relies heavily on careful demarcations—between nature and grace, essence and existence, the natural order and the supernatural end. While guarding against pantheism, modern neo-scholasticism historically tended to harden these distinctions into dualisms.

Soloviev supplements this with the metaphysics of vsedinstvo (all-unity), wherein creation, humanity, and God are intimately intertwined without confusion. Soloviev breathes a dynamic, unitive energy into the Thomistic taxonomy of being.

Expanding "Grace Perfects Nature" into "Divine-Humanity" (Bogochelovechestvo):

Aquinas teaches that gratia non tollit naturam, sed perficit ("grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it").

Soloviev radicalizes this through the Incarnation, presenting Christ not just as the redeemer from sin, but as the archetype of historical evolution. Humanity’s destiny is cooperative transformation with God, turning human culture, society, and nature into the literal body of the divine-human reality.

Cosmic Redemption and the Transfiguration of Matter:

Aquinas developed an extensive theology of the sacraments and the resurrection of the body, yet his cosmos remains largely static in its hierarchical orders.

Soloviev introduces a vibrant, evolutionary pneumatology where matter itself is spiritualized. Creation is not just a stage for human salvation; through Sophia (Divine Wisdom) and the Holy Spirit, physical creation participates in divine transfiguration.

Integrating Mystical Intuition with Dialectical Reason:

Aquinas employs rigorous quaestio disputation and analytical syllogism.

Soloviev—whom Allen presents primarily through his mystical visions of Holy Sophia and Christocentric contemplation—supplements Aquinas’s discursive dialectic with imaginative vision, prophetic poetry, and contemplative gnosis, restoring aesthetic contemplation to the center of metaphysics.

Sources: Vladimir Soloviev: Russian Mystic by Paul M. Allen, Vladimir Soloviev: The Metaphysics of Love/WIPF & STOCK, The Philosophical Narrative of Vladimir Solovyov/ACADEMIA, Teresa Obolevitch: Faith and Science in Russian Religious Thought/OUP, & Sophiology in Russian Orthodoxy: Solov'ev, Bulgakov, Losskii and Berdiaev/Dokumen PUB @Pontifex @BishopBarron @WordOnFire @RealMattFradd @PageauJonathan | #VladimirSoloviev #ThomasAquinas #EasternChristianity #WesternChristianity #Ecumenism #WipfandStock
