text:
Yes—a battery-powered aircraft carrying one or two people is feasible today. The difficult part is making it affordable, certified for autonomous passenger service, and practical across Los Angeles. I would start with a two-seat aircraft operating between a few fixed stations.

The vehicle

A simple design would have an enclosed cabin, multiple electric rotors, fixed landing gear, and standardised batteries and motor assemblies. Independent power and flight-control systems would be essential.

Two seats offer better potential economics: the second passenger adds revenue without doubling station and dispatch costs. A one-seater would be lighter, but every trip earns only one fare.

An existing benchmark is EHang’s two-seat pilotless EH216-S, which publishes a 19-mile range and announced a $410,000 international suggested price. It demonstrates the concept, but its Chinese approvals do not authorise an LA service. Specifications, pricing.

Range and cost

These are preliminary planning estimates, not guaranteed specifications or supplier quotes:
ItemReasonable starting assumptionSimple multicopter route5–12 miles, allowing headroom below advertised maximum rangeWinged electric aircraft routeInvestigate 20–50 miles, subject to aircraft selectionOne-seat commercial aircraft$250,000–$500,000Two-seat commercial aircraft$400,000–$800,000Small station at an existing suitable aviation site$1–5 million, excluding land and major reconstructionNew urban or rooftop station$5–20 million or more
Multicopters are mechanically simpler, but use substantial energy staying airborne. Wings improve efficiency during forward flight, making them more attractive for longer LA journeys. Actual range depends on passenger weight, wind, battery condition, and required reserves.
Mass production could reduce manufacturing costs through standardised components and repeatable assembly. It would not eliminate certification, maintenance, or insurance costs.
How autonomous trips would work
Your automated-route idea is the best starting point:
Book a trip → arrive at a station → board → fly an approved route → land → connect to a car or transit.
AI could schedule aircraft, predict demand, and support maintenance. Flight automation would need validated responses to weather, other aircraft, navigation failures, and an unavailable landing pad. Fixed routes help, but cannot eliminate those situations.
The FAA expects initial air-taxi operations to resemble helicopter services using existing infrastructure. A fully pilotless fleet requires approvals beyond simply having an aircraft that flies automatically. FAA overview
What stations would look like
Think of a compact airport terminal:
One takeoff-and-landing pad with clear approaches and an area protected from rotor airflow.
Two to four aircraft parking and charging positions.
A small waiting room and controlled boarding area.
Maintenance access and battery-fire provisions.
Convenient connections to transit and car pickups.
Ground-level stations at existing airports would be easier starting points than rooftops. Rooftops introduce structural, evacuation, access, and wind challenges. FAA guidance also requires attention to downwash and site safety. Vertiport guidance

Where to put them in LA

I would investigate these areas—not assume they are available or approved:

AreaPotential roleHawthorne / South BayOperations base and airport-area connectionsDowntown / LA Live / USC vicinityEmployment, visitors, and eventsBurbank AirportAirport passengers and northern LA accessVan Nuys AirportValley access and maintenance facilitiesLong Beach AirportRegional connections

Aircraft range would determine which pairs could connect directly. The winning routes must save time door to door, including station access and boarding—not just offer a short flight.

Fleet economics and feasibility

An illustrative 20-aircraft, three-station launch could require roughly $26–71 million, including aircraft, basic facilities, operational setup, spares, and initial operating funds. That excludes developing and certifying a new aircraft and major property purchases.

Electricity would be a relatively small expense. Aircraft financing, battery replacement, maintenance, insurance, station staffing, and empty repositioning flights would determine fares. For example, an assumed $180 cost per departure, divided across 1.5 paying passengers on average, means $120 per passenger to break even. That illustrates the economics; it is not a fare forecast.

My recommendation is to partner with an aircraft manufacturer and launch one valuable route between two stations. A limited premium service is credible enough to investigate today. An inexpensive, autonomous “Waymo of the skies” throughout LA still needs substantial technical, regulatory, and commercial progress.

text:
10 WAYS HOW TO HOLD HER ATTITUDE AND MOOD SWINGS WITH LOVE

She is not chaos.
She is weather.
She is tide.
She is the moon pulling hidden waters to the surface so they can be seen, named, and blessed.

When her atmosphere shifts, do not become the storm. Become the mountain that remains.

1.  Remember she is a living temple of the Divine Feminine. Mood is incense rising from an inner altar you cannot always see. Bow first.
2.  Meet her weather with stillness, not strategy. Your calm is the sacred geometry that holds her expanding universe.
3.  Listen beneath the words. The attitude is rarely the message. The message is almost always “See me. Stay. Do not abandon the mystery.”

4.  Offer presence instead of solutions. Solutions are the mind’s attempt to control the ocean. Presence is the shore that never leaves.
5.  Speak only after your own heart has returned to its original frequency of love. Words spoken from irritation become spells of separation.
6.  Hold her like the night holds the moon: without trying to change her phase.

7.  When she is sharp, become water. Water does not argue with the blade; it simply remains itself until the blade rusts or rests.
8.  Bless the mood instead of fearing it. Every swing is a sacred initiation asking both of you to go deeper into trust.
9.  Protect the space between you as holy ground. Do not let ego, pride, or old wounds set up tents there.
10.  Love her the way the cosmos loves the earth: fiercely, quietly, without condition, through every season of light and shadow.

This is not weakness.
This is mastery.
This is the ancient art of holding the Beloved without dimming her fire or losing your own.

Stay rooted. Stay open. Stay in love.
The storm will pass.
The temple remains.

text:
LET US EXTEND A HELPING HAND TO OUR TEMPLE PRIESTS 
Just pause for a minute… and open your heart.
We go to a temple.
We have Darshan of Swami.
We perform Archana.
We offer Abhishekam.
We put our offerings into the Hundi.
We pray for our family… our health… our children's future… our prosperity.
But…
Do we ever stop and think about the person who stands behind that Sanctum every single day?
The Kurukkal…
The person who wakes up before sunrise…
Who opens the temple doors…
Who cleans the Sanctum…
Who lights the lamp…
Who rings the bell…
Who chants the Mantras…
Who performs Abhishekam…
Who prepares and offers Naivedyam…
And who, with folded hands, prays for our families before Swami.
And then…
He goes back home.
Perhaps to a house with a leaking roof.
Perhaps to an empty kitchen.
Perhaps to medicines that need to be purchased.
Perhaps to a child's school fees waiting to be paid.
Perhaps to an ageing wife who needs treatment.
Perhaps to his own tired and ageing body.
Yet the next morning, he is back again.
Because there is one thought in his heart:
“Swami's Puja must never stop.”
Especially in the small, interior villages of Tamil Nadu, there are temples where only a handful of devotees visit.
There may be little income.
There may be no regular support.
There may be almost no facilities.
But…
THE PUJA CONTINUES.
The lamp continues to burn.
The bell continues to ring.
The Mantras continue to echo.
Because one Kurukkal refuses to abandon his Kainkaryam.
Sometimes, he may not even know where his next month's income will come from.
But he knows one thing:
Swami must be worshipped.
That is his dedication.
That is his Dharma.
That is his Kainkaryam.
And perhaps…
we can become the support that he desperately needs.
We can provide groceries for a month.
We can provide oil for the temple lamp and Abhishekam.
We can provide Puja materials.
We can help with medical expenses.
We can support a child's education.
We can repair a small portion of a damaged priest's house.
 We can help with an urgent family need.
It may be only a few hundred rupees for us.
But for them…
it may mean food for a family.
It may mean medicine for an elderly priest.
It may mean a child's school fee being paid.
It may mean a lamp continuing to burn.
And above all…
It may tell a Kurukkal:
“You are not alone. We are with you.”
We go to the temple to receive blessings from Swami.
They remain in the temple to serve Swami.
Let us therefore serve those who serve Him.
 The lamp they light should never go out because of poverty.
The daily Puja should never stop because the Kurukkal has no means to survive.
A family that has dedicated its life to Swami should never feel forgotten.
Remember…
Protecting a temple is not merely about protecting its walls, Gopuram or Vimanam.
A temple can have a magnificent Gopuram.
It can have a newly renovated Sanctum.
It can have beautiful stonework.
But…
Who will perform the Nitya Puja if there is no Kurukkal?
Who will light the lamp?
Who will chant the Mantras?
Who will offer Naivedyam?
Who will stand before Swami and pray for us?
That is why…
KURUKKAL FIRST… THEN THE TEMPLE.
Let us wipe away a Kurukkal's tears.
Let us reduce a family's burden.
Let us support a child's education.
Let us help an elderly priest obtain medical treatment.
Let us put groceries into an empty kitchen.
Let us put oil into a temple lamp.
Let us ensure that the Nitya Puja continues without interruption.
This is not charity alone.
This is Kainkaryam.
This is Dharma.
This is our responsibility towards our Sanatana heritage.
We seek Swami's blessings every day.
Let us also remember the person who stands before Swami every day seeking nothing for himself, but praying for all of us.
A small contribution from us can become a great support in his life.
Let us not wait for them to ask.
Let us reach them before they are forced to give up.
Save Our Priests.
 Support Our Kurukkals.
Keep the Nitya Puja Alive.
Let the Temple Lamp Continue to Burn.

text:
Washington State 

If Washington Were Its Own Country 

TAX FAIRNESS 

To become more economically competitive, Washington must prioritize tackling tax fairness and securing sustainable revenue

A just-launched effort called the Partnership for a Competitive Puget Sound contends that we must create tax structures that are simple, fair, competitive, and predictable. That work is actually already underway in the Legislature, but there's a lot still to do. 

Will business leaders join organizations like NPI in supporting revenue legislation to modernize our tax code and fund the schools, transportation, and public services that make prosperity possible?

Sept. 16, 2026

If Washington State were its own country, it would rank as having one of the top twenty-five economies in the world, at least as measured by gross domestic product. The Evergreen State today is a major tech and aerospace hub with a large agricultural sector to boot, and has been growing exponentially for decades, yet a host of business and political leaders are warning that the state at risk of falling behind and losing jobs if it doesn’t prioritize economic competitiveness. On Monday, a large group of them assembled in Seattle to launch the Partnership for a Competitive Puget Sound at a media event that was covered by The Seattle Times, KUOW, and other local media outlets.

The premise of the Partnership was laid out in a letter penned by former Democratic Governor Chris Gregoire, the CEO of Challenge Seattle. She writes:

We are at a defining moment that will shape Puget Sound for a generation. The choices we make today will determine whether this remains a region where good jobs open doors, bold ideas become new industries, and people in every community can build their futures. I am confident about what we can accomplish together.

The data in this report tell two truths at once.

First, our foundation is strong. Over the past decade, Puget Sound added jobs and wages grew faster than the national average. We are home to companies that employ hundreds of thousands of people, a worldclass research university, some of the nation’s deepest technology and aerospace capabilities, major defense and maritime assets, clean-energy resources, and a workforce known around the world for its ingenuity. We also offer an exceptional natural environment and quality of life. From the Olympics and the Cascades to Puget Sound and communities across the region, there is no better place in the country to build a life, raise a family, and enjoy the outdoors. These strengths have given generations of people the opportunity to build careers, support families, start businesses, and succeed here.

Second, those jobs and opportunities are not guaranteed. For too long, we have assumed that our advantages and our history of success would carry us forward. They will not. Other regions are working every day to win the jobs, talent, and investment we once assumed would come here and stay here.

The warning signs are clear. 

Puget Sound lost jobs, marking the first time in two decades that regional job growth has trailed the nation. Washington’s cost-of-doing-business ranking has fallen from 32nd to 47th. Employers and residents alike tell us it has become too difficult to build, too expensive to operate, too unpredictable to plan, and too unaffordable for workers and families. This moment calls on us to act together with greater focus, guided by two principles: restoring our competitiveness and building partnership.

In recent years, Washington has become a more challenging place to do business, while other states and regions are competing aggressively to attract employers, investment, and talent. The pace of tax and regulatory change has accelerated, while rising operating costs and growing challenges in attracting and retaining talent have made it harder to plan for the future.

text:
Asia trades in the shadow of a hawkish Fed hike. The dollar is at a seven-week high, the 10-year Treasury yield is pinned near 5%, and oil is sliding on supply relief. 

Japan is the epicentre - the BoJ is hours away from its own hike, and the 10-year JGB yield is hovering just below 3% for the first time since 1996.

1. Equities: A fractured open

Asian markets opened mixed, with a clear divergence between North Asia and Greater China.

Japan - Nikkei 225: 
Opened at 64,643.58 (+1.12%, +720.58 points) but gave back most gains, trading just 64 points higher before noon. The rally was driven by tech and semiconductor names, but a stronger yen (USD/JPY at 156.20) capped upside for exporters.

South Korea - KOSPI: 
Opened 61 points (+0.91%) higher at 6,779, but the rally faded to just two points above flat before lunch. Samsung Electronics traded flat at 253,500 KRW, while SK Hynix fell 0.9%. The chip sector is conflicted: AI spending optimism vs. higher borrowing costs.

Hong Kong - Hang Seng: 
The worst performer in the region. Opened down 233 points (-0.94%) at 24,480, with the tech index falling 1.03% to 4,281 and the China Enterprises Index down 0.97% to 8,127. Alibaba-backed https://t.co/FCOG7HVKzI rose 4.7% and MiniMax added 5.3%, but the broader index was dragged by property and financials.

Mainland China - Shanghai Composite: 
Opened down 14 points (-0.38%) at 3,877. The Shenzhen Component fell 0.33% to 13,409 and the ChiNext Index shed 0.43% to 3,297. Chinese equities remain the laggard, weighed by trade tensions and a lack of stimulus surprise.

Australia - ASX 200: Modestly higher, up 0.16% to 0.34%.

FX: Dollar at Seven-Week High, Yen in the Intervention Zone

The dollar hit a seven-week high against major peers, underpinned by a jump in short-term Treasury yields. Markets have fully priced a December hike and are now assigning roughly 50% odds to an October move.

USDJPY: ¥156.07–¥156.24, holding near intervention territory. The yen has lost ground for three consecutive sessions. All eyes are on the BoJ decision tomorrow, with markets pricing a 98% probability of a 25bp hike to 1.25% - a level not seen since 1995.

EURUSD: $1.146 (-0.05%), pressured by dollar strength.

GBPUSD: $1.337 (-0.03%), with the Bank of England decision later today expected to hold steady.

AUDUSD: $0.7087–$0.7090, supported by easing oil prices but capped by broad dollar strength.

NZDUSD: $0.5718–$0.5725, near recent lows after the GDP deceleration earlier this week.

Commodities: 
Oil Extends Losses, Gold Surges Unexpectedly

Oil fell for a second consecutive session after Saudi Arabia offered additional crude cargoes through Oman, easing fears of Middle East supply disruption.

· Brent crude: $104.59 (-1.2%, down $1.24)

· WTI crude: $101.29 (-1.1%, down $1.14)

· Both contracts fell about $3 on Wednesday

Gold staged a counterintuitive rally, rising $41 to surpass $4,311.89 (+1.12%) in Asian hours. This is the classic "fiscal hedge, not rate trade" signal - the marginal buyer is pricing political risk and fiscal deterioration, not the rate cycle.

Silver: $63.938 (+1.53%)

Copper: $6.380 (+0.83%), supported by the LME inventory draw earlier this week.

Bonds: Yields retreat after the hike

U.S. Treasury yields fell across the board as the market digested the Fed's decision. The 10-year yield dropped 3bp to 4.99%, ending an eight-day rally. The 2-year yield fell 1bp to 4.72%, after hitting a 2024 high of 4.73% the prior session.

The 10-year JGB yield fell 0.5bp to 2.99%, holding just below the 3% threshold - its highest level since September 1996. The BoJ decision tomorrow is the binary event for Japanese rates.

U.K. 10-year gilt: 5.305% (+1.58%), with the BoE decision due later today.

Bank of Japan decision (Friday, Sept 18): Markets price a 98% chance of a hike to 1.25%. The yen's reaction and any intervention signal from Tokyo - is the single largest risk event for Asian FX this week.

Sjoe! Somebody Left the Political Theatre Running Overnight 🎭💡😂 ~ Sjoe! The Performance Has No Final Act — But Someone Is Paying for It 🎭💸 ~ Sjoe! Five Asks Walk Into a Waiting Room… ⏳🇿🇦🇺🇸
The lights are still on. The audience is still seated. And the ticket price is about to go up. South Africa has a durable political habit. High-stakes processes open on low thresholds that deliver immediate headlines, moral positioning and identity signalling. Final thresholds remain high enough that decisive closure stays distant for years. 

That unfinished interval itself becomes the useful product. 

The same habit is now being applied to relations with the United States. Pretoria’s replies to Washington’s five specific asks continue as process language—“still drafting a reply,” “dialogue ongoing”—while the United States has already moved from persuasion to targeted visas and explicit warnings of further measures. 

What once functioned as low-risk domestic currency is being reclassified by an external power as delay that carries escalating cost. Ordinary citizens, largely unaware of the script, remain the eventual underwriters.

Sjoe. Familiar stage. Rising meter.

1. The Stage Lights Stay On

South African institutional life has repeatedly favoured processes that open easily and close slowly. The 2001 World Conference Against Racism produced an early anti-racism framing that outlasted documented problems at the parallel NGO forum and the subsequent boycotts by democratic states. 

The Phala Phala Independent Panel required only prima facie material to open a parliamentary sequence; removal of a president under Section 89 still demands a two-thirds majority never previously achieved. 

The ICJ application secured provisional measures on a plausibility standard while the merits phase, governed by exacting evidentiary requirements for specific intent, stretches across multiple years of pleadings.

Political science offers a useful lens. Incomplete institutions—those that generate continuous procedural activity without forcing terminal decisions—create what scholars of comparative politics call “process rents.” 

Actors on multiple sides extract visibility, differentiation and mobilisation value from the open interval. Closure becomes the risk rather than the goal. The architecture is not accidental. 

South Africa’s constitutional negotiators, drawing on the bitter lessons of the 1980s and early 1990s, deliberately multi-staged certain accountability mechanisms to protect against pure majoritarian removal on thin material. The same protective logic appears in international adjudication. 

Yet when the protective design is applied across domains as a default operating mode, the protective feature becomes a renewable political asset.

That asset is now visible in the bilateral track. After more than a year of clear United States asks concerning rural safety prioritisation, public condemnation of inflammatory rhetoric, fair compensation standards in expropriation, relaxation of mandatory ownership requirements under broad-based black economic empowerment, and clearer non-alignment, the South African response has remained process. 

On 11 September 2026 the Presidency confirmed it was still drafting a reply. 

Five days later the United States imposed targeted visa restrictions under Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act and stated, through both the Secretary of State and the Ambassador, that this constituted only the first escalatory step. 

The time for endless dialogue, the Ambassador noted, had run its course.

What was previously tolerated as domestic process has been reclassified as insufficient engagement. The lights stay on. The external meter has started.

Sjoe!
A stage designed so the first door opens with a gentle push and the last door almost never closes is not primarily a machine for reaching truth. It is excellent lighting with no final curtain call.

Stirring Questions:
Why does a process that opens easily and closes almost never become the preferred vehicle for high-stakes engagement?
What incentive remains to force closure when the unfinished interval itself supplies renewable political returns?
How should citizens distinguish genuine constitutional caution from an institutional preference for permanent stage lighting?

These questions matter together because they test whether the current delay is an isolated diplomatic episode or the latest performance of a structural habit already visible across multiple domains of public life.

2. The Audience Has Not Been Told the Script

Most South Africans encounter friction with the United States as distant noise—another headline about visas or tariffs that will somehow resolve itself among elites. Public language routinely collapses “still drafting a reply” into the appearance of engagement. 

The majority therefore does not register that the identical design which has kept other high-visibility files open is now being applied to relations with the world’s largest economy.

This opacity is not neutral. 

Comparative work on incomplete contracts and political theatre shows that when citizens cannot distinguish opening acts from final verdicts, elite incentives tilt further toward prolongation. Short-term returns—sovereignty signalling, base mobilisation, international differentiation—continue while cumulative costs remain diffuse and incompletely attributed. Aid freezes, elevated tariffs and targeted visas have already arrived. 

The next transmission channel under discussion is the bond market.

South Africa’s foreign-currency debt remains relatively modest, limiting traditional sanctions leverage. Rand-denominated government bonds, however, carry material foreign ownership. An executive restriction on American purchases—precedented in other jurisdictions—could trigger forced selling, sharp yield spikes, rand depreciation and transmission of pain through bank balance sheets and inflation into ordinary households. 

Citizens who never saw the programme notes will still be asked to pay for the performance.

The knowledge gap itself forms part of the incentive structure. When the audience cannot see the recurring pattern, the political cost of keeping the lights on stays low until the fiscal costs arrive.

Sjoe!
It is remarkable how long a performance can run when the audience has never been handed the programme and the theatre management is paid by the hour.

Stirring Questions:
If the public conversation treats process statements as substantive engagement, what mechanism remains for early recognition of escalatory risk?
How does civic unawareness itself become part of the incentive structure that prolongs unfinished stages?
When costs finally transmit more broadly, will the population recognise them as the logical outcome of a long-running pattern or as sudden external hostility?

These questions matter together because they reveal that the danger is not only elite calculation but the knowledge gap that keeps ordinary citizens from seeing the calculation in time.

3. When Redress Becomes the Cover Story

The current delay does not stand alone. It rests on a longer administrative sequence. Cadre deployment—loyalty-based appointments formalised after the 1997 Mafikeng conference and operated through deployment committees—systematically placed political reliability above competence in the state institutions that administered post-apartheid redress instruments. 

Preferential procurement, BEE equity deals and land programmes became channels through which connected networks concentrated benefits. Mass employment and broad-based ownership outcomes lagged. 

The Judicial Commission of Inquiry into Allegations of State Capture documented how the practice facilitated extraction.

Section 217 of the Constitution requires procurement systems that are fair, equitable, transparent, competitive and cost-effective, while allowing preference. Hard binary ownership gates test that boundary. 

When under-delivery became undeniable, the institutional response was not to dismantle the loyalty filter. It was to intensify the racial eligibility rules that surround it. 

Employment Equity targets tightened. In 2026 the National Treasury published draft General Public Procurement Regulations that would make 100 percent ownership by designated groups a condition of entry for an entire band of state contracts. A firm that is 90 percent black-owned does not qualify. A listed company with dispersed shareholding does not qualify. 

Long-compliant firms are locked out if any residual non-designated ownership remains.

The dual movement—retention of the loyalty filter plus radicalisation of the racial cover—is the operational core. The language of accelerated redress remains intact on the surface. 

The administrative practice has evolved into a self-reinforcing model: shortfalls are met with further intensification of the rules that protect the original extraction logic. Political science describes this as path-dependent self-protection. 

Failure is diagnosed as insufficient intensity of the existing instrument rather than as a problem with the appointment practice that administers it.

Sjoe!
A system that answers its own under-performance by raising the racial threshold for entry has a peculiar genius: it can fail at its stated purpose indefinitely and still succeed at its operational one.

Stirring Questions:
Why was the loyalty filter treated as non-negotiable while the intensity of racial eligibility was treated as indefinitely expandable?
If under-delivery is repeatedly met with more of the same racial instruments rather than reform of appointments, what mechanism remains for course correction?
Does a system that answers its own shortfalls by raising the racial threshold for entry still operate under the original constitutional wager that race would cease to be the organising principle of the state?

These questions matter together because they force a choice between two incompatible accounts: one in which radicalisation is the cure for historical injustice, and one in which radicalisation is the method by which an extraction model protects itself.

4. The External Critic Has Read the Rewritten Script

Because the loyalty filter and the subsequent racial intensification are observable in statute, regulation and practice, they convert what might otherwise be dismissed as ideological disagreement into a documented pattern of governance outcomes. 

Farm-attack tracking that records elevated violence and recurring patterns of extreme brutality among commercial farmers further thickens the evidentiary base cited by the United States. 

Once that record is treated as established, personal visas become only the first step.

The remaining high-impact instrument identified by South African economists is a potential restriction on American purchases of rand-denominated government bonds. Foreign holdings are material. An executive measure could force yields higher, pressure the rand and transmit fiscal pain through the banking system and inflation. 

Unlike targeted visas, this lever does not distinguish between elites and ordinary households. It hits the fiscal foundation that funds salaries, infrastructure and social grants.

International comparisons are instructive. Jurisdictions that retained loyalty-based appointment systems while intensifying group-preference rules have repeatedly discovered that external capital markets eventually price the resulting institutional risk. 

The cover story of redress remains useful domestically. Externally it has become legible as something else: a sequence that began with legitimate historical correction, passed through extraction, and then protected itself by hardening the very categories it was meant to transcend.

Sjoe!
It is one thing to keep a domestic audience convinced that the cover story is still the whole story. It is another thing when the external critic has already read the footnotes and is holding the bond prospectus.

Stirring Questions:
If an internal administrative sequence is legible abroad as governance failure, how long can the domestic cover story continue to function without external cost?
What is the precise threshold at which personal sanctions give way to instruments that transmit fiscal pain to the broader population?
Can critical minerals or alternative capital sources offset a bond-market restriction quickly enough to protect ordinary households?

These questions matter together because they shift the discussion from elite political returns to the distribution of eventual costs—and because those costs will not ask whether citizens were shown the script.

5. Signals Before the Stick

The unfinished-process architecture is now being applied to the bilateral dispute itself. Each additional month of drafting and dialogue language extracts further domestic political returns while the external actor has already moved past persuasion. 

Ordinary South Africans, kept largely unaware of the recurring pattern, risk discovering its price only after broader levers have been pulled.

The next national or local vote will not merely choose a government. 

It will be read, whether intended or not, as a signal of public tolerance for continued radicalisation and delay. High tolerance may be interpreted in Washington as confirmation that the oxygen stage can continue. 

Lower tolerance may be read as a reason to keep the remaining stick sheathed. 

Either way, the electoral signal will form part of the calculation about whether delay remains low-cost theatre or has become an invitation to economy-wide measures.

Comparative experience shows that external actors ultimately respond less to official process language than to observable domestic incentives. When those incentives continue to reward unfinished stages, the probability of higher-impact instruments rises. 

The stage lights are still on. The audience has not been given the programme. And the ticket price is no longer set solely in Pretoria.

Sjoe!
The appointment with clarity has been booked. The waiting room, however, appears to have excellent coffee and no shortage of newspapers.

Stirring Questions:
What electoral outcome would register in Washington as evidence that public tolerance for the current sequence has limits?
If the bond stick is eventually raised, will citizens recognise it as the logical endpoint of a long-running domestic habit or as sudden external punishment?
How long can a democracy afford to keep high-stakes processes permanently lit when the eventual underwriters of the performance have never been shown the script?

These questions matter together because they determine whether the next performance continues under the old incentive structure or whether the costs of unfinished oxygen finally force a different calculation—inside South Africa and beyond it.

Synthesis

Independent lines of evidence—institutional design across multiple domains, the historical sequence of cadre deployment and subsequent regulatory intensification, observable policy texts, violence-tracking data, and the progressive external response—converge on a coherent observation. 

Low-threshold openings and high-threshold closures generate renewable political returns. The loyalty filter converted redress instruments into extraction channels; the radicalisation of racial eligibility rules protected that model while retaining the language of historical justice. 

Ordinary citizens remain largely unaware that the same architecture is now being applied to relations with the United States. 

The external actor has treated prolonged process responses as exhaustion of patience and has begun imposing personal costs while retaining higher-impact economic levers. 

The next electoral signal will form part of the calculation about whether those levers remain sheathed.

The claim is testable. If final thresholds were routinely met, if the loyalty filter had been dismantled after the State Capture Commission, if racial eligibility rules had been relaxed rather than intensified, if public comprehension of the pattern were high, or if the United States treated continued process language as sufficient engagement, the argument would fail. 

It has not failed on the available record.

Objections

Some will say these processes are simply careful constitutional and international law, and that high final bars protect against hasty injustice. The objection is fair in principle. Yet the consistent gap between low opening thresholds and high closing thresholds, combined with the political returns extracted from the unfinished interval, suggests the design is doing more than protecting justice.

Others will argue that criticism of the radicalisation of racial rules is itself an attempt to reverse historical redress. The historical record does not support the claim that the only available response to under-delivery was further intensification of racial gates while leaving the loyalty filter intact. The State Capture findings and the subsequent draft regulations are public.

A third view holds that South Africa’s moral voice on the international stage is a hard-won asset that should not be diluted by external pressure. The asset is real. The question is whether an asset extracted from unresolved founding events and sustained by selective hierarchies remains an asset once the costs are forced into view and transmitted to ordinary households.

Final Resolution and Takeaway

The political oxygen extracted from unfinished processes is no longer a cost-free domestic currency. What began as a habitual method of generating headlines and moral positioning has, through the cadre-deployment sequence of looting followed by radicalisation, supplied an external power with both the justification and the leverage to impose economy-wide costs. 

Ordinary South Africans, kept largely unaware of the script, are positioned as the eventual underwriters of the performance.

The next electoral signal will not merely choose a government. It may decide whether Washington continues to treat delay as tolerable theatre or as confirmation that the bond stick—and the fiscal pain it would transmit—has become the rational next act.

The stage lights are still on.

The question is how long the audience can afford the ticket.
Sjoe.

The Lead
On the Brink of an All-Out Regional War in Southwest Asia

by Dennis Small (EIRNS) — Sep. 16, 2026

With the Sept. 10-13 surprise seizure of control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait by the Houthis, which controls passage from the Indian Ocean into the Red Sea and from there to the Suez Canal, another huge portion of global sea traffic has been disrupted, if not stopped altogether. There is scrambling in capitals around the world over how to address the new crisis situation.

Bab al-Mandeb is one of the busiest maritime chokepoints in the world, with almost 9% of all global seaborne trade passing through it, including 20% of both cars and containers and some 15% of crude and refined oil products. Add to that the effect of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and the near-total stoppage of Russian and Ukrainian grain and fertilizer exports through the contested Black Sea, and the shape of a meltdown of massive proportions of the world’s physical economy begins to come into focus.

The war party crews in Washington, London, and Tel Aviv have leapt into immediate action. US Centcom confirmed that Adm. Brad Cooper called an urgent closed-door meeting in Germany of the military chiefs of staff of Israel, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and numerous Gulf states, to discuss military steps for reopening Bab al-Mandeb, including Israeli “offers to help” Saudi Arabia against Iran—who are allies of the Houthis. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is also considering jumping into the fray with military “help.”

This is a recipe for generalized warfare throughout Southwest Asia—on Russia’s southwestern flank—in a strategic context in which the United States has just announced that it has begun an arms race in space, while introducing a change in nuclear doctrine to promote the use of tactical nuclear weapons for supposedly “limited” nuclear war—an oxymoron, if ever there was one.

But an alternative to the growing probability of nuclear war is also starting to come into focus.

The Sept. 12-13 BRICS summit more than held its own against London-Washington efforts to fracture that grouping, which represents half the world’s population, as did the SCO summit two weeks earlier. Serious discussions were held, as Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov stated, “regarding the creation of alternative payment platforms, settlement and depository mechanisms, a reinsurance mechanism, an investment platform, and a grain exchange.”

More is scheduled for September, including the crucial Sept. 24 meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump at the White House, where President Xi will continue to offer the U.S. the opportunity to work together on infrastructure and other major projects in the Global South, which would be beneficial to all parties. In preparation for that trip, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, telling him that Beijing is “willing to strengthen dialogue and cooperation with Iran, and safeguard Iran’s legitimate rights and interests.” This is a message that Xi is expected to deliver personally to Trump when they meet, in the face of American threats and demands that all nations must cut off economic ties with Iran as decreed by the Treasury Department’s Operation Economic Outcast. Xi will also present Trump with options for the peaceful resolution of the entire Southwest Asia crisis, and that of Ukraine as well.

Wang Yi also met on Sept. 16 with Celso Amorim, the Special Advisor to Brazilian President Lula, for related discussions. Brazil is a founding member of the BRICS, as are Russia, India, China, and South Africa. On his way to China, Amorim also stopped in New Delhi, the host of the latest BRICS summit, for strategic discussions with the Modi government.

When the United Nations General Assembly begins its annual high-level General Debate on Sept. 22, as is traditional, the opening speech will be delivered by the Brazilian President Lula. Useful alternatives to onrushing global warfare, options based on the concept that development is the new name for peace, could well be placed on the world’s agenda at that time, and in the deliberations that follow.

‼️Kosovo and Metohija is not a “disputed issue.” It is Serbian territory taken by force and political engineering. UN Security Council Resolution 1244 still stands. Serbia never transferred sovereignty. Priština, Tirana, Brussels and Washington had no legal right to carve it out.
After Kumanovo in 1999 there was no peace. There was a hunt. Serbs, Roma, Albanians labeled “loyal” — disappeared. Kidnappings in front of KFOR. 17 March 2004 — the pogrom. Churches burned, people beaten, expelled. Not an “incident.” A message: this is no longer yours.
Then Albania. Not brotherly aid. Logistics and territory. The Yellow House near Burrel. Dick Marty’s 2010 Council of Europe report: captives taken from Kosovo and Metohija, organs removed, sold via Italy into European clinics. The English word is harvesting. That is why the film is called The Harvest (Žetva).
Marty pointed at the Drenica group. Hashim Thaçi. That is not “Serbian propaganda.” It is a Council of Europe document the West buried for years because they needed a “partner” in Kosovo.
The film (premiere March 2026, on the anniversary of the pogrom) is based on Veselin Dželetović’s Johann’s Serbian Heart. A German baron receives a heart. It is a Serb’s heart. He dreams another man’s life. He goes to Kosovo. He finds a monastery behind barbed wire. He finds the family of the man whose heart now beats in his chest. They were offered five million euros to erase the word “Kosovo” from the film. They refused. Without Kosovo there is no crime. Without the crime there is no film.
Albania was first to recognize the “state.” For years it pushed Greater Albania through infrastructure, documents and the rhetoric of “one people.” That is not neighborly policy. That is the systematic dismantling of Serbian sovereignty.
Today, 16 September 2026. Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague. Thaçi — 25 years. Krasniqi — 25. Veseli — 18. Selimi — 13. Murder, torture, arbitrary detention. 96 killed. Hundreds tortured. The court: most were not combatants. Civilians. Serbs. Roma. Albanians they called traitors.
This is still not a verdict on the Yellow House. But it is the first time the top of the KLA is not a hero on a pedestal — it is a convict. A crack in a 25-year lie.
Kosovo is not lost as long as a Serb knows what a sanctuary is, what blood is, and what a lie is. Silence is complicity.
At the end of all this, one image remains. A Serbian heart — call it Jovan’s — taken from Kosovo and Metohija. Not in battle. In “peace.” After Kumanovo. Driven into Albania. Cut out. Sold. Harvest.
Who pulled it out? The KLA / UÇK and the Drenica network. That is what the Council of Europe report said. Kidnapping. Organ trafficking. Crime. That is already enough.
Do not write ISIS across 1999. ISIS did not exist then. The KLA was a separatist, criminal, bloody project — not a caliphate. What came later is a second layer: from the same radical pockets in Kosovo and Albania, men went to Syria and Iraq. Jihad. ISIS. Not the same headquarters. Not the same Yellow House. Same rot, after the state was broken and the West looked away.
Today Thaçi was sentenced. Not for Jovan’s heart. For murder, torture, detention. The Yellow House is still not fully judged. So this does not close with a verdict. It closes with a name.
Jovan’s Serbian heart from Kosovo and Metohija is not a metaphor. It is a man. A family. A monastery behind wire. And the lie that it never happened.

Developments over the past two days point to an effort by the British, the Israelis, and their allies in Washington to rapidly escalate the U.S.-Israeli war of aggression against Iran into a full-fledged regional conflict. Efforts are underway to induce Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries to accept Israeli and British offers of “help” to reopen the Bab al-Mandeb strait, which the Houthis recently brought under their control.

Axios’s Barak Ravid, citing leaks from Israeli sources, reported on Wednesday that U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Bradley Cooper convened a meeting of top Arab military chiefs, along with the head of the IDF, in a private meeting in Germany to discuss the war with Iran and broader tensions in the region. In addition to Cooper, the meeting was attended by the military chiefs of staff of Israel, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan, and Egypt. https://t.co/wIhSpoMcoL

According to Ravid’s Israeli sources, Cooper reassured the group that the U.S. military would not withdraw its forces from the region, despite Iranian attacks on U.S. bases. An Israeli official said Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gen. Eyal Zamir briefed the other participants on IDF operations on various fronts. CENTCOM confirmed the meeting in a statement, but said little about it. “The leaders discussed opportunities for enhancing security cooperation in the Middle East,” it said.

A source with knowledge of the matter also told Ravid that Israel and Saudi Arabia—with the assistance of CENTCOM—are discussing how Israel could support Saudi military operations against the Houthis and provide ISR assistance modeled on its support for the UAE.

Additional chatter on possible Israeli involvement against the Houthis came from the Arabic-language Al Akhbar, which, according to Middle East Eye https://t.co/2OPCKKj1PA, reported that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has offered “Israel’s services” to countries in the Arabian Peninsula and has expressed a willingness to participate in a “comprehensive war” against Ansar Allah. The report, by Al-Akhbar editor Ibrahim al-Amin, said that Netanyahu was also pressing Israel’s security establishment and military to prepare for possible action against Iran and Hezbollah. The proposed Israeli role was part of a “wider regional effort” to counter the Houthis and the threat to shipping through the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb, one of the world’s main maritime corridors, Israeli media said.

Bloomberg, in a report updated early on Tuesday, reported that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is considering whether to help Saudi Arabia counter attacks from the Houthis in Yemen “amid British concerns about a worsening economic hit from the escalating conflict.” https://t.co/6qqshwqm7n

According to the Bloomberg report, Burnham has received requests from Saudi Arabia for a range of diplomatic and military support. text:
Washington State 

RENTON ACADEMY FOR SPECIAL NEEDS CHILDREN 

Exclusive: A counselor assaulted a 7-year-old, slamming him into a wall. The school won't let him transfer.

A family is fighting Renton School District after an educator assaulted their child. In this exclusive report, the KING 5 Investigators expose exactly what happened.

Sept. 16, 2026

RENTON, Wash. — Malia Carter thought she had finally found her son the help he needed.

Jerome, 7, has ADHD and an individualized plan for behavior issues. Day to day, Carter said, that shows up through frustration and emotional outbursts.

"As his parent, I have to be patient with him," Carter said. "I thought that was what they were doing, too."

She is referencing Renton Academy, a school built for students who need more support than a standard school can offer. She transferred Jerome there in March.

"I thought he was going there to get help and support his special needs that he needed," said Carter. "That wasn't the case."

Surveillance video obtained by KING 5 shows, just seven weeks after Jerome arrived at Renton Academy, a school employee grabbing and slamming her son into a wall.

The video starts with Renton Academy's hallway on May 4, 2026. An employee and Jerome come into frame.

Jerome is visibly angry in the video – pushing and kicking as the educator tries to de-escalate him. Five other adults gather nearby, including counselor Nila Griffin.

Jerome, in his own words, said he was coming down from the outburst.

"I was mad and calming down," said Jerome. "And she (Griffin) said something mean, and then I walked up to her and she grabbed me by my shirt."

The video shows Griffin grab him, push him, and then do something Jerome's family attorney said no one trained to manage children in crisis should ever do: slam him into a wall.

"Horrible," Jerome said, describing the moment. "I hit my head and it feel like I had a bruise on it."

Recalling the video, Carter grows visibly emotional.

"Because I couldn't help him," Carter said. "I couldn't help him at all."

Carter said the school wasn't clear on exactly what happened. She didn't see the video, and didn't get the full picture of what her son had gone through, until two weeks later.

"A lot of questions, not enough answers," she said. "I was getting pushback from the school district and I was like, 'OK, so you guys are protecting her, and not my son.' So I'm going to protect my son."

She called police, child protective services, and Loren Cochran, an attorney who specializes in cases where kids are harmed at school.

"I was horrified. Absolutely horrified," Cochran said, describing his reaction to the video. "Because you take a kid like Jerome and you put him in a school like Renton Academy so he's safe."

A counselor trained for exactly this
Renton Academy's website states the school has a "team of specifically trained teachers and counselors."

Records explain the school is "for students who have difficulty succeeding in a traditional classroom environment," and that "many students have mental or behavioral health issues that can sometimes manifest in aggressive or violent behavior. For that reason, school employees are trained to de-escalate students who are agitated, and routinely do so successfully."

Griffin wasn't a teacher or assigned to a classroom, records say, but her role was solely focused on providing "extra support to students who are agitated and acting out to the point where they cannot remain in the classroom."

"She was listed before as a counselor/interventional behaviorist," Cochran said. "So my understanding is she was supposed to have training to deal with kids like Jerome."

Griffin told police she acted in self-defense, saying that when Jerome came toward her, she feared for her safety and felt the need to physically control him.

‼️Kosovo and Metohija is not a “disputed issue.” It is Serbian territory taken by force and political engineering. UN Security Council Resolution 1244 still stands. Serbia never transferred sovereignty. Priština, Tirana, Brussels and Washington had no legal right to carve it out.
After Kumanovo in 1999 there was no peace. There was a hunt. Serbs, Roma, Albanians labeled “loyal” — disappeared. Kidnappings in front of KFOR. 17 March 2004 — the pogrom. Churches burned, people beaten, expelled. Not an “incident.” A message: this is no longer yours.
Then Albania. Not brotherly aid. Logistics and territory. The Yellow House near Burrel. Dick Marty’s 2010 Council of Europe report: captives taken from Kosovo and Metohija, organs removed, sold via Italy into European clinics. The English word is harvesting. That is why the film is called The Harvest (Žetva).
Marty pointed at the Drenica group. Hashim Thaçi. That is not “Serbian propaganda.” It is a Council of Europe document the West buried for years because they needed a “partner” in Kosovo.
The film (premiere March 2026, on the anniversary of the pogrom) is based on Veselin Dželetović’s Johann’s Serbian Heart. A German baron receives a heart. It is a Serb’s heart. He dreams another man’s life. He goes to Kosovo. He finds a monastery behind barbed wire. He finds the family of the man whose heart now beats in his chest. They were offered five million euros to erase the word “Kosovo” from the film. They refused. Without Kosovo there is no crime. Without the crime there is no film.
Albania was first to recognize the “state.” For years it pushed Greater Albania through infrastructure, documents and the rhetoric of “one people.” That is not neighborly policy. That is the systematic dismantling of Serbian sovereignty.
Today, 16 September 2026. Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague. Thaçi — 25 years. Krasniqi — 25. Veseli — 18. Selimi — 13. Murder, torture, arbitrary detention. 96 killed. Hundreds tortured. The court: most were not combatants. Civilians. Serbs. Roma. Albanians they called traitors.
This is still not a verdict on the Yellow House. But it is the first time the top of the KLA is not a hero on a pedestal — it is a convict. A crack in a 25-year lie.
Kosovo is not lost as long as a Serb knows what a sanctuary is, what blood is, and what a lie is. Silence is complicity.
At the end of all this, one image remains. A Serbian heart — call it Jovan’s — taken from Kosovo and Metohija. Not in battle. In “peace.” After Kumanovo. Driven into Albania. Cut out. Sold. Harvest.
Who pulled it out? The KLA / UÇK and the Drenica network. That is what the Council of Europe report said. Kidnapping. Organ trafficking. Crime. That is already enough.
Do not write ISIS across 1999. ISIS did not exist then. The KLA was a separatist, criminal, bloody project — not a caliphate. What came later is a second layer: from the same radical pockets in Kosovo and Albania, men went to Syria and Iraq. Jihad. ISIS. Not the same headquarters. Not the same Yellow House. Same rot, after the state was broken and the West looked away.
Today Thaçi was sentenced. Not for Jovan’s heart. For murder, torture, detention. The Yellow House is still not fully judged. So this does not close with a verdict. It closes with a name.
Jovan’s Serbian heart from Kosovo and Metohija is not a metaphor. It is a man. A family. A monastery behind wire. And the lie that it never happened.

Kalif Raymond enters his eleventh NFL season in a new uniform with Chicago, holding down a WR3 role on an offense projected for 25.4 market-implied team points per game while running 64.5 plays a game. A massive opening week burst changed the immediate optics when Raymond commanded 9 targets against Carolina, catching 8 passes for 16.4 PPR points while separating at an elite 4.20 yards of separation. Despite that explosive first outing, the overarching profile remains anchored by thin volume and a projected 1.96 targets per game. Raymond is a veteran playing through a bench tier with a historical baseline that typically suppresses fantasy output outside of spike weeks. The primary risk lies in the thin volume, which can easily regress toward his historical floor once the offense settles and higher-priority options dominate the distribution. While the Chicago offense operates with a pass rate over expected of minus 3.9, the sheer volume of 64.5 plays per game offers enough ambient opportunity for occasional production, especially with 30.3 percent of team targets sitting vacant in the room. Skill-wise, the high separation metric confirms he can still beat coverage cleanly when called upon, but expecting weekly reliability from a receiver who historically hovered around a 36.6 percent snap share is a dangerous bet. The upcoming schedule features a strength index versus position of 0.958, indicating a slightly tougher than average overall slate for receivers, compounded by a Minnesota defense that allowed just 23.7 fantasy points per game to the position last year compared to the 30.7 league average.

He offers Jas the .357, barrel down.

Jas grips the .357, hands trembling. His mind whirs, tracing angles pure as Chrono's code.
He raises it, arms braced, barrel aligned with the left can, and pulls the trigger.
The .357 roars, recoil surging through his wrists.
The left can soars off the stump, spinning into the mud with a soft thud.

text:
Yesterday I asked a simple question:

What if the answer to Hormuz isn't just protecting the waterway?

What if you move the barrel?

MOVE THE BARREL.

Hormuz is vulnerable. Saudi Arabia built a pipeline to bypass it. 

That pipeline can be attacked. 

Move the crude west to Yanbu and now the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb matter.

So maybe the real answer isn't just finding another route for the same Middle Eastern barrel.

Maybe you move the barrel itself.

Guyana. Brazil. Argentina. Canada. The United States. Maybe Venezuela.

And now something very interesting is already showing up in the market:

Two very different barrel prices.

A barrel trapped behind geopolitical risk can trade at a steep discount.

A barrel sitting outside those chokepoints, ready to move, can command a substantial premium.

Reuters just reported Basrah Medium being offered more than $43 below Murban, while Australia's Pyrenees crude reached about $138 a barrel.

Different grades, yes. 

But the market is sending a message:

Location matters.

Deliverability matters.

That creates what I call the "SAFE BARREL."

Not because nothing can ever happen to it.

Because it is deliverable.

It doesn't need Hormuz.

It doesn't need Bab el-Mandeb.

It doesn't need a vulnerable bypass pipeline just to reach the customer.

And that is where the cognitive shift begins.

The question changes from:
“How do we get this barrel through the danger?”

to:

“Why are we producing so much of the marginal barrel inside the danger in the first place?”

Once refiners, insurers, traders and governments start asking that question, something changes.

The barrel has two values:
What the oil is worth.

And what getting the oil actually delivered is worth.

Spot cargoes tell us where traders run during a crisis.

Long-term contracts tell us where the world thinks energy is going.

Follow the pipelines. 

Follow the ports. 

Follow the contracts. 

Follow the money.

MOVE THE BARREL.

The safe barrel may become the valuable barrel.

And this may be much bigger than oil.

If you want to follow the story, stay with The American Doctrine here on my page.

We are working our way through the history first, looking closely at the decisions, people, money and events that moved pieces across the board.

As the story approaches the present, we'll slow down and look even closer.

Because now some of those pieces are moving in real time.

We'll follow the receipts, test the connections and watch the board change as it happens.

No line goes on the board without receipts.

More soon.

Silas Truth,
Sons of Liberty

🚨 5 THINGS WE LEARNED FROM THE GAME VS. RACING CLUB:

1. ADEYEMI WAS A BARGAIN: Barcelona paid just €22m + €7m in variables for Karim Adeyemi, and right now that looks like outstanding business.

Against Racing, he was unstoppable: 1 assist, 2 penalties won, constant runs in behind and relentless intensity from start to finish. 

He never stopped running and creating danger. He now has 5 G/A in 7 appearances for Barça across all competitions.

2. GABRIEL JESUS WILL BE IMPORTANT: Another brilliant goal today after already scoring in the Champions League this season. 

Gabriel Jesus could become extremely important when Flick needs to rotate or give Raphinha some rest.

When healthy, he offers so much: movement, pressing, technical quality, versatility and experience. He looks like a player perfectly suited to Flick's football.

3. JOÃO CANCELO IS IN TOP FORM: 2 goals vs. Racing, and both were absolute ROCKETS. After another strong performance against Feyenoord, Cancelo looks full of confidence again.

Barça's depth at left-back is ridiculous right now: Xavi Espart, João Cancelo and Alejandro Balde. Three completely different profiles for Flick to choose from.

4. ALL BARÇA ATTACKERS ARE SHINING: Raphinha. Lamine Yamal. Anthony Gordon. Karim Adeyemi. Gabriel Jesus. Dani Olmo. Fermín López.

Everyone is contributing. Everyone is competing. And most importantly, the competition looks healthy — they celebrate each other's goals, press together and play like a family.

Barça have now scored 33 goals in their first 7 games, winning all seven, and have scored 5+ goals in five of them. These are video-game numbers.

5. BARÇA NEED TO SHARPEN UP DEFENSIVELY: Yes, Barça are winning. Yes, the football has been spectacular. Yes, the attack looks almost unstoppable.

But there is still one warning sign: too many of the few chances Barça allow are ending in goals.

It happened against Levante, and it happened again against Racing. Barça have now conceded 5 goals in their last 3 games.

Against teams Barça can overwhelm with five, six or seven goals, those mistakes may not matter. But against Bayern, Arsenal or Manchester City in the Champions League, the margins will be much smaller. 

Barça may not create as many chances, while those teams will punish defensive errors far more aggressively... The attack is already operating at an extraordinary level. The next step is making the defence just as reliable.

Goodmorning Beautiful Souls. 🤍

With even the smallest glance toward the news,
it becomes difficult not to feel
the trembling beneath the surface of our world.

Another tragedy.
Another family shattered.
Another place swallowed by water, earth, or fire.
Another body left behind
while a soul quietly crosses beyond the veil.

Where there was once devotion,
hatred sometimes takes its place.
Where there was tenderness,
pain can become a language.
And everywhere, it seems,
the old world is revealing its deepest wounds.

But perhaps these moments are not asking us
to drown in the darkness.
Perhaps they are asking us to wake up.

How much more must we witness
before we understand
that nothing here is promised forever?

The Earth groans beneath the weight of what we have created,
while humanity stands at the threshold
of remembering what truly matters.

Time is precious.
Love is precious.
This breath is precious.

The old age trembles,
and something new begins to stir
beneath the ashes of what no longer serves us.

So let your heart become a sanctuary.
Let compassion be stronger than fear.
Let consciousness rise above chaos.
And where the world offers darkness,
become a small and unwavering flame.

The shift of the ages
does not begin somewhere beyond the stars…

It begins
within you.

✨ Wake gently. Love deeply.
Choose light consciously.
The dawn is already approaching. 🌍🕊️

text:
Who else is gonna pull up with this aura to the best Cathedrals in Europe? 

😎

What is the best Cathedral in Europe?

Europe’s greatest cathedrals are some of the most extraordinary buildings ever created, combining faith, engineering, art, sculpture, and centuries of history into places that can still overwhelm you the moment you walk inside.

Cologne Cathedral in Germany may be the ultimate Gothic cathedral. Its enormous twin spires rise more than 500 feet above the city, and its dark stone exterior gives it an almost intimidating presence. Begun in the 13th century and completed more than 600 years later, it feels impossibly ambitious.

Milan Cathedral is perhaps the most visually excessive of them all. Covered in pinnacles, statues, flying buttresses, and white marble, the entire building looks carved rather than constructed. The rooftop, where visitors can walk among the spires, is one of the most remarkable cathedral experiences in Europe.

Notre-Dame de Paris is smaller than some of the others but arguably the most famous Gothic cathedral in the world. Its rose windows, towers, sculpted portals, and flying buttresses helped define the popular image of medieval Christianity and Gothic architecture.

Chartres Cathedral in France may offer the purest surviving medieval Gothic experience. Its extraordinary stained glass casts deep blues and reds across an interior that has remained remarkably intact for centuries.

Florence Cathedral is dominated by Brunelleschi’s enormous Renaissance dome, one of the great engineering achievements in architectural history. Combined with the green, white, and pink marble exterior, it creates one of Europe’s most recognizable skylines.

Seville Cathedral in Spain is massive. Built partly on the site of a former mosque, it combines Gothic grandeur with the famous Giralda tower and contains one of the most enormous church interiors in the world.

St. Vitus Cathedral in Prague rises dramatically from Prague Castle and dominates the city. Its soaring Gothic interior, royal tombs, chapels, and connection to the kings of Bohemia give it an almost mythical atmosphere.

Burgos Cathedral in Spain is famous for its unbelievably intricate openwork spires. Its exterior seems almost too delicate to be made from stone and represents some of the finest late Gothic craftsmanship anywhere in Europe.

Santiago de Compostela Cathedral is important not only because of its architecture but because it marks the end of the Camino de Santiago, one of Christianity’s great pilgrimage routes. The building contains Romanesque, Gothic, and Baroque elements accumulated over centuries.

Finally, St. Paul’s Cathedral in London represents a completely different tradition. Christopher Wren’s immense Baroque dome dominates the London skyline and shows that Europe’s greatest cathedrals are not limited to medieval Gothic architecture.

Together, these ten buildings represent some of humanity’s greatest architectural achievements, places built not simply to impress, but to make visitors feel small beneath something intended to point beyond themselves.

Have you visited any of these before?

text:
Pop Culture Flashback

Mafia Files

(In Case You Missed It)

Mafia rat who inspired Goodfellas had real-life criminal career steeped in blood - 14th June 2012

Gangster turned informant whose life and crimes were immortalised in the film Goodfellas

Henry Hill, who has died aged 69, was a mobster whose nefarious exploits with the Lucchese family on the New York crime scene of the 1970s were made famous by the Martin Scorsese film Goodfellas (1990).

In the film, an adaptation of the book Wiseguy by the journalist Nicholas Pileggi, Hill, played by Ray Liotta, is the narrator and central figure, running the gamut of mob crime over a 25-year period from 1955.

Among many other misdeeds, he dangles a tardy loan repayer over the lion's den in a zoo and helps organise a robbery at JFK airport in New York, known as the Lufthansa heist, which nets millions but results in a bloody feud between the thieves.

But though Hill's real-life criminal career was steeped in blood, he insisted that he never "whacked" anyone himself. "I never killed anybody," he said last year. "I was a money man." He did, however, confess to burying "a lot of bodies". As for the film, he was happy to admit that it was "99.9 per cent dead on". His character's opening line is: "As far back as I can remember I always wanted to be a gangster."

Henry Hill was born on June 11 1943, one of eight children in a poor family in Brooklyn, New York. His father, also Henry, was Irish-American, while his mother, Carmella, was of Italian extraction. Henry Jr's mixed heritage meant that he could never become a "made" man in the Mafia, a status which offers certain protections and privileges.

He began his criminal career innocently enough, running errands for Paul Vario, a capo in the Lucchese family who ran a cabstand near the Hills' house. But soon Henry was being given glimpses of the mob lifestyle, learning how Vario ran loan sharking operations and protection rackets. He was awed by the easy money on display.

By the time he was 14 he had dropped out of school, and his position with Vario was formalised when he was made a member of a local construction union, which allowed him to collect a salary for a no-show job. He became a youthful mascot for the Vario crew, which included Jimmy Burke, the charismatic and brutal gangster played by Robert de Niro in Goodfellas.

Henry's first major crime came after he was ordered to put a rival cab rank out of business. Smashing his way into the opposition taxis, he doused them in petrol and set them on fire. But he was not arrested for the first time until 1959, when he attempted to buy goods with a stolen credit card. He was soon released, however, and his unwillingness to talk during his detention only added to the affection in which he was held by the Vario crew.

For three years, between 1960 and 1963, Hill served with the 82nd Airborne Division of the US Army. It is not clear whether this was an attempt to "go straight", but in Wiseguy Hill claims that the move to Fort Bragg was made to wait out the "heat" of police attention.

On his return to New York he duly picked up the threads of his old life, enjoying the perks of the mob life. Perhaps the most celebrated scene in Goodfellas is a single shot which shows Hill and his girlfriend Karen (later to be his wife) bypassing the long queues outside the Copacabana nightclub by greasing many palms until they are sitting right in front of the stage. "What do you do?" she asks him, dazzled. "I'm in construction," he lies.

In 1972 Hill and Burke went to jail, sentenced to 10 years for extortion. But life inside did not dent his mob career. Hill peddled drugs and made books and, in 1978, was released for good behaviour.

Back on the outside Hill, along with Burke and Tommy DeSimone (played in the film by Joe Pesci), made ever more money, notably robbing trucks and fencing stolen goods. But as the stakes grew higher, so the mutual mistrust and fear of betrayal, never far beneath the surface, rose. "The money," Hill recounted in an interview recently, "was unbelievable. We never robbed nothing small."

The biggest job of all, the Lufthansa heist of 1978, started with Hill. He had previous experience of robbing the cargo terminal at JFK airport, having stolen $US420,000 in 1967 with DeSimone from the poorly-secured Air France lot. Eleven years later a Lufthansa worker at the airport, with serious gambling debts to a bookmaker called Martin Krugman, revealed that the airline regularly moved millions of dollars in cash destined for US servicemen in Germany. Krugman told Hill, and Hill told Burke, who planned the theft, to be carried out by a team that once again included DeSimone.

It was a success beyond the gangsters' wildest dreams. They scooped more than $US6 million, a sum now equivalent to $US20 million, making the robbery one of America's biggest ever. Within days, however, the fallout had begun. With the FBI scrutinising their every move, the robbers assumed one of their number would crack, and began to turn on each other. Edward "Stacks" Parnell, a getaway driver who had failed properly to dispose of his truck, was the first to go, shot on December 18, a week after the raid. Over the next six months, at least eight more mobsters connected with the robbery would die, as Burke launched a vicious campaign to stamp out potential "rats".

As the body count mounted, Hill feared he too would be "whacked". He escalated his drug dealing, and - a cardinal sin in the Mafia - eventually became addicted himself. It was this business that got him arrested, in April 1980. When the police moved in, they played Hill wiretaps of his erstwhile allies in the mob, Vario and Burke, discussing the need to kill him. Hill, who had said that he would rather "put a gun in my mouth" than become a "snitch", recognised that "the whole crew were homicidal maniacs" and agreed to become an informant.

His evidence helped secure 50 convictions, earning Hill and his family a place in the Witness Protection Program. That is where Goodfellas ends, with Hill looking out of a bland housing lot in Omaha. In fact, his life subsequently remained anything but placid. The Mob continued to hunt him. One of the 10 moves he had to make was completed with just a few hours' notice. On each occasion Hill would have to assume a new identity. Peter Haines and Martin Todd Lewis were two of the names he used.

His problems with drink and drugs endured. He was arrested in 1987 on drugs charges and, though he recognised that the FBI "kept me safe when I didn't know how to keep myself safe", he left witness protection in the early 1990s.

He reassumed the name Henry Hill, but few of his adversaries were left to track him down. Vario had died in 1988, and Jimmy Burke was in jail, where he would die in 1996. None the less, Hill was always looking over his shoulder for "some punk kid trying to make a rep for himself".

The money had all gone. "The government said a couple of hundred million dollars went through my hands," he revealed. "But I just blew it on slow horses, women, drugs and rock-and-roll. We partied five, six nights a week and I was making $US15,000 to $US40,000 a week. But I was a degenerate gambler. I could lose $US40,000 in a week."

He made several hundred thousand dollars from Goodfellas and turned himself into something of a consultant for mob films and television series. Recently, when asked if the Mafia might kill him, he replied: "The mob? They don't care about me anymore. Are you kidding? They send me their scripts and treatments to sell in Hollywood."

He continued to be a victim of his various addictions, making regular visits to the tables at Las Vegas and having to check in and out of drying-out clinics. Unlike many of his fellow mobsters, however, he died in bed, in a Los Angeles hospital.

Henry Hill married, in 1965, Karen Friedman. They divorced in 2002, and he subsequently married Kelly Alor and then Lisa Caserta. He is survived by a son and a daughter of his first marriage.

Henry Hill, born June 11, 1943, died June 12, 2012.

text:
Remembering the Soviet Invasion of Poland on 17 September 1939: Did the Absence of This Key Piece from the West’s Collective Memory Blind It to Russia’s Imperial Ambitions in the Post-Soviet Era?

The Soviet invasion of Poland on 17 September 1939 was a direct consequence of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, the agreement between Hitler and Stalin that helped make the Second World War possible. The Soviet Invasion unleashed terror against the Polish population: the systematic destruction of the country’s elites, four waves of mass deportations to remote settlements, places of exile and forced-labour camps across the Soviet Union, and widespread murder and repression. It also marked the beginning of a historical trajectory that would ultimately exclude Poland from the political West for nearly half a century.

Yet the anniversary is not merely a matter of historical remembrance. It offers a revealing insight into both the Soviet and contemporary Russian imperial modus operandi, especially as manifested in Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. Officially, the Soviet Union intervened to “rescue” national minorities in an allegedly defunct Polish state, a pretext Moscow continues to invoke to this day. In reality, it was implementing the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact.

Concluded on 23 August 1939, this ostensible “non-aggression pact” between two totalitarian regimes paved the way for war. Its secret additional protocol provided for the partition of Poland and Eastern Europe. The Soviet Union subsequently supplied Nazi Germany with raw materials, including oil, grain, cotton and metals, that were indispensable to the Third Reich’s war machine. The two regimes also cooperated directly through logistical arrangements, shipments across Soviet territory and joint military ceremonies, including the German–Soviet parade in Brest-Litovsk. Against this backdrop, the Red Army invaded eastern Poland on 17 September 1939.

In October, sham elections were held in Soviet-occupied Poland to legitimise the incorporation of the annexed territories into the Soviet Union. A ruthless policy of Sovietisation began immediately afterwards. Executions, arrests and sentences were followed by mass deportations to remote settlements, places of exile and forced-labour camps across the Soviet Union. On the night of 9–10 February 1940, the first of four waves of deportations began. The initial targets were Polish military and civilian settlers, forestry employees and their families. They were later joined by teachers, civil servants, business owners, and Polish and Jewish refugees from the German-occupied General Government. Some died during the journey; many others succumbed to hunger, disease and the inhuman living and working conditions they encountered in exile.

In the spring of 1940, the Soviet regime murdered approximately 22,000 Polish officers, police officers, officials and other prisoners in the Katyn massacre and at other killing sites: a deliberate strike at the heart of the Polish elite. The historian Professor Andrzej Paczkowski estimates that around one million Polish citizens were affected by Soviet repression in its various forms including arrest, deportation, torture and other forms of persecution between 1939 and 1941. He puts the number of deaths at between 90,000 and 100,000.

These historical patterns remain visible today. Putin’s Russia is once again resorting to the same instruments: the pretext of “protecting” minorities: first in Georgia in 2008, then in Crimea and the Donbas in 2014, and again during the full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022; the deportation of civilians and children from occupied territories; political assassinations and show trials of opposition figures; and the systematic suppression of culture and education in occupied regions. 

Video: Roger Moorhouse for the Embassy of the Republic of Poland in London, 2019.
