text:
Nobody warned the cats. That's the part nobody talks about.
There's a wooden box behind a barn. No sign on it. No name. Just planks, some straw, a heat lamp glowing orange in the dark, and a plastic flap for a door. If you didn't know what it was, you'd walk past it a hundred times and never think twice.
But that box is a survival system. Somebody built it, on purpose, to keep two animals alive through a winter that would otherwise kill them.
And for months, it worked exactly the way it was supposed to. Two cats. One heat source. One tiny warm rectangle of straw in an otherwise freezing world, and an unspoken agreement between them about who sleeps where and how close is too close.
Then the door flap moved. And it wasn't a cat.
I need you to sit with that for a second, because most people scroll past videos like this thinking "oh, cute, an animal walked into a place it doesn't belong," and they miss what's actually happening. This isn't cute. This is a five-alarm event in the nervous system of two animals who have spent their entire lives calculating threat in real time, every second, with no days off.
Feral and stray cats do not get to relax. That's not an exaggeration, that's biology. A housecat sleeping on your couch has outsourced survival to you — food, shelter, safety — and its brain knows it, which is why it can sleep sixteen hours a day with its belly exposed. A cat living outside, even one with a shelter and a feeding schedule and someone who loves it from a distance, does not get that luxury. Its brain is still running the same threat-detection software its ancestors ran ten thousand years ago. Every rustle is a maybe-predator. Every shift in temperature is a maybe-danger. Every closed space is a maybe-trap. The only thing that lets a feral cat actually sleep, actually drop its guard, is when it has fully mapped the risk of a space down to zero.
These two cats had mapped this box. They knew every board. They knew the heat lamp didn't move, didn't bite, didn't growl. They knew the straw didn't hide anything that could hurt them because they'd slept in it every night and woken up fine every morning. This box, for them, was the one place on Earth where the threat-detection software could power down for a few hours.
And then something walked through the door that broke every rule the map was built on.
I'm not going to tell you what happens next, because honestly, telling you would rob you of the fifteen best seconds of your week. But I will tell you why your brain is going to lock onto this video the second you press play, because it's not an accident, and it's not just "animals are funny." There's something deeper going on and once you see it you'll notice it in every animal video that has ever gone properly viral.
Here it is: we are obsessed, at a level below language, with watching creatures encounter something their instincts have no category for.
Humans do this too, constantly, we just don't notice it in ourselves because we have language to paper over the confusion instantly. An animal doesn't have that luxury. When something happens that its genetic programming has literally no folder for, you can watch the confusion happen in real time on its face and its body, unedited, unfiltered, completely honest. There's no faking that expression. There's no animal method-acting "shock." What you are looking at, when you watch a cat's pupils and ears and shoulders do something weird in response to an unexpected animal walking into its space, is a raw, unrehearsed readout of a brain trying to solve a problem it has never encountered before in its evolutionary history.
That is rarer and more valuable than almost any other kind of footage on the internet, and most people don't consciously know why they can't stop watching it, they just know they can't stop.
Now let's talk about the duck. Because the duck is the other half of why this works.
Ducks are not creatures we associate with soft indoor spaces. We associate ducks with ponds, with cold water, with feathers that shrug off rain like it's nothing, with waddling around parking lots looking mildly annoyed at the concept of dry land. We do not, generally, picture a duck making an executive decision to walk into a wooden shelter built for cats and treat it like personal real estate. It breaks the category in our heads the same way it breaks the category in the cats' heads, just from the other direction — we don't expect the duck to want warmth and company that badly, and the cats definitely don't expect the duck to just show up and act like it owns the place.
That double confusion, animal and human both hitting the same wall of "wait, that's not supposed to happen here," is exactly the kind of thing your nervous system was built to pay very close attention to. It's the same wiring that makes you snap your head around when something in your peripheral vision doesn't match the pattern it's supposed to match. Except here, nothing dangerous is actually happening. Your brain gets the full alertness spike, the full "wait, WHAT" jolt of attention, with zero actual risk attached. That combination — high alert, zero danger — is basically the dictionary definition of the kind of content that people watch three times in a row before they even think about tapping the caption.
Let's go deeper on the shelter itself, because I think most people scrolling past this have no idea how deliberate a structure like this actually is, and understanding it changes how you watch what happens inside it.
Winter shelters for outdoor and feral cats are not casually thrown together. People who build these — and there is an enormous, largely invisible community of feeders and caretakers who do this every single year, unpaid, unrecognized, often working alone in the dark before sunrise — follow a set of very specific rules, because the margin for error in freezing temperatures is exactly zero. The entrance has to be small enough to trap body heat but large enough for the cat to get in without hesitating, because a cat that has to squeeze or struggle at the door won't use the shelter at all, it'll just find somewhere worse and colder instead. The insulation has to trap warmth without trapping moisture, because a damp shelter is more lethal than no shelter, the same way wet clothes kill hikers faster than the cold air alone ever could. The bedding has to be something that doesn't absorb and hold water — straw, not hay, and definitely not blankets, despite what every well-meaning first-time cat feeder tries to put in there before someone corrects them. And the heat source, if there is one, has to be positioned exactly right: close enough to matter, far enough to never risk burning fur or paws, running on a system reliable enough that it doesn't fail on the one night it's needed most.
Every inch of that box is a decision made by someone who understood, at a gut level, what it actually takes to keep something alive when the temperature drops below what its body was built to survive alone.
Which is what makes the moment in this video hit differently once you know that. That heat lamp isn't just a lamp. It's the only thing standing between two animals and a night that could kill them. It is, in the most literal sense, the single most valuable resource in that entire structure. And what you're about to watch is a negotiation over who gets access to it — a negotiation nobody agreed to have, initiated by a party nobody invited, settled entirely through body language, because none of the three participants speak a common tongue.
I promise you, the way it plays out is not what you're expecting. I've watched hundreds of these interspecies videos over the years, professionally, for a living, trying to figure out why some of them explode to tens of millions of views and most just quietly disappear. And the ones that actually break through, every single time, share the same structural trick: they set up a clear expectation in the first two seconds — you already know, instantly, what "should" happen when a duck walks in on two cats guarding a heat source — and then the actual footage refuses to give you that expectation back. It gives you something stranger, slower, and much more interesting than a chase or a fight.
That gap, between what you brace for and what actually happens, is where all the good stuff lives. It's where laughter comes from, it's where "aww" comes from, it's where the compulsive urge to send a video to five different group chats comes from. Your brain built a prediction, the video violated it, and now your brain wants to understand why, and rewatching is the fastest way to try to figure that out, so you rewatch, and somehow it's even better the second time because now you're not bracing for the wrong outcome anymore, you're just watching the actual, absurd, specific thing that unfolds.
There's a reason nature documentaries spend millions of dollars and years of patient camera-trap footage trying to capture thirty seconds of unscripted interspecies interaction, and here it is, happening in a plywood box behind someone's house, on a night-vision trail camera that cost less than a nice dinner. Nobody scripted this. Nobody could have. You cannot direct a duck. You cannot cue a feral cat's reaction on command. What you're looking at is one of the very few genuinely unrepeatable moments the internet has to offer, and once it's over, it's over — there is no second take, because none of the three animals involved know they're in a movie.
Let's talk for a second about why cats specifically react the way they do to sudden, non-threatening intrusions, because it matters for what you're about to watch.
A cat's very first move when something unexpected enters its space is almost never aggression. People assume cats are hair-trigger creatures ready to hiss and swipe at anything unfamiliar, but that's a myth built from watching cats that are already cornered or already in pain. A cat that has room to retreat, room to observe, room to reassess — which these two absolutely had, inside that shelter — will almost always choose observation first. Freeze. Widen the pupils. Flatten slightly. Gather data. The fight-or-flight response in cats is actually a fight-or-flight-or-freeze-and-figure-it-out response, and that third option, the freeze, is where the most interesting footage always comes from, because it's the moment where you can see the cat's whole internal committee meeting happening on its face in real time: is this a threat, is this food, is this a rival, is this... nothing? Do I know what this is?
And a duck, meanwhile, operates on a completely different social operating system. Ducks that have grown up around humans and other animals, especially ones that have been hand-raised or lived closely with mixed farm animals, develop something close to social confidence that doesn't map onto "wild duck" behavior at all. A duck like that doesn't experience a cat as an automatic predator the way its wilder cousins might. It reads the room the way any animal reads a room it's comfortable in — where's warm, where's safe, where's mine now — and it commits to that read with a kind of casual, unbothered confidence that, frankly, most humans could stand to learn from.
Put those two operating systems in the same six square feet of straw, at night, with one heat source between them, and you get something that isn't quite comedy and isn't quite drama, it's this specific, rare third thing — a genuine cross-species social negotiation, happening in real time, with real stakes (nobody wants to lose the warm spot on a cold night) and zero real danger. That combination is exceptionally hard to find in nature, and even harder to find on camera.
I also want to talk about why this particular kind of video — night-vision, grainy, a little bit rough, filmed by a trail camera instead of a film crew — hits harder than a polished, well-lit version of the same event ever could. There's a rawness to infrared footage that your brain automatically codes as "true." No lighting rig. No camera operator adjusting position for a better angle. No editing to smooth over an awkward moment. Just a fixed lens recording exactly what happened, whether or not it happened to be cinematic. That unfiltered quality is precisely why trail-camera and security-camera footage has become one of the most trusted visual formats of the last decade — we've all learned, on some subconscious level, that footage like this doesn't lie to you the way a produced video can. What you see is what actually occurred, full stop, no notes.
And what actually occurred here, in that little wooden box, on that particular night, is something I genuinely don't think you'll predict, even having read this whole thing, even knowing every piece of context I've just given you about cat psychology, duck confidence, shelter design, and why your brain is wired to love exactly this kind of footage. Knowing the setup doesn't spoil the punchline. If anything, it makes the punchline better, because now you'll actually understand what you're looking at instead of just reacting to it.
Here's a small, strange detail that I think about a lot: none of these three animals will remember this in the way we will. The cats will forget the specifics of this night by next week, replaced by a thousand other nights of straw and heat and quiet. The duck almost certainly has no idea it did anything worth mentioning. But because someone mounted a small camera on a small box, behind a barn, on a random cold night, this exact moment gets to exist forever, gets to be watched by strangers on the other side of the planet who will never meet these animals, will never see that barn, will never know their names, and will still, somehow, feel something real when they watch it.
That's the whole magic trick of this kind of footage, and it's not a small thing. In a feed full of things designed and produced and optimized to make you feel something, this is just... a thing that happened. Unplanned. Unrepeatable. True. And the fact that it happened to be this specific combination — a duck, two cats, a heat lamp, a night that could have gone a hundred boring ways and instead went this way — is either extraordinary luck or proof that the universe has a sense of comedic timing that none of us fully understand.
One more thing before you go watch it, because I think it changes how you'll feel about the ending.
The people who build and maintain shelters like this one — the ones who show up in freezing weather to refill food, swap out bedding, check the heat source is still working, do this for animals that will never thank them, never love them back the way a pet would, sometimes never even let them get close — are doing some of the quietest, least celebrated animal welfare work that exists. There's no parade for it. No badge. Most of the time, nobody even knows it's happening except the animals themselves and whoever's holding the flashlight at 6am in the cold checking that everyone made it through the night. This video exists because someone cared enough to put a camera on a box they built with their own hands to keep two animals alive, and in doing that, they accidentally captured something that's now about to make a lot of strangers laugh, or gasp, or feel a weird unexpected rush of tenderness toward two cats and a duck they've never met and never will.
That's it. That's the whole thing. A box. A lamp. Two cats who thought they had this figured out. And a duck that didn't get the memo, or got a completely different memo, or decided the memo didn't apply to it.
Watch it. Watch what the cats do in the first three seconds — that's the real tell, that's where all the honesty lives, before anyone, animal or human, has had time to decide how to feel about what's happening. Watch what happens after that, when the shock wears off and something has to actually be decided about who stays and who goes and who gets to be warm tonight.
You will not see it coming. I've told you almost everything except the one thing that actually matters, and I did that on purpose, because some things are better discovered in real time, with your own eyes, at full volume, with the sound of straw shifting and a heat lamp humming in the background of a night that, for one strange, small, perfect moment, belonged to all three of them at once.
Go watch it. You'll understand everything I just said the second you see the first frame, and you still won't see the ending coming.
Let me give you a bit more, because once you start pulling on this thread, it doesn't stop giving.
Think about every viral interspecies video you've ever actually remembered, the ones that stuck in your head for years instead of dissolving the second you scrolled past them. The elephant that seemed to grieve. The crow that brought gifts to the person who fed it. The dog that waited at the exact spot every day. The fox that curled up next to a farm cat like it had done it a hundred times before. None of those videos are "produced." None of them have a script, a hook written by a marketing team, a call to action. What they have in common is a single unbroken take of something that should not, by any normal rule of the animal kingdom, be happening — and yet it is, right there, undeniable, on camera.
We remember those because our brains are pattern-matching machines running on millions of years of "figure out what's normal so you can spot what's dangerous," and every single one of those clips is our own pattern-matching machine hitting a wall and rebooting in real time. Fear evolved first to keep us alive. Curiosity evolved right alongside it, because the animals that stopped to actually look at the weird thing — instead of just running — were the ones who learned faster, adapted faster, and survived longer when the weird thing turned out to matter. You are, in a very real sense, biologically rewarded for staring at exactly this kind of footage. Your ancestors' survival depended on people in the group who paid close attention to things that broke the pattern. You inherited that wiring. It's still running. It's running right now, which is probably part of why you've read this far into a post about a duck.
Here's something else worth sitting with: interspecies tolerance like this isn't actually as rare in nature as we assume, it's just rarely filmed well, and even more rarely filmed at the exact right moment. Farm sanctuaries and rural properties are full of quiet, undocumented arrangements between animals that "shouldn't" get along — barn cats that share space with chickens, goats that adopt orphaned lambs from other species entirely, working dogs that develop genuine, lifelong bonds with the horses they're supposed to just be herding. Proximity plus low threat plus repeated exposure is basically the recipe for interspecies tolerance across the entire animal kingdom, humans very much included. The difference here is that this arrangement wasn't repeated exposure. It wasn't built slowly over weeks. It happened once, suddenly, on camera, with zero warm-up period — which is exactly why it's rare enough to stop you mid-scroll instead of blending into the enormous pile of "cute animal" content the internet produces every single hour of every single day.
There's a specific kind of tension that builds when you're watching two animals that each have every reason, biologically, to be wary of the other, and instead of resolving that tension the way your gut expects — a hiss, a lunge, a scramble, a retreat — the moment just... keeps going. It doesn't resolve on the timeline you're braced for. Your brain wants a clean beat: threat detected, threat resolved. When that beat doesn't land where you expect it, when the tension just keeps stretching a half-second longer than feels comfortable, that's exactly the sensation that keeps a thumb frozen on a screen instead of flicking to the next video. It's the same mechanic that makes a good magic trick work — not the reveal itself, but the extra half-second right before it, where your brain knows something is about to break and doesn't yet know what.
I'll also say this, because it's easy to forget once you're several paragraphs deep into overanalyzing a video: none of this needed to be smart to work. It works on toddlers. It works on people who've never thought about animal behavior for a single second in their life. It works on people scrolling at 2am who couldn't care less about feral cat shelter architecture or duck social confidence. All of the psychology above is real, but the video doesn't need you to know any of it to land. It lands on instinct alone. Everything I've written is just an explanation, after the fact, of why something that already works on a gut level works on a gut level. The video doesn't need the essay. The essay exists because some of us can't just enjoy a good clip without also wanting to know why it's good.
So here's the honest pitch, stripped of all the analysis: two cats had a warm spot on a cold night. A duck decided that spot was now a shared spot, or possibly just its spot, and nobody consulted the cats about it. What happens between the moment that duck commits to the doorway and the moment everyone settles into whatever the new arrangement turns out to be is fifteen-ish seconds of the most purely, accidentally cinematic animal footage you will see this month, filmed by nobody trying to make cinema, using a camera that exists purely so someone could check on two cats they care about.
Watch the ears. Watch the tail. Watch who moves first and who refuses to. That's where the whole story is, and no amount of me describing the psychology behind it will do what fifteen real seconds of it will do the moment you press play.
One last thought, and then I'll actually let you go.
Somewhere out there tonight, that same box is probably sitting exactly where it always sits — behind the same barn, straw a little more flattened than it used to be, heat lamp still humming its quiet orange hum into the cold. The cats are probably back to whatever their normal looks like now. Maybe the duck comes back. Maybe it never does, and this was a one-night arrangement that nobody but a small trail camera will ever be able to prove happened at all. Either way, something shifted in that box on that particular night, some tiny renegotiation of who this space belongs to and who gets to feel safe in it, and it happened without a single word being exchanged, because none of the three parties involved have words to exchange in the first place. They just have bodies, and instinct, and whatever it is that passes, between animals, for a decision.
We don't get to see this kind of thing very often, not really seen it, not the honest unscripted version. Most of what passes for "animal content" online is staged, or baited with treats just off camera, or cut together from twenty takes to make one perfect ten seconds. This isn't that. This is one continuous, unbroken slice of something that happened exactly once, to three specific animals, in one specific box, on one specific cold night, and got caught on camera purely because someone cared enough to be watching in the first place.
That's rare. That's worth fifteen seconds of your scroll. That's worth watching twice, honestly, because the first time you'll be too busy processing what you're even looking at to catch everything happening in the background — the shift of a paw, the angle of an ear, the exact moment the tension either breaks or doesn't.
Go watch it now, before someone spoils the ending for you in the replies.
And if you've made it this far into a post about a duck and two cats and a heat lamp, do yourself a favor and actually press play instead of just imagining it from the description. Your imagination, no matter how good, is not going to land on the same beat the real footage lands on. It never does. That's the entire point of unscripted footage — it doesn't follow the story your brain would have written for it, it follows its own logic, animal logic, weather logic, straw-and-heat-lamp logic, and that logic is always stranger and better than whatever a human mind would have guessed in advance.
So don't guess. Watch.

text:
The Loneliest Monarchy in the Red Sea

Riyadh has built one of the world's most lavishly funded militaries, yet it faces an existential maritime crisis entirely alone. 

As Houthi forces entrench themselves along Yemen’s critical Red Sea coastline, targeting Saudi oil tankers and shuttering exports at key Red Sea hubs like Yanbu, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman confronts a stark reality: deep pockets cannot buy victory without boots on the ground.

Saudi Arabia’s air force (which is actually slightly bigger than the Israeli air force) can bomb targets with precision, but controlling territory along the Bab el-Mandeb strait requires ground combat - a cost Riyadh has historically outsourced. 

When the Saudi-led coalition launched its campaign, the heavy lifting was undertaken by UAE-backed forces, local Yemeni militias like the Southern Transitional Council (STC), and hardened Sudanese contractors. That proxy coalition has collapsed. Following a bitter rift over influence in southern Yemen, Saudi Arabia bombed UAE-aligned STC positions, prompting Abu Dhabi to withdraw its troops, logistics, and foreign forces. Furthermore, Sudan’s domestic crisis has drained the supply of Sudanese contractors who once manned the frontlines. Riyadh isolated the very partners who provided its infantry shield.

Desperate for ground forces, Riyadh turned to its regional partners, only to find the cupboard bare. The newly minted Mecca Joint Defense Agreement - a mutual defense pact between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey - was touted as a new security umbrella. Yet when asked to intervene, both Islamabad and Ankara demurred. Pakistan pointed to non-retroactive clauses and unratified treaties, while Turkey offered empty calls for diplomatic restraint.

Nor can Washington be relied upon to save the day. The relationship has deteriorated sharply after Saudi Arabia restricted the U.S. military from using American bases and Saudi airspace to conduct strikes during the war with Iran. Having already negotiated a separate 2025 ceasefire with the Houthis to protect American vessels, Washington has no intention of deploying troops to bail out Riyadh.

This leaves the kingdom backed into a corner while Houthi strikes - guided by sophisticated targeting data and advanced Iranian weapons - effectively block energy exports via the Red Sea - which was a bypass route to Hormuz. With native forces unwilling to enter high-casualty urban warfare, Riyadh is left with three bleak alternatives: pay exorbitant rates for an army of foreign mercenaries, wait for a U.S. campaign to eventually decapitate the regime in Tehran, or completely capitulate to Iran in hopes that the Ayatollah orders the Houthis to lift the blockade.

Until one of these plays out, the Houthis hold the upper hand in the Red Sea corridor. Riyadh stands exposed as a regional titan with infinite capital, empty defense pacts, and no allies willing to bleed for Saudi oil.

Have you tried praise? No, really! Have you? 

I was told the story, recently, of a middle-aged couple who had tried for quite a while to give birth - but had not attained that dream.

They attended this spiritual retreat of sorts and decided to "not continue with just asking" but, instead, "simply praise God" for doing what they believed only He could.

They found out they had conceived shortly after they wrapped up the retreat and went home.

Little wonder we are told in Psalm 33:1, "Let the godly sing for joy to the LORD; it is fitting for the pure to praise him."

I am not saying praising God is like some magic switch you can turn on at will - whenever you want something. No. I am saying, however, that praise moves mountains!

This is not the first testimony I have heard about people praising God - from the depths of their hearts, in their brokenness and grief, in their sheer despair, and getting their heart's desires.

In fact, in the Bible it is written about how many people "praised," and through it, secured many blessings. I shall share only 3 of them with you to remind you of what God is capable of:

1. In the biblical account of the fall of Jericho (Joshua 6), God instructed the Israelites to march around the city in silence - but with their priests blowing trumpets. On the 7th and last day, there was a massive, coordinated shout of praise - and this brought down the famous walls of that great city!

2. In Acts 16:25​-26, we are told of how Paul and Silas, stripped, beaten, and locked up in the deepest dungeon with their feet bound in stocks, neither despaired nor complained. What did they do instead? They sang and praised the Living God, singing hymns while the other prisoners listened. Around midnight, a violent earthquake shook the very foundations of the prison, the doors flew open, and everyone's chains came loose - though they refused to run away. This episode led to salvation coming to the jailer and his entire household.

3. Hannah, childless after years of deep sorrow, wept and prayed fervently at the tabernacle, vowing to dedicate the child God would give her back to Him - to work in His service. After receiving a word of peace from Eli, the priest, she switched to "worship." That is how Samuel, God's own prophet and the last Judge of Israel, came to be born. When this happened, Hannah offered a prayer of ecstatic praise and thanksgiving to God (1 Samuel 2).

You know what? Let me add a bonus:

4. Judah found itself in a very prickly spot that could spell disaster: a massive, invading coalition of Ammonites and Moabites had arisen to attack it (2 Chronicles 20). King Jehoshaphat led his people in prayer and fasting to the LORD. He then appointed singers to walk ahead of the army, "praising" God for the beauty of His Holiness - for a victory which, at the time, they had not yet seen. In the end, because the LORD set ambushes against Judah's enemies, they destroyed one another. Guess what? Judah did not even have to lift a finger in battle! Judah won against a formidable foe - without having to fight!

Are you still in doubt about the power of praise?

You've tried everything else. You've poured your heart out and begged God. Still nothing. Now, try praise!

May the God of praise raise you up and fill your cheeks with laughter!

AMEN!

text:
Bypassing the CoWoS Bottleneck: The Technical Logic and Geopolitical Constraints of SK Hynix-Intel Ohio

If the Ohio arrangement is packaging and EMIB-T interconnect rather than HBM wafer fabrication, it addresses the other half of the CoWoS bottleneck

SK Hynix is evaluating a lease of part of Intel's Ohio fab and discussing a joint venture with Intel and major cloud customers, according to Reuters. No agreement is signed. SK Hynix's official statement says it is "reviewing various options, including establishing additional production bases, to strengthen the competitiveness of its memory business," but "no matters have been determined at this stage." The market's first read was "SK Hynix HBM front-end lands in the U.S." The more accurate technical read is that if the Ohio arrangement involves packaging and EMIB-T interconnect rather than HBM wafer fabrication, it addresses the other half of the CoWoS bottleneck.

The other half: CoWoS gap is narrowing too slowly relative to AI packaging consumption

J.P. Morgan's July supply chain check puts TSMC's internal CoWoS monthly capacity at roughly 115,000 wafers by the end of 2026, roughly 190,000 by the end of 2027, and roughly 220,000 to 225,000 by the end of 2028. Non-TSMC OSAT capacity from Amkor and JCET expands from about 12,000 to 15,000 wafers per month by end-2026 to about 85,000 by end-2028. Even on that trajectory, J.P. Morgan's core conclusion is a supply-demand gap remaining at roughly 20% through 2027 and 2028.

The reason the gap persists is that AI chip packaging consumption grows faster than capacity expands. High-end GPUs, AI CPUs, and custom ASICs all need logic and HBM in the same package. TSMC's CoWoS has entered 5.5-reticle mass production and targets 14-reticle size by 2028, at which point a single package can hold up to 10 large processor dies and 20 HBM stacks. Larger packages make thermal expansion mismatch, mechanical stress, and heat dissipation harder to manage, and yield management more difficult. J.P. Morgan's model explicitly states that "CoPoS, EMIB-T, and outsourced assembly test yields are still variables," which means the sell-side itself acknowledges uncertainty in the single-path CoWoS supply forecast.

EMIB-T's technical position: the second path

Intel's EMIB-T offers a different technical path. EMIB is a 2.5D packaging platform Intel has deployed in high volume since 2017. Its core mechanism embeds small silicon bridges inside an organic substrate to connect multiple dies, replacing a large silicon interposer. In 2024, Intel Foundry upgraded EMIB to EMIB-T, adding TSVs inside the silicon bridge so power and high-speed I/O signals can pass directly through the bridge rather than routing around it.

The technical significance: HBM4 doubles I/O count from 1,024 to 2,048, requiring denser vertical power delivery and signal paths. EMIB-T's TSV approach makes I/O physical layer design compatible with 2.5D interposer technology while keeping the cost and size scalability advantages of organic substrate packaging. EMIB-T supports roughly 8x to 10x reticle-size chip integration.

Cost is the other key variable. Industry analysis puts the price difference between EMIB-T and CoWoS at up to 50%, depending on whether an expensive silicon interposer is required. For SK Hynix, that means customers can redirect the packaging savings into more HBM capacity, increasing memory bandwidth per chip.

SK Hynix made its technical position explicit at Hot Chips 2026: its next-generation HBM packaging roadmap includes Intel EMIB alongside TSMC's CoWoS-L, CoWoS-S, and CoWoS-R. This is not a procurement decision. It is a technology blueprint disclosure. But it marks a shift from single-source TSMC dependency to multi-source packaging.

The 350 km packaging corridor between Ohio and Indiana

SK Hynix has already invested over $4 billion in an advanced HBM packaging plant in West Lafayette, Indiana. The cleanroom is scheduled for October 2028, with mass production of next-generation HBM in the second half of 2029. That plant is positioned as back-end packaging: wafers produced in Korea ship to Indiana, where they are packaged and tested before being supplied to U.S. customers.

Indiana to Intel's Ohio fab is roughly 350 km straight-line, 400 km by road, about four hours. That proximity enables a division of labor: SK Hynix performs some HBM wafer fabrication or packaging steps in Ohio, then completes final packaging and testing in Indiana. Intel's first Ohio fab is slated for 2030 production and the second for 2032, which overlaps with the Indiana plant's 2029 mass-production timeline.

The more specific possibility is SK Hynix doing HBM stacking and EMIB-T packaging inside Intel's Ohio facility, using Intel's advanced packaging capacity while staying close to its Indiana back-end base. Intel's EMIB-T validation yield has reached 90%, and MediaTek has confirmed it will use EMIB-T for a next-generation custom chip project, with tape-out targeted for Q4 2026 and mass production in Q4 2027.

Korean export review: front-end HBM in Ohio is the hardest scenario to clear

A key geopolitical constraint sits here. South Korea's Industrial Technology Protection Act designates advanced DRAM and HBM manufacturing as national core technology. Overseas transfer requires statutory government review. Technology leak cases referred to prosecutors rose from 9 in 2021 to 33 in 2025, with semiconductors the most frequent domain. South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said its position is that "cases related to national core technologies will be subject to review under the Industrial Technology Protection Act."

That makes "HBM wafer fabrication in Ohio" the hardest scenario to clear in Seoul. The Korean government faces pressure from Washington to build U.S. capacity, but also needs to weigh the outflow of advanced memory technology. SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won acknowledged in July that the company faces "enormous pressure and lobbying from customers and countries to supply more," but domestic opposition exists as well.

The more likely approval path is producing conventional DRAM for Intel server CPUs in Ohio, or performing additional HBM packaging steps inside Intel's facility. Neither triggers the core national technology review that front-end HBM wafer fabrication would. Reuters noted that it could not learn which chip types SK Hynix might produce in Ohio.

Actual impact on the CoWoS queue: diversion or addition?

If the Ohio arrangement is packaging and EMIB-T rather than HBM wafer fabrication, does it actually shorten the CoWoS queue?

Two variables matter. The first is EMIB-T's actual packaging throughput. Intel's external packaging customer count is increasing, but it has no mass-production wafer foundry anchor customer yet. EMIB capacity is far smaller than TSMC's CoWoS in the near term, but it can take orders for mid-to-high-end AI chips where cost sensitivity matters more than extreme package size — cloud custom ASICs or AI CPUs, for instance. That demand moves out of the CoWoS queue, indirectly relieving pressure on the highest-end CoWoS-L capacity.

The second variable is whether J.P. Morgan's 20% gap model includes EMIB-T supply. The report explicitly states that "CoPoS, EMIB-T, and outsourced assembly test yields are still variables." If EMIB-T ramps faster than expected, the 20% gap assumption may overstate the real shortage.

That does not make EMIB-T a CoWoS replacement. Counterpoint Research notes that TSMC still leads in high-volume manufacturing, maturity, and JEDEC standard ecosystem lock-in. Intel's ability to challenge CoWoS depends on timely execution, ecosystem adoption, and solving thermal management and integration trade-offs. EMIB-T is better understood as a second supplier that diverts cost-sensitive, package-size-tolerant demand rather than directly replacing CoWoS-L in the highest-end AI accelerators. Unimicron stated on its earnings call that EMIB-T is "not yet mature," and the yield target for three EMIB-T substrate suppliers during initial mass production at the end of 2027 is only 50%.

Signals to watch

First, the specific technical scope of the SK Hynix-Intel negotiation. If the disclosed plan is "HBM packaging in Ohio, wafer fabrication stays in Korea," it will not trigger Korea's core technology review, but it does divert CoWoS packaging demand. If the plan involves front-end DRAM or HBM wafer fabrication, Korea's government review becomes the decisive variable. SK Hynix's wording — "reviewing various options" — is notably distant from "decision made."

Second, the actual EMIB-T capacity ramp. A 90% validation yield and volume delivery are separated by an engineering gap. MediaTek's Q4 2027 mass production target is the first external large-customer reference point. Google's ninth-generation TPU has also reportedly adopted EMIB-T, targeting 2028 mass production with MediaTek co-design.

Third, whether J.P. Morgan's CoWoS gap model incorporates EMIB-T supply in the next update. If the 20% gap is revised down due to EMIB-T capacity release, the SK Hynix-Intel collaboration's impact on the CoWoS queue gets a quantified answer.

The Ohio arrangement is not a simple "HBM goes to America" story. It is a signal of packaging path diversification, and its actual effect depends on EMIB-T ramp speed and the boundaries of Korean export review. For analysts tracking the advanced packaging supply chain, the thing to watch is not whether SK Hynix signs a lease, but what type of packaging equipment actually runs inside Intel's Ohio facility — that is the evidence that determines whether the CoWoS queue is genuinely diverted.

text:
This guy messaged me on one of my socials and said, “This is my fake account. I have an original account too, please bear with me. You won’t regret it.”

I said okay, let’s continue 

He told me he’s divorced with two kids, lives in Dallas, Texas, and runs his own health business. I said okay, no problem. Then he started talking about how, if everything goes well, I’ll become his girlfriend.

I asked myself: girlfriend for what? 😭

You’re a divorced man with two kids, and I’m a single girl just starting my life. I didn’t even bother asking his age because from everything he was saying, I already knew he was probably in his 40s.

Then he started with, “Being divorced doesn’t mean It can’t work” and all that.

I told him plainly: I would rather start my life with a single man who has never been married than enter a relationship with a divorced man simply because he lives in Dallas, Texas.

He then said, “That’s fine, if that’s my preference.”

I said, “No problem, but let me advise you. Don’t feel like because you live in Texas, you can just come to Nigeria and any girl will automatically want you.”

Omo, he got offended. 😂

Next thing, he blocked me.

I blocked him back because I’m not interested in an international blocking competition. 😂

But honestly, this is for my girls: BE WISE.

Someone living abroad is not automatically a prize. Someone having dollars, a business or an American address doesn’t mean you have to accept whatever relationship they offer you.

Know what you want. Know your standards. And don’t let “I live in America” make you forget them.

text:
I very strongly co-sign this (yes, I'm biased, but it helps to offer a more detailed inside view). Here's a plug for some of my favorite projects at Stanford. It's a non-exhaustive list, with so much more I'm missing and still to come, but you'll see for yourself why Stanford is so well positioned in the ways @chrmanning describes.

Terminal Bench Science, which Stanford helped build with @StevenDillmann and many other brilliant collaborators, evaluates real-world agentic tasks that scientists actually care about. Program Bench was also co-developed at Stanford with @jyangballin (Stanford PhD, co-advised by Diyi and Ludwig), who co-created SWE-bench at Princeton.

Open datasets and open training: DataComp (@lschmidt3), OpenThoughts with @etash_guha, Marin's (very!) open-source experiments and training runs led by @percyliang with @WilliamBarrHeld and so many other brilliant folks there and in Open Athena, and @houjun_liu's SecureForge plus all the red-teaming work he and @aiprof_mykel's students are doing (huge shoutout to @SISLaboratory!). Human-AI interaction: @Diyi_Yang's work on sycophancy & evaluating human-AI collaboration, grounding models in the context of people (+@oshaikh13), @michaelryan207 aligning models with diverse human cultural values, and more.

The mechanics of how models are evaluated in the first place: @jennjwang's work, the paper that first showed context gets lost in the middle (@nelsonfliu) way back when, and the clear case for the power of test-time scaling with Large Language Monkeys and all the research that followed (@brad19brown, @jordanjuravsky, @ryansehrlich, + @RylanSchaeffer and many others), and @sanmikoyejo push for making measurement a science + Emmanuel Candes grounding evals in stats + @ChrisGPotts on interpretability + much more I'm leaving out.

Being this close to Silicon Valley makes Stanford a unique nexus: building openly while keeping a finger on the pulse of which problems frontier AI can actually help solve. Stanford researchers are often best positioned to see which direction to go before the rest of the world even knows labs are hill-climbing on it, let alone has the infrastructure to evaluate it. And they do it while maintaining independence and excellence.

I couldn't agree more with the role Prof. @chrmanning describes for the @stanfordnlp and @StanfordAILab, and I'm excited for Stanford to keep playing such an important part in this ever-evolving ecosystem.

text:
Sjoe! “Nil” Just Got a Luggage Tag from Washington 🇿🇦🧳🇺🇸 ~ The Political Sign Says “Nil”; the Deeds Office Says “Check Again” 📜🚨 ~ South Africa’s Land Debate Has Arrived at the Spreadsheet 📊🇿🇦😂
Sjoe. A single word—“nil”—has been travelling farther than most title deeds in this country. It appears in legislation, in political speeches, in market calculations and, more recently, in the fine print of American visa restrictions. 

The word does not build a single house or plant a single hectare. 

Yet it has acquired the strange power of a political sign that can move independently of the systems meant to give it practical meaning. When that sign meets external costs and domestic administrative failure, something modest but useful becomes visible: the price of treating ownership as permanently provisional rises, and the space for more predictable rules briefly reappears.

This is not a story of villains and saviours. It is a story of a sign, the costs that reattach to it, and the ordinary institutional work required if South Africa is to keep its land contest inside courts and deeds offices rather than letting it drift into ambient uncertainty.

1. The Sign That Outruns the System

The Expropriation Act 13 of 2024, signed into law in early 2025, allows for the possibility of nil compensation in defined circumstances when land is taken in the public interest and the outcome remains “just and equitable.” Courts retain the final word. On paper the architecture is orderly. 

In political life the word “nil” has become something more ambient: a circulating promise of decisive transformation that can outrun the slower realities of capacity, post-settlement support and clear title (Expropriation Act 13 of 2024).

The political history of the word matters. 

A formal attempt to amend section 25 of the Constitution to make nil compensation explicit for land-reform purposes failed to secure the required two-thirds majority in December 2021. The ordinary legislation that followed therefore operates inside the existing constitutional text while carrying much of the mobilising force of the failed amendment. 

The sign survived the legislative constraint. That survival is itself an institutional fact.

In September 2026 the United States announced targeted visa restrictions against individuals linked to the enactment or implementation of policies enabling uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination or the incitement of violence against minority groups (United States Department of State, 2026). 

The measures sit inside a broader set of diplomatic “asks” that have included farm security, inflammatory rhetoric and ownership requirements under Black Economic Empowerment. The American framing places particular weight on the security of tenure of Boer and other minority property holders. 

Whether one regards that framing as overdue protection or selective concern, the functional effect is the same: the political sign of “nil” now carries an external price tag.

Markets notice first. Lenders lengthen investment horizons. Title begins to feel provisional even before any large volume of nil-compensation decisions is recorded. Domestic institutions register the same signal. The pairing of an ambient slogan with concrete external costs converts an abstract contest into a higher-stakes calculation. 

It does not erase historical grievance. It simply makes the gap between rhetorical ambition and system performance more expensive to ignore.

Sjoe! 
A word that once travelled freely now finds itself with a luggage tag issued in Washington. The tag does not stop the journey, but it does make the journey more noticeable.

Stirring Questions:
How many actual nil-compensation decisions would it take before the formal narrative of restraint becomes impossible to sustain? 
How are commercial lenders already pricing the contingency created by a statute that is simultaneously described as limited and celebrated as transformative? 
If the political arithmetic inside the Government of National Unity shifts, which track—official restraint or enabling possibility—is designed to move first? 

These questions matter because they test whether the sign can remain ambient once real costs are attached to it.

2. Predictable Title as Shared Interest

South Africa’s Constitution already balances the protection of property with the duty to foster equitable access to land (Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, s 25). Lawful restitution, redistribution and carefully justified expropriation remain available. What the external signal elevates is the practical price of ambiguity. 

When ownership rules are expected to be enforced, both historical claimants and current holders gain something rare in the current climate: calculability.

The institutional pathway—courts, the Special Investigating Unit, the deeds registry—offers a different tempo from permanent provisionality. Clearer expectations reduce the incentive for pre-emptive occupation on one side and defensive mobilisation on the other. 

In an environment some monitors have described as polarised, that reduction is not trivial. It does not dictate the content of redress. It merely privileges the procedures through which redress is more likely to remain orderly.

Economic incentives reinforce the point. 

Title uncertainty raises the cost of capital for every producer who must borrow against land. It complicates municipal rates bases. It slows the conversion of public land into serviced stands. The same calculability that protects a commercial farmer’s planning horizon also protects the state’s ability to deliver housing at scale. 

The external pressure, by raising the cost of the most radical reading of the statute, indirectly strengthens the relative attractiveness of the institutional route.

The irony is structural rather than personal. A country that has spent decades debating the moral weight of historical dispossession still struggles to keep the ordinary machinery of title honest and functional. 

External pressure that raises the cost of the most radical reading of the statute does not rewrite the Constitution. It simply makes the institutional route relatively more attractive than the symbolic one.

Sjoe! 
The Constitution already wrote the balance. The rest of us are still arguing about the interest rate on ambiguity.

Stirring Questions:
What incentives would most effectively align political rhetoric, legislative text and the daily practice of the deeds office? 
How should the state weigh the legitimate demand for faster delivery against the equally legitimate requirement that public land not vanish through forged paper?
Can clearer rules serve both the family waiting for a stand and the producer who needs to plan beyond the next season? 

These questions matter because every constituency that depends on land—housing beneficiaries, commercial farmers, restitution claimants—relies on the same underlying assumption: that the formal record still means something.

3. The Place of Peace That Lost Its Stands

Ekurhuleni means “place of peace” in XiTsonga. The name was chosen with the early-1990s violence of the East Rand still fresh in memory. Between 2018 and 2022, more than two hundred vacant municipal stands in Villa Liza, valued at approximately R58 million, were fraudulently transferred into private hands without council resolution or payment to the municipality. 

A conveyancing firm not on the municipal panel of approved attorneys lodged forged rates clearance certificates and fabricated powers of attorney at the Johannesburg Deeds Office. The firm’s principals personally acquired dozens of the stands through related entities, recorded at low prices and later resold at substantially higher figures. 

Some of the stands have since been developed; the municipality still receives no rates revenue from them (Special Investigating Unit, 2026).

The Special Investigating Unit, acting under presidential proclamation, has interdicted further dealings and is asking the Special Tribunal to set the transfers aside and recover the losses. Criminal referrals are planned. 

This is ordinary fraud, not high-policy land reform. Yet it occurs inside the same legal and administrative system that is supposed to manage restitution, redistribution and secure title. When public land can still be moved by forged paper in a municipality whose name aspires to peace, the gap between political sign and institutional machinery becomes impossible to ignore.

The case illustrates a deeper governance problem. Political energy has concentrated on the outer edge of the constitutional text while the everyday systems that make any land policy credible—deeds integrity, municipal oversight, rates collection—remain permeable. 

Symbolic restraint without administrative repair leaves the system open to both ideological escalation and ordinary predation. External pressure that raises the cost of radical legislative signals can, in limited conditions, create time and incentive for domestic bodies to close integrity gaps. 

Closing those gaps serves every group that depends on reliable records.

Sjoe! 
A place named for peace lost more than two hundred stands to paperwork. The name remains. The stands do not.

Stirring Questions:
How many more municipal assets must disappear through paperwork before the repair of everyday title systems becomes a non-negotiable priority? 
What happens to public trust when a place named for peace cannot protect its own vacant stands? 
Can the high-level debate about historical redress remain credible while the ordinary machinery of ownership remains this permeable? 

These questions matter because they ground the abstract contest in a documented failure that no political slogan can paper over.

4. Interrupting the Worst-Case Loop

Polarisation intensifies when each side treats the other’s most extreme reading as the only realistic future. The political sign of nil compensation sustains one reading of imminent uncompensated dispossession. The perceived absence of restraint sustains the reciprocal reading of permanent blockage of redress. 

United States measures attaching tangible costs to the outer legislative edge, together with domestic litigation against the Expropriation Act and SIU enforcement of title integrity, can interrupt that mutual worst-case assumption.

Neither mechanism eliminates legitimate historical claims nor freezes the constitutional settlement. They raise the price of treating the polarising interpretation as inevitable. 

In a setting already characterised by some observers as polarised, any reintroduction of contingency and institutional mediation reduces the emotional fuel available to extremes. 

The effect is modest and contingent. It operates by restoring a degree of calculability that pure symbolic contestation tends to erode.

Political incentives matter here. A governing arrangement that must manage coalition partners, court challenges and external diplomatic costs faces different pressures from one that operates under ambient permission. The current combination of internal litigation and external cost-raising does not dictate outcomes. 

It changes the relative attractiveness of the most polarising path. That change is itself a form of institutional mediation.

Sjoe! 
Worst-case assumptions travel in pairs. Raise the price of one and the other begins to look less inevitable.

Stirring Questions:
Can the present scale of institutional resistance—court challenges, investigative action, market caution—slow or reshape the dual track before political arithmetic shifts? 
What happens to the legitimacy of governing arrangements when one partner litigates against legislation supported by another? 
Is the current mobilisation of courts and civil society a temporary brake or the beginning of a longer contest over the practical meaning of section 25? 

These questions matter because the strength of remaining checks will determine whether early conditions of polarisation remain early or become the next phase.

5. The Narrow Convergence

The apparent clash between the political utility of the “nil” sign and external insistence on property predictability converges on a practical requirement for peace: rules clear enough for investment, housing delivery and social trust to resume. 

Concern for security of tenure, once stripped of maximalist rhetoric, aligns with the broader principle that no group’s title should be rendered permanently provisional by political atmosphere. South Africa’s own courts, investigative institutions and constitutional text already supply the domestic architecture for that principle.

External pressure that reinforces rather than rewrites that architecture can, under limited conditions, help keep the contest inside institutional channels rather than allowing it to migrate into ambient occupation or defensive mobilisation. 

Containment of this kind does not resolve historical grievance. It reduces the immediate drivers of polarisation and thereby supports the conditions under which more durable arrangements become feasible.

The cumulative evidence points in one direction. Legislative text, diplomatic measures, investigative findings, court activity and historical record converge on the same practical observation: an ambient political sign, external costs and visible administrative failure do not settle the land question. 

They do reintroduce calculability. That reintroduction is modest. It is also the necessary precondition for any reform that hopes to last longer than the next election cycle.

Sjoe! 
The sign still travels. The costs are clearer. The paperwork still needs watching. 
South Africa gets to decide which of those three facts will shape the next chapter.

Stirring Questions:
What would a genuinely shared interest in calculable rules look like in legislative, administrative and political practice? 
How can the legitimate demand for redress be pursued without rendering title permanently provisional for any group? 
Can South Africa keep its land contest inside the Constitution, the courts and the deeds office long enough for capacity and honesty to catch up with aspiration? 

These questions matter because durable peace will still require domestic capacity, political will and honest delivery. The linked dynamics of sign and cost merely make the price of avoiding those requirements more visible.

Synthesis

The converging evidence is consistent across independent domains. The legislative text of the Expropriation Act makes nil compensation possible under defined conditions. United States diplomatic measures attach tangible costs to the outer edge of that possibility. The SIU investigation into Ekurhuleni demonstrates that everyday title systems remain vulnerable to fraud. Domestic courts continue to test the Act’s compatibility with section 25. Historical Trek-era written agreements exist in the archival record yet do not create absolute modern titles under the 1996 Constitution. 

Together these strands show that a powerful political sign, external cost-raising and visible administrative failure do not settle the land question. They do reintroduce calculability and institutional mediation into a debate that otherwise risks remaining locked in reciprocal worst-case readings.

The argument is falsifiable. Clear evidence that nil-compensation powers remain unused, that occupation rhetoric is actively contradicted by the governing party, that succession produces continuity of constraint, or that institutional capacity expands faster than political demand would require revision of the picture. 

The stakes are practical: agricultural investment, housing delivery, the residual authority of courts, and the social temperature of a country that still aspires to peace.

Objections

Some will argue that any external pressure on land policy constitutes unacceptable interference in sovereign redress. The concern is legitimate. Sovereignty remains with South Africa. The functional observation is narrower: external costs can raise the price of treating the most radical reading of domestic legislation as inevitable, thereby creating modest space for institutional mediation.

Others will contend that focusing on administrative fraud and title predictability distracts from the moral urgency of historical dispossession. The urgency is real. The reply is that moral urgency without functional title systems tends to produce either symbolic victories or disordered outcomes. Both historical claimants and current holders benefit when the formal record is honest and enforceable.

A third view holds that the political sign of nil compensation is itself a necessary mobilising force. Mobilisation has its place. The risk is that an ambient sign can outrun the systems required to give it constructive content, leaving the country with heightened expectation and diminished capacity.

Conclusion

Sjoe. The word “nil” still travels. The costs attached to it have become more visible. The administrative failures that undermine every side’s confidence in the system have been documented in a place that calls itself the place of peace. 

None of this resolves South Africa’s land contest. It does, however, make the price of permanent provisionality clearer and the value of calculable rules harder to dismiss.

Durable peace will require domestic capacity, political will and honest delivery. The linked dynamics of sign and cost merely make the cost of avoiding those requirements more difficult to ignore. 

The argument remains open to evidence. 

The country still gets to decide how much weight to give the sign, how much urgency to give the repair of its own systems, and how much patience to give the institutional path that alone can turn aspiration into something that lasts.

The converging evidence shows that the simultaneous presence of an ambient political sign, external cost-raising measures and visible title fraud does not settle South Africa’s land question, but it does reintroduce calculability and institutional mediation into a debate that otherwise drifts toward mutual worst-case assumptions.

The shift away from employer-sponsored group insurance toward individual coverage accounts is one of the quietest structural changes in American benefits. Thatch is building the infrastructure for that future: a world where your health benefits follow you across jobs, clients, and life changes. A unicorn valuation signals that investors think this shift is not just coming but accelerating.

text:
Technical facts disproving political and tech claims on online child safety:

Protecting children online requires knowing who is a child. Knowing who is a child requires knowing ages. Knowing ages requires knowing everyone's age across all devices, apps, and internet services. That requires age checking services.

Age checking services cannot comply with government mandates to be "robust". "Robust" age checking originated in Australia and is now in US and EU legislation. It means "best endeavours" with specific legal intent.

"Robust" age checking requires proving age beyond doubt. Age estimation services can never be "robust". You cannot have a "robust" service without verifying everyone's identity through government issued ID or extensive personal, financial, or behavioural data. Without enough data, device, app, or service access is denied until official ID is provided.

Verifying every identity destroys privacy. Storing verification data on servers creates instant risk. Identity verification enables governments to monitor citizens and censor speech. As Larry Ellison said, people change behaviour when monitored through digital surveillance.

Parents can already protect children from online harms using existing technology. In 2012, I demonstrated poor parental controls on BBC Newsnight, leading me to build early safety tools for Samsung and Apple. I also built the first Android time curfew capability 14 years ago.

Today, iOS and Android offer built in controls to block unsuitable apps, websites, and content by age rating, alongside granular curfews. Real world risks like bullying exist online, but parents can manage access just as they manage real world exposure.

Exhibit A: If parents can already block access for free on their own phones, why do governments push legislation that forces identity collection, exposing data to cybercriminals and tech companies?

Exhibit B: Why are governments, tech companies, and NGOs not educating parents on existing settings that are free of charge and "robust", even while citing tragic cases to push legislation?

In 2004, I co-founded the W3C standard for Content Labelling and URI Classification, co-inventing account and folder classification to label content based on risk and compliance. I advocated for voluntary account verification to stop impersonation long before people knew it was even possible.

Mandatory identity verification to use a phone or internet service is dystopian control. I would never advocate or support that.

I have advised the US DOJ, NCMEC, CEOP, and IWF on child exploitation detection. EU Chat Control and UK image scanning mandates will not tackle exploitation. They break end to end encryption and VPNs, introducing dangerous spyware, and puts more children at risk.

I was contacted by a company I wouldn't work for to see if I'd be interested in a position. I moved forward with the process, and failed the tech screen.
In truth I have zero plans to leave my current company, or the project I've been working on for years, but while going through the process I learned more about the company and the team and the work and my opinion was swayed. The rejection stung, not only because of my failure to show my worth to strangers when asked, but because I might have entertained an offer if given.
It did make it clear that I've lost the ability to interview well, and that is scary.
Employed software engineers should actively apply to positions at companies they would potentially never work for, just to build the skills they need specific to interviewing. At worst, you get rejected and learn a few things, at best you get an offer that tells you your current value and keeps you up to date with what you should expect when it's time to move on.
Not all the time. It's time consuming, and stressful. But maybe at least every 6 months you should try to go through an entire interview loop. That's what I'll be doing from now on. I'm older now, and I've forgotten what it's like and if I had to really try for a job I really wanted I'd be ignored.
I can't allow that. Lessons learned.

text:
📜 HOOK & AUTHENTIC QUOTE

"All humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone." 

— Blaise Pascal, Pensées (1670)

Over three centuries ago, Pascal diagnosed the exact spiritual sickness that defines the modern condition. He didn't live to see the smartphone, the algorithmic timeline, or the notification bell, yet he understood the human aversion to silence better than any modern psychologist. 

We are living through the death of contemplation. And with it, the quiet extinction of genuine inner peace.

⚡ THE MODERN MIRROR

Look around. We have engineered a society where solitude is treated as an emergency. 

Waiting for the elevator? Out comes the phone. Standing in line for coffee? Scroll, refresh, consume. A five-second pause in a conversation creates an unbearable social itch that must be scratched by noise. 

We are perpetually stimulated, permanently connected, and chronically exhausted. We carry supercomputers in our pockets that offer infinite escape routes from the one place we are terrified to visit: our own minds. 

Pascal’s warning has metastasized. We no longer just struggle to sit quietly in a room alone—we have made it socially and psychologically impossible to do so.

🧠 DEEP ANALYSIS

1. The Industrialization of Attention
Our attention is no longer our own; it is the primary currency of the digital economy. Tech corporations employ armies of behavioral psychologists to hijack the ancient human desire for connection and novelty. Every ping is a dopamine hit designed to pull you outward, away from introspection, and into the collective hive-mind of outrage and trivia. 

2. The Terror of the Unfiltered Self
Why do we run from silence? Because silence strips away our armor. In the quiet, the distractions fade, and the unaddressed grief, the quiet anxieties, and the existential questions finally demand an audience. Constant entertainment is not a luxury; it is a sophisticated, socially acceptable form of anesthetic. We drown our inner turmoil in a deluge of external noise so we never have to ask ourselves: *Who am I when nobody is watching?*

3. The Illusion of Productivity
We have conflated motion with meaning. Because we are constantly reacting to emails, texts, and news cycles, we feel productive. But this frantic busyness is actually a profound form of stagnation. We mistake the consumption of information for the cultivation of wisdom. True depth requires stillness, yet we reward the frantic surface-swimmer and ignore the diver.

4. The Extinction of Sanctuary
Inner peace is not something you find; it is something you protect. By inviting the entire world into our bedrooms through glowing screens, we have demolished the inner sanctuary. Without solitude, there is no original thought. Without original thought, there is no conviction. We become echoes of algorithms rather than authors of our own lives.

💡 THE PHILOSOPHICAL TAKEAWAY

Pascal’s insight offers both a diagnosis and a prescription. The loss of contemplation is not merely a modern inconvenience—it is a spiritual crisis that hollows out the human soul. 

If we are to reclaim our inner peace, we must relearn the lost art of radical stillness. This does not mean retreating to a mountain cave; it means reclaiming sovereignty over your own mind in a world designed to rent it out. 

Turn off the notifications. Close the tabs. Sit in the uncomfortable silence until the noise in your head subsides and the deeper voice beneath it finally speaks. 

Peace is not the absence of chaos in the world. It is the ability to remain anchored in the quiet room of your own soul, entirely unafraid of your own company.

text:
When you study the UK Enclosure Acts (15th–19th c.), the parallels to today’s tech and resource grab are hard to ignore.

The commons were stolen. Then the people were made dependent. Then they were managed.
Same playbook. New tools.

For centuries, “peasants” survived on the commons  shared land for grazing, foraging, farming.

Parliament, controlled by landowners, passed Enclosure Acts. Fences went up. Traditional life became illegal overnight.
Dispossession was legalised.

Today’s version: the digital commons.
AI is trained on humanity’s collective knowledge, art, and language. Then that value is walled off behind paywalls, APIs, and copyright.
The public creates it. A tiny elite encloses it.

Historical enclosure wasn’t just about owning land. It was about ending self-sufficiency.
Lose the commons, and you can no longer feed yourself. You migrate to the city and take whatever wage the factory offers.
Dependency was the point.

Watch the same move now: private control of arable land, water rights, seeds, and supply chains.

‼️If you don’t own the inputs of survival, you don’t have independence. You have a subscription to existence.

After enclosure, poverty exploded. The response wasn’t to return the land.
It was Poor Laws tightly managed charity to keep people just stable enough not to revolt.
Not freedom. Containment.

The modern sequel is UBI talk and corporate philanthropy.
A stipend can look humane. It can also function like the old Poor Laws: keep a displaced population compliant, dependent, and politically quiet.
Charity is not ownership.

Then came the walls.
Hedges. Stone barriers. Guards. The public was kept off the newly private land by force.

Today the walls are biometric gates, drone perimeters, surveillance grids, and proprietary algorithms.
Same function.

The lesson of enclosure is simple:
Whoever owns the infrastructure of survival holds power over everyone who needs it.

Land then. Compute, data, water, food, and energy now.
The fences changed. 
The intent didn’t.

So what actually works for building real income alternatives in 2026? Let me be specific.

The three models that consistently produce results for regular people — not influencers, not tech insiders — are:

1. Skill monetization through service arbitrage
You learn a high-demand digital skill (copywriting, video editing, paid ads management). You charge clients. Then you document your process and package it into templates or courses later. You start active. You build toward passive.

2. Content-driven affiliate revenue — but narrowed down
Broad niches are dead. The people winning are hyper-specific. A newsletter about budgeting for single parents in their 40s outperforms a generic 'personal finance' blog every single time. Specificity is the new SEO.

3. Digital products tied to a real problem you solved
Not an ebook about productivity. A specific spreadsheet tracker that solves an exact painful problem. A template pack. A system. The more specific the problem, the less competition, the higher the conversion.

The pattern across all three? They start with active effort and transition to passive over time. There is no version where you skip the active phase and land in the passive phase.

Also worth saying: most people fail not because their idea is bad. They fail because they switch ideas every 60 days. Consistency is the actual product.

The market in 2026 rewards depth over breadth. It rewards staying power over novelty. It rewards people who show up long enough to be trusted.

I have watched people with mediocre offers outperform brilliant ones simply by refusing to quit.

So here is my honest question — what has actually stopped you from building something consistent in the past? Was it the wrong model, or the wrong timeline expectation? 👇

Worth noting what else changed in the same revision. Alongside Jane Eyre's inclusion, an article on creative thinking was removed, and new texts were added on becoming well-rounded socialist builders and on China's athletic and space achievements.

Which makes the choice of novel more interesting than the romance framing suggests. The engine of Jane Eyre is refusal. She walks out on Rochester the moment she learns about Bertha, with no money and nowhere to go. She then refuses St John Rivers and the respectable, useful life he offers her as a missionary's wife. The book is a sustained study of what it costs to say no, and whether a person has anywhere to go afterwards.

Charlotte Brontë published it in 1847 as Currer Bell, a man's name, because she judged that her own would change how the book was read before anyone had opened it. The novel now being used to teach sounder values arrived in the world wearing a disguise the market required.

Fourteen-year-olds are quite good at working out which part of a book they were meant to notice and which part they actually did.

📌 In his keynote address, H.E. Ambassador Zhou shared the following reflections:

77 years ago, China rose from a century of foreign aggression and domestic unrest. It has grown into a prosperous nation with a USD 20-trillion economy, ranking as the world’s largest manufacturer and goods trader, forging steadily ahead on the path of Chinese modernisation.

Anchored in an innovation-driven and people-centred development philosophy, China’s growth delivers tangible benefits to its own people, while creating global business opportunities and improving livelihoods across the world. Amid persistent global uncertainties, China continues to offer new solutions to challenges facing world peace and global governance. It strives to build a more equitable, orderly multipolar world and advance inclusive, mutually-beneficial economic globalisation together with like-minded partners.

China and Zimbabwe stand as steadfast partners in safeguarding international fairness and justice. China fully supports Zimbabwe playing a greater role in regional and international affairs. Standing side by side, we uphold genuine multilateralism and champion the purposes and principles of the UN Charter.

📌 Looking back on our bilateral journey over the past year, H.E. Ambassador Zhou expressed deep pride, joy and gratitude, summing-up our fruitful cooperation under three core themes:

🔹 Heritage ❤️
President Xi Jinping’s heartfelt reply letter to Zimbabwe’s liberation war veterans rekindles shared memories of our heroic struggles. Forged through common trials and shared values, the time-honoured China-Zimbabwe friendship carries a profound legacy of liberation-era camaraderie, bringing our two nations ever closer. 

🔹 Harvest 💪

A host of people-centred cooperation projects have been delivered nationwide, including the High Performance Computing Centre, the Belt and Road Joint Laboratory on Agriculture, the Juncao Technology Assistance Programme, 300 newly drilled boreholes, the donation of 5,000 metric tonnes of rice, drought-relief interventions, and maternal and child health initiatives.

China remains Zimbabwe’s largest source of FDI. Pragmatic cooperation in steel, lithium, cement and solar energy is advancing steadily, yielding concrete results on the ground.

🔹 Heart 💞

🇨🇳🤝🇿🇼 Acting Foreign Minister Dr. Shava and other distinguished guests graced the reception. They extended warm National Day greetings, spoke highly of the robust all-weather China-Zimbabwe community with a shared future, and praised vibrant cooperation across the steel sector, digital infrastructure, education and trade. Iraq is emerging as the next strategic pressure point in the US-Iran confrontation, not because Baghdad seeks another war, but because its geography, militias and political system connect several regional fronts.

The September attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline, reportedly launched from Iraqi territory, has intensified pressure on Baghdad. Iraq has opened an investigation, dismissed a local security commander and moved against border crossings, while responsibility for the strike remains contested.

The timing matters. The US military withdrawal from Iraq is scheduled to be completed by 30 September, while Baghdad faces growing pressure to disarm the Iraqi resistance militias. Several powerful factions reject disarmament, leaving the Iraqi state caught between Washington, Riyadh and Tehran.

Strategically, Iraq offers something Lebanon and Yemen do not: a direct land bridge to Iran and a dense network of armed and political actors embedded within the Iraqi state.

The emerging contest is therefore not simply about Iraqi militias. It is about whether Iraq becomes a sovereign buffer between competing regional powers or another operational theatre in the wider US-Iran war.

If pressure on Baghdad intensifies, the central question will be whether Iraq remains a mediator and sovereign actor, or becomes the next battlefield through which the regional balance is contested.
