text:
🇨🇦🇪🇺 Canada could become the EU’s first-ever “associate member,” but before anyone starts printing blue passports, Brussels still has to decide what that actually means.

Ursula von der Leyen floated the idea as a way to pull Canada much closer to Europe economically and strategically without offering full membership, which Canada cannot legally qualify for anyway because it is not a European country.

The likely arrangement would sit somewhere between today’s CETA trade deal and the much deeper access enjoyed by countries like Norway or Switzerland.

That could mean easier trade, closer cooperation on defense, energy, technology and the Arctic, plus expanded travel and education rights.

And some of that is already moving beyond theory.

Ottawa and Brussels are reportedly discussing Canadian participation in Erasmus+ and deeper access to the EU’s Horizon Europe research program. 

They’re also looking at broader mutual recognition of professional qualifications, potentially covering doctors, engineers and professors.

Canada is also already the first non-European country participating in the EU’s €150 billion SAFE defense-procurement program, so the integration has been quietly getting deeper for a while.

Canada’s trade fight with Washington has intensified, Trump slapped 50% tariffs on around $20 billion of Canadian goods, and Ottawa is openly trying to reduce its dependence on the U.S.

Still, this is nowhere near a done deal. 

“Associate membership” does not currently exist as a defined EU status. 

Member states and Parliament would have to agree on what Canada actually gets, what rules it follows and how much it pays. 

Countries already waiting years to join may not love seeing Ottawa offered its own bespoke lane.

Trump has already called the idea “laughable,” suggested deeper Canadian integration with the EU could amount to a “hostile act,” and threatened Europe with serious tariffs if he decides the arrangement harms U.S. interests.

So this is no longer just a quirky new EU membership category.

It’s starting to look like part of something much bigger: Canada trying to build itself a lot more room between Washington and Brussels.

Sources: Bloomberg, Reuters, AP, Euronews, Financial Times, Government of Canada / Writer: Julie

text:
Good Thursday morning and welcome to September 17th...

Not Charles Lindbergh. Not Amelia Earhart.

On this date in 1911, a pilot you've never heard of---Calbraith Perry Rodgers, of Pittsburgh---took off from Sheepshead Bay, New York, in his biplane, with the goal of flying across the United States.

The feat had not yet been done, and a grand reward of $50,000 had been publicly offered by newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst to anyone who could make the transcontinental flight in 30 days or less.

Rodgers flew at low altitude, following train tracks by sight since he had no instruments. A special train followed him with spare parts.

His route would cover over 4200 miles, and he spent over 80 hours in flight time.

Due to an average speed of only about 50 miles per hour, and many unscheduled stops, Rodgers accomplished the feat in 49 days, landing in Pasadena, California in November.

Rodgers passed away in a plane crash in April of 1912. His biplane that made the historic trip is at the Smithsonian Air & Space Museum.

text: A lot of Europeans don't quite understand how problematic this is for many Americans. I visited Southern California a couple of times, and while it is one of my favourite places in the world, I cannot imagine it being possible to live there without owning a car. Nothing seemed walkable. You can't just wander along to the corner shop to pick up the newspaper, a pint of milk and a pack of bacon in the morning. There didn't seem to be many bus stops in residential areas. And while there was a rapid transit system, having looked at the map, it seems to offer little coverage for the size of the urban area. The point isn't to criticise, because it is such an intoxicating, wonderful place to be and no doubt live; however, for good or ill, Southern California has designed its transport, and thus all its urban and suburban areas, around the motorcar. This means that a political leader telling the proles to drive less for Israel sounds completely different to American ears than to Europeans.

text:
A Profile Is Not Evidence: A Skeptical Examination of the Conley-Did-It Theory

Your chronology is off, and too much of your argument rests on assumptions presented as evidence.

You tell us what Jim Conley probably did, why he lied, where Mary Phagan supposedly went after leaving Leo Frank’s office, where Conley supposedly attacked her, how he moved her, where he assaulted her, and why he wrote the death notes.

Where is the evidence for each step?

A murder case cannot be solved by choosing the suspect with the uglier biography and then building a story around him because the story sounds simpler.

The question is not which man looks more like a murderer.

The question is what evidence connects each man with the murder of Mary Phagan.

A Criminal Profile Is Not Proof of Murder

Conley drank. He had a criminal record. He lied by omission. He gave changing accounts. He came from a rough background.

Frank was educated, married, professionally employed, socially respectable, and portrayed by the prosecution as a man living two very different lives.

If nothing else were known about the case, Conley might reasonably have attracted greater initial suspicion.

But how does a statistical profile prove who murdered one particular 13-year-old girl on Saturday, April 26, 1913?

It does not.

Aggregate crime statistics tell us about populations. They do not identify an individual murderer.

A criminal trial asks whether one specific defendant committed one specific crime.

If you want to argue Conley killed Mary, show evidence connecting Conley to the killing.

His drinking does not do it.

His arrests do not do it.

His race does not do it.

His social class does not do it.

His lies do not do it by themselves.

Where is the evidence of the murder itself?

Frank Was Indicted Before Conley’s Full Body-Moving Account

The chronology creates a serious problem for any claim portraying Conley’s final account as the event which caused the State to proceed against Frank.

Leo Frank was indicted for murder on Saturday, May 24, 1913.

The Atlanta Journal reported the indictment was returned at 12:23 p.m. after the grand jury considered the evidence (AJ, 1).

Conley’s fuller body-moving account developed afterward.

The Atlanta Journal’s July 27 chronology records Conley’s May 24 admission concerning authorship of the death notes, followed later by the body-moving account (AJ, 2).

Frank was already under indictment before Conley supplied his fully developed account of helping move Mary’s body.

So how could Conley’s final body-moving story have caused Frank’s indictment when the indictment already existed?

The dates do not fit such an argument.

Twenty-One Participating Grand Jurors Signed the Indictment

The Atlanta Journal reported twenty-one of the twenty-three members of the Fulton County grand jury signed Leo Frank’s murder indictment. The other two were absent (AJ, 1).

Twenty-three grand jurors.

Two absent.

Twenty-one participating.

Twenty-one signatures.

Among the participating members, the indictment was 21 to 0 as reflected by the signatures reported in the contemporary press.

Steve Oney identifies four Jewish men on the grand-jury panel: George A. Gershon, A. L. Guthman, Sol Benjamin, and Victor H. Kriegshaber. Oney reports Kriegshaber was away, leaving three Jewish members among the participating grand jurors when the indictment was returned (Oney, 3, p. 116).

Does this prove antisemitism did not exist in Atlanta in 1913?

No.

Does it prove Frank was guilty?

No.

But how does one reconcile this record with a simple claim saying an antisemitic grand jury indicted Frank because he was Jewish?

Three Jewish grand jurors participated in a grand jury whose twenty-one participating members signed the murder indictment.

And this happened before Conley’s later body-moving account.

Conley Lied. Frank’s Accounts Changed Too.

Nobody has to pretend Jim Conley was an honest man.

He lied.

He concealed information.

He changed his story.

Rosser spent days attacking him over those changes.

The jury heard all of it.

But why does Conley lying automatically mean Conley murdered Mary?

A murderer can lie.

An accomplice can lie.

A witness can lie.

A frightened person can lie.

A person protecting himself can lie.

A person protecting someone else can lie.

A lie raises a credibility problem. It does not identify which crime the liar committed.

Conley gave his own explanation for withholding information. He said he believed Frank would “get out and help me out.”

Perhaps Conley lied about this too.

But where is your evidence establishing another motive?

When you say Conley denied involvement because “murderers do this,” you claim knowledge of what was inside his head.

How do you know?

Did Conley say so?

Did someone hear him say so?

Did he write it?

Where is the evidence?

Why should your interpretation of his motive replace his own recorded explanation?

And if changing accounts make Conley suspicious, why not apply the same scrutiny to Frank?

Frank’s Noon Timeline Did Not Stay Fixed

In State’s Exhibit B, dated Monday, April 28, Frank placed Mary in his office between 12:05 and 12:10, “maybe 12:07” (State’s Exhibit B, 4).

Monteen Stover testified she entered Frank’s office at approximately 12:05 and remained about five minutes.

Frank was not there (AC, 6).

Later Frank allowed for a possible trip toward the toilet during this interval. The toilet was reached through the second-floor metal-room area.

So where was Frank between approximately 12:05 and 12:10?

Why did his April 28 account place Mary with him during roughly the same period when Stover said his office was empty?

Why did his later account introduce the possibility of movement toward the metal-room area?

No single point proves murder.

But these facts concern opportunity, location, chronology, and credibility.

If Conley’s changing accounts deserve microscopic examination, why should Frank’s chronology receive a pass?

Frank Was Not Simply “A Bit of a Nuisance With the Ladies”

Your description of Frank as little more than “a bit of a nuisance with some of the ladies” leaves out a considerable amount of prosecution evidence.

Numerous female employees testified concerning his conduct and reputation around women (AJ, 8).

Dewey Hewell said Frank spoke frequently with Mary, called her by name, stood close to her, and placed a hand on her shoulder.

Under cross-examination she admitted she did not know what they discussed and could not say the conversations were improper (AG, 9).

Both portions belong in a fair account.

Myrtice Cato and Maggie Griffin testified concerning Frank and Rebecca Carson entering the fourth-floor women’s dressing room together. Carson denied those visits.

Mamie Kitchens testified concerning Frank opening the women’s dressing-room door while a woman was undressed. Frank offered an innocent explanation.

Nellie Wood made allegations involving unwanted familiarity and an indecent proposal, followed later by disputes involving a defense affidavit.

None of this proves Frank murdered Mary.

But why describe Conley’s entire criminal history in detail while reducing prosecution testimony concerning Frank’s behavior around female employees to “a bit of a nuisance”?

If character evidence matters against Conley, why should character evidence concerning Frank disappear?

Conley’s Lookout Testimony Has Been Misstated

You describe the prosecution story as if Frank saw Mary arrive, suddenly recruited Conley, and asked him to help arrange an assault upon her.

Conley did not testify to this sequence.

He claimed Frank had previously used him as a lookout and gave him instructions before Mary appeared.

According to Conley, Frank told him:

“There’ll be a young lady up here pretty soon” (AJ, 11).

Conley also described signals involving Frank stamping his foot and Conley locking the door.

Was Conley telling the truth?

Possibly.

Was he lying?

Possibly.

But why attack a version of his testimony different from what he actually said?

If Conley fabricated the lookout account, show where it fails.

Which detail was impossible?

Which witness disproved it?

Which physical fact contradicted it?

Which time interval could not work?

“Too Many Moving Parts” Does Not Prove Anything

You call Conley’s story “a whopper with a lot of moving parts.”

Fine, your entitled to have an opinion. 

You find it unbelievable.

But why does complexity make a story false?

Real crimes can involve panic, concealment, movement of bodies, improvised explanations, conflicting stories, and later lies.

The useful questions concern evidence.

Which portions of Conley’s testimony were disproved?

Which portions were corroborated?

What information could investigators have supplied him?

What facts did he know independently?

Could his timeline work?

Could Frank’s timeline work?

What physical evidence fits the second floor?

What physical evidence fits the basement?

Calling one story complicated answers none of those questions.

The Jury Heard Conley Under Cross-Examination for Days

The jury watched Conley testify.

They heard his lies.

They heard his contradictions.

They heard Rosser attack his drinking, arrests, criminal history, changing accounts, and credibility.

They watched his face.

They heard his voice.

They saw how he answered questions during days of examination and cross-examination.

They still convicted Frank.

Juries can make mistakes.

Human judgment is not infallible.

But those twelve jurors possessed something nobody debating this case more than a century later possesses.

They saw Conley testify in person.

On August 25, 1913, the verdict was returned unanimously, and each juror individually affirmed the verdict when polled (AJ, 12).

The Georgia Supreme Court later affirmed Frank’s conviction four to two and wrote:

“The evidence supports the verdict” (Georgia Supreme Court, 13).

You can disagree with the jury.

You can disagree with the Georgia Supreme Court.

But where is the evidence showing your modern reconstruction deserves greater weight than the evidence heard at trial?

Look Closely at the Conley-Alone Story

Your alternative account goes roughly like this:

Mary receives her pay from Frank.

She leaves Frank’s office.

She walks downstairs.

Conley sees her.

Conley somehow knows she is alone.

He attacks her.

He knocks her unconscious.

He moves her to the trap opening.

He throws her living body approximately fourteen feet into the basement.

He follows her downstairs.

He sexually assaults her.

He strangles her.

He writes the death notes.

He stages the scene.

You call this simpler.

Where is the evidence?

Who saw Mary descend the stairs after leaving Frank?

Who saw her on the first floor?

Who saw her with Conley?

Who saw Conley waiting for her?

Where is the first-floor crime scene?

Where is the blood?

Where is the hair?

Where are signs of a struggle?

What object did Conley supposedly use to strike her?

What physical evidence places Mary near the trap opening?

How did Conley move an unconscious girl weighing roughly 107 pounds?

Where is evidence showing Mary entered the basement alive?

Where is evidence placing the sexual assault downstairs?

Where is evidence showing Conley strangled her there?

Each step sounds simple after being stated.

Each step still needs evidence.

The Fourteen-Foot Fall Creates a Physical Problem

Your theory proposes a living 13-year-old girl falling roughly fourteen feet onto an earthen basement floor.

Mary had injuries.

But the medical testimony did not describe broken bones or a fractured skull from an uncontrolled fourteen-foot fall.

William Gheesling testified the skull was not fractured. Dr. J. W. Hurt likewise described the head injuries without finding a skull fracture (AJ, 14).

Could a person fall fourteen feet without breaking a bone?

Yes.

But if you propose such a fall actually happened, where is the medical evidence supporting it?

Where are the injuries one would expect from a roughly 107-pound body dropping fourteen feet?

Why was her skull not fractured?

Why were no bones broken?

What evidence shows she struck the basement floor alive?

The later defense developed versions involving use of the ladder and lowering Mary through the opening rather than an uncontrolled drop.

An uncontrolled fourteen-foot fall creates a serious physical question requiring an answer.

What About the Second-Floor Evidence?

You say the death notes are the only physical evidence linking either man with Mary’s body.

The record is broader.

Conley admitted writing the notes.

Writing them proves authorship. It does not automatically prove he handled Mary’s body.

Meanwhile, Robert Barrett testified he found strands of hair on the L-shaped handle of his bench lathe in the second-floor metal room.

He also described a larger red spot and smaller spots near the women’s dressing room, with a white substance spread over part of the area.

The defense disputed both items.

The blood testing was primitive compared with modern forensic science.

The hair identification was contested.

But why does disputed evidence become no evidence?

If your theory places the murder entirely downstairs, what explains hair resembling Mary’s on a second-floor lathe handle?

What explains the suspected blood spots near the women’s dressing room?

What explains the white substance spread across part of the area?

Why should those physical findings be ignored while the death notes are treated as decisive evidence against Conley?

The prosecution presented physical evidence supporting its second-floor theory (AJ, 15).

A basement theory has to account for it.

Monteen Stover Is Still Standing in an Empty Office

Monteen Stover entered Frank’s office at approximately 12:05.

She stayed about five minutes.

Frank was absent.

Frank’s April 28 statement placed Mary with him during essentially the same period.

Later he allowed for a possible trip toward the metal-room toilet.

If Mary left Frank and walked downstairs directly into Conley’s hands, where was Frank?

Why was his office empty?

Why did his earliest detailed account place Mary there?

Why did his later account allow for movement toward the metal-room area?

Why does your reconstruction have an answer for every movement Conley supposedly made, but no clear answer for Frank’s whereabouts during one of the most important five-minute intervals in the case?

Drinking Does Not Prove Murder

You emphasize Conley’s drinking.

What does it prove about Mary’s murder?

There were also allegations concerning Frank drinking after Mary’s death, including Minola McKnight’s later repudiated affidavit.

Because Minola repudiated her affidavit, it should not be presented as settled fact.

The point is narrower.

If drinking does not prove Frank killed Mary, why should drinking prove Conley killed her?

You Cannot Read Conley’s Mind

You write:

“Unlike Frank, he was determined to keep himself as far from the actual crime as possible because that’s what murderers do.”

Where is your evidence for this motive?

Did Conley say this?

Did a witness hear him say it?

Did he write it?

Is there a contemporaneous document supporting it?

Or are you assigning him a motive because your theory requires one?

Conley might have lied because he killed Mary.

He might have lied because he helped move her.

He might have lied because he feared prosecution.

He might have lied because he expected Frank to help him.

He might have lied for several reasons at once.

We do not get to select one motive and call it fact without evidence.

The Conley-Alone Theory Has More Unanswered Questions Than Its Simplicity Suggests

The Conley-alone argument begins with Conley’s character and then works backward.

Conley lied, so he becomes the murderer.

Mary must have gone downstairs because Conley needed access to her.

Conley must have attacked her there because the theory places him there.

He must have moved her to the trap opening because her body ended in the basement.

He must have thrown her downward because the theory needs a route to the basement.

He must have sexually assaulted and strangled her downstairs because the reconstruction places the crime there.

He must have written the notes to frame someone because he admitted writing them.

But where is the evidence establishing each link?

Where is the evidence Mary went downstairs after Frank paid her?

Who saw her?

Where is evidence Conley encountered her?

Where is the first-floor assault scene?

What caused the blow to her head?

Where is the physical evidence of an assault near the trap opening?

Where is the blood?

Where is the hair?

Where are signs of a struggle?

And why would Conley choose one of the most exposed places in the factory to attack Mary Phagan?

The front of the National Pencil Company opened toward the street through wood-and-glass doors. Anyone approaching from outside could potentially look in. Anyone entering the building could interrupt what was happening.

Now place this scene in Atlanta in 1913, in the Jim Crow South.

A Black man caught assaulting a 13-year-old White girl could expect enormous danger to himself, both legally and physically. He would have been lynched on the spot. Why would Conley carry out such an attack near the glass-front entrance, where discovery could occur at any moment? 

Saturday was memorial day, the streets were packed with people from all over Atlanta and visitors from Georgia as a whole.

Things were different during Jim Crow. Blacks did not commit crimes out in the open around White people, the fear of lynching was ever present. 

And according to this theory, he supposedly did so without first securing the front door, according to the bogus Alonzo Mann confabulation.

Why?

If Conley intended to assault Mary, why leave the glass main entrance accessible?

Why risk a worker, passerby, customer, policeman, or anyone else entering unexpectedly?

Why choose a location exposed to the front entrance when a far more secluded area existed upstairs?

The defense presented its theory of the lobby near the entrance, and the prosecution presented it's second floor theory where Frank's office was located. 

The second-floor machine department offered privacy. The women’s dressing-room area was toward the rear of the floor near the men's and women's toilets. Doors separated portions of the area from public view. Someone standing outside on Forsyth Street could not simply look through the factory entrance and see what was happening back there.

Physical evidence was also reported in this secluded second-floor area, including suspected blood near the dressing room and hair found on the lathe handle.

So compare the two theories.

Under the Conley-alone theory, Mary is attacked near the front of the building, close to the street entrance, with no identified blood, hair, or struggle evidence near the trap opening, while the front door supposedly remains unsecured.

Under the prosecution’s theory, the attack occurs in the rear machine department on the second floor, away from the street, near the women’s dressing room, in an area where physical evidence was reported.

Which location better fits an attacker seeking privacy?

And if the answer is supposed to be the exposed front entrance, where is the evidence supporting it?

The Jim Crow setting makes the problem even sharper looking back in time.

The jury would have to ask itself:

Would a Black factory worker in Atlanta in 1913 seriously choose to assault a White teenage girl beside an entrance visible from the street, then move her body while leaving the front door unsecured? (Alonzo Mann)

Why take such an extraordinary risk?

Why select the location offering the greatest chance of interruption or discovery?

The streets were filled with White Confederate Patriots just outside the glass and wood framed doors. 

The theory needs more than a possible route to the basement.

It needs evidence.

Where is the physical evidence of the attack near the trap opening?

Where is the blood?

Where is the hair?

Where are the signs of struggle?

Who saw Mary downstairs with Conley?

Who saw Conley near the trap opening with her?

And why would a man supposedly trying to commit and conceal a capital crime choose one of the most exposed locations in the factory while leaving the front entrance unsecured? (Alonzo Mann supposedly walked in)

On its face, this part of the Conley-alone theory does not pass a basic common-sense test.

How did Conley move roughly 107 pounds of unconscious weight by himself when he testified he needed Frank's help?

Where are injuries supporting a fourteen-foot fall?

Why was her skull not fractured?

Why were no bones broken?

Why was hair resembling Mary’s reported on the second-floor lathe in the machine department?

Why were suspected blood spots found near the second-floor dressing room?

Why did Frank initially place Mary with him between 12:05 and 12:10, “maybe 12:07”?

Why did Monteen Stover find Frank’s office empty during approximately the same interval? 

Frank said Mary was in his office with him during that time. 

Why did Frank later allow for a possible trip toward the metal-room toilet in the machine department?

Why does your description of Conley’s lookout account differ from his testimony?

Why should your 2026 interpretation of Conley’s motive replace the explanation he gave in 1913?

And most importantly:

What evidence proves your Conley-alone sequence actually happened?

Calling Conley violent, drunk, criminal, dishonest, or statistically more likely to commit murder does not answer any of these questions. It's not evidence that Leo Frank didn't commit the crime.

A profile is not a crime scene.

A criminal record is not an autopsy.

A statistical probability is not an eyewitness.

A simpler story is not automatically the true story.

If you want to replace the prosecution’s case with a Conley-alone theory, then show the evidence for the Conley-alone theory, but it needs evidence, not wishful thinking.

Not assumptions. 

Not demographic probability.

Not a psychological guess about what Conley was thinking. Neither you nor me has a time machine or the ability to read Leo's and Conley's mind in 1913.

Evidence.

An elderly, demented woman in Belgium was euthanized after her family decided that she should be killed. Since it was claimed that the woman didn’t understand what was happening, the doctor laced her coffee with her sedatives – while she was chatting with her family. The doctor then gave another sedative by injection. The woman then stood up. Family members held her down while the doctor injected her and killed her. In court later the judges declared that ‘given the deeply demented condition of the patient, the doctor did not need to verify her wish for euthanasia.’

A gunshot would be quicker and probably more painless than drugs.

Why don’t advocates of euthanasia be blunt and endorse the idea that doctors should simply shoot patients? Patients could, like Nurse Edith Cavell, be put on a chair and shot in a scruffy courtyard. It would be faster and more certain than any other way of killing. A firing squad could be made up of euthanasia campaigners and politicians.

In more than half of the cases where individuals in Oregon, USA were subjected to euthanasia, there is no record of whether or not there were any complications. I bet there were. Complications which have been recorded during euthanasia include: difficulty in finding a vein, spasms, twitching, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, sweating, gasping. One instance of euthanasia failed because the doctor had ordered the wrong drug. Another attempt was delayed when the doctor had to leave to fetch a second batch of lethal drugs.

Contrary to the reassurances offered by campaigners for ‘death by doctor’ schemes, taking lethal drugs by mouth can be traumatic. It is not unusual for patients to take many hours to die. One patient took 104 hours to die. One patient became unconscious 25 minutes after swallowing lethal medication but woke up and regained consciousness 65 hours later.

One report showed that lethal injections caused severe pain and severe respiratory distress with associated sensations of drowning, asphyxiation, panic and terror in the overwhelming majority of cases.

A study of more than 200 autopsy reports after executions in nine American States showed evidence of pulmonary oedema in the lungs (likely to cause a feeling of drowning or suffocation)

Midazolam used in executions has caused signs of pain – including gasping, choking and coughing, with patients heaving against their restraints.

Evidence shows that some people who choose assisted suicide vomit their lethal dose of drugs before it can be absorbed.

So, we’re on about day 100 of this never-ending Julytember... because apparently Mother Nature forgot the “-ber” months are supposed to come with cooler weather.

And what better way to celebrate than highs once again climbing into the upper 90s to near 100° today?

The NWS HeatRisk map shows Major to Extreme heat risk across parts of the area, with heat index values between 105° and 110°. HeatRisk is a little different from simply looking at the heat index. It considers how unusual the heat is for this time of year, how long it lasts, daytime AND nighttime temperatures, and the potential for heat-related impacts. When our area is highlighted in the red and purple temps, I pay attention.
So yes... take the heat seriously again today. Stay hydrated, take plenty of breaks if you’re working outside, and spend as much time as possible in air conditioning.

As for some relief, I’m still optimistic that this stubborn ridge of high pressure finally begins breaking down early next week. Before you roll your eyes, it's really all we can look forward to! As the ridge breaks down, rain chances should increase into the 30–50% range, particularly Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday.

The heat, on the other hand? Heh...
Will it be as ridiculously hot as it is today? Nope!
Will temperatures suddenly feel like fall? Nada!
Right now, it still looks like above-average warmth will continue into next week, just hopefully without the upper 90s and 105–110° heat index values we’re dealing with now. More like 85-90°🤞🏼.

text:
A former Restore Britain candidate has accused the party of being hijacked by racists and of sliding rapidly toward the hard Right, saying the organisation he briefly represented no longer matches the civic patriotism he thought he had joined. 

Jez Hermer, a former Royal Marines officer who stood for Restore in a Dover district council by-election last month, says that during his short but intense involvement he saw what he regarded as overt antisemitism, racism and misogyny among activists and in party-linked forums. He also describes an increasingly rigid ethno-nationalism in which debate about heritage and demographic change gave way to hostility toward anyone who argued that Britishness is not defined by being white.

Hermer says he was branded a “traitor” after telling voters and journalists that someone does not need to be white to be British. In comments that triggered a backlash from hardline supporters, he said he did not believe “for a second” that Restore stood for a “pure white” test of nationhood, and that he had to reassure nervous local voters that the party was not an ethno-nationalist vehicle. 

Those remarks, made during the campaign in Guston, Kingsdown and St Margaret’s-at-Cliffe, were denounced by some activists as “completely unacceptable.”
Writing in The Telegraph, Hermer argues that leader Rupert Lowe and senior figures have done little to halt what he calls a “rapid charge to the hard-Right.” 

He says there is a widening gap between the public proposition offered by Lowe and the culture taking hold in parts of the activist base. More troubling, he suggests, is that the shift no longer looks entirely organic: there appears to be “agency within the party’s organisational heart” that is, whether deliberately or not, aiding a slow-motion takeover by the hard Right.

Hermer, who served 23 years as a Royal Marines officer after earlier Army service and later worked as an engineer and businessman, presents himself as someone who joined Restore because of concerns about immigration, cultural change and national identity. He insists those subjects can and should be debated. What he says he will not accept is the normalisation of racism, antisemitism or extremism under the cover of that debate.

The intervention adds to a run of allegations about Restore’s activist culture. Other whistleblowers have described slurs, pressure on women in politics, and campaigners treating civic nationalism as betrayal. Figures associated with “total remigration” and open ethno-nationalism have been prominent online supporters; some have clashed publicly with candidates such as Hermer who reject a racial definition of Britishness. Critics say the party has become a magnet for people who want to push it beyond Lowe’s stated positions. Supporters of the leadership reply that a noisy fringe should not be allowed to define the whole organisation.

Hermer finished with around 10 per cent of the vote in the Dover contest, which the Greens won by a handful of votes. Reform UK accused Restore of splitting the right-wing vote. For Hermer, the more serious split is inside Restore itself: between those who want a hard line on borders and those who treat ancestry as the only test of belonging. He says the latter group is winning ground, and that the party’s centre is not stopping them.

News Flashback

Early 2026

Jan-March

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

“Y’all Keep That Sh*t”: Chris Brown Rejects Texas Honor After Rep. Venton Jones Apologizes on Don Lemon

A Texas lawmaker tried to walk back an onstage honor for Chris Brown. Brown told him to keep the award.

What started as a concert-stage celebration of R&B turned into a public split in three days: two Texas Democrats recognized Chris Brown in Arlington, one of them apologized after the backlash, and Brown rejected the honor while accusing the lawmaker of “tap dancing.”

The honor

On Saturday, September 12, U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett and Texas State Rep. Venton Jones took the stage at AT&T Stadium during Chris Brown and Usher’s R&B Tour stop. Crockett entered both artists into the Congressional Record, calling the moment “Black joy” and saying she wanted their work documented at the congressional level. Jones presented Brown with a separate State of Texas legislative recognition. Producer RoccStar helped coordinate the appearance. 

Jones later said the visit was also about voter turnout ahead of the November midterms, that they were brought in to reach people already in the building. The clip that traveled was not a get-out-the-vote speech. It was two elected officials onstage hugging and honoring a man whose legal history has followed him for 17 years.

Why it blew up

Brown pleaded guilty in 2009 to felony assault after attacking then-girlfriend Rihanna, one of the most widely covered domestic-violence cases in modern music. Other former partners have sought restraining orders. That record is not a rumor. It is the reason the honor landed like a slap to a lot of people who heard “we see you” from politicians on other days and “celebrate his artistry” on this one. 

Critics did not argue Brown can’t sell out stadiums. They argued elected officials do not have to put the state’s name on it.

Jones apologizes. Brown does not play along.

By Tuesday, Jones was on Don Lemon’s morning show doing damage control.

“I want to offer an apology,” he said. “I want to offer my apology to Black women, to women, and to anyone who has experienced domestic violence and really express that it was not my intention to stoke the traumas that go into that.” 

He followed with a written statement that went further: he acknowledged the Black women his actions had hurt and said an apology needed to be as loud as the original moment. He also said he is himself a survivor of sexual violence and domestic abuse, and that his experience does not cancel the impact of the honor. 

Brown’s first reaction had been gratitude. He thanked Crockett and Jones, said he was “not political,” and even apologized to Crockett for any backlash she might catch for recognizing him.

That tone died after Jones went on Lemon.

Responding to coverage of the apology, Brown wrote: 

“I don’t want the award anymore, my brother. You went on with Don Lemon and started tap dancing. Y’all keep that sh-t.”

He went further on Instagram: the lawmakers came to him, not the other way around. His Dallas shows were already sold out. He said he never asked to be honored because he knew this exact reaction was coming — and that Jones started apologizing because he did not want to lose voters and support. His closer was blunt: leave him alone and let him focus on the fans who paid to see him. 

The split on the stage

Crockett has not issued a matching public walk-back. That contrast is now part of the story. One lawmaker treated the honor as something that needed an apology to Black women and survivors. The other has so far let the Congressional Record entry stand. Brown drew a line between them: grace for Crockett, contempt for Jones.

That is the part a lot of people are sitting with. Not whether Brown is “canceled.” He is touring stadiums with Usher. The question is why two officials thought a formal state and congressional recognition was the right vehicle — and why only one of them decided the optics were no longer worth defending.

text:
Your account leaves out evidence in the trial record that directly answers several claims.

Several statements in your reply do not fit the sworn testimony or the newspaper record.

You say Mary screamed in Frank’s office and then somehow fled toward the metal room. You say Mary’s hair was not found there. You say Dorsey gave up on the hair. You say the large red spot was paint rather than blood. You suggest a nosebleed or cut finger explains the blood evidence.

Where is the evidence for those statements?

Conley placed the scream after movement toward the metal room which was located at the back of the second floor.

You ask why Mary would run away from the stairs and toward the metal room after being attacked in Frank’s office.

But where did Conley testify this happened?

In his sworn testimony, Conley described movement away from the office and toward the metal department before the scream.

His testimony was:

“After they went back there [to the machine department], I heard the lady scream” (BOE Conley, 1).

The Atlanta Journal reported Conley’s story the same way on August 4, 1913, saying he heard Mary scream in the metal room (AJ, 2).

So where is the testimony saying Mary screamed in Frank’s office?

Where is the testimony saying she broke away from Frank?

Where is the testimony saying she ran toward the metal room?

Your question about why she supposedly ran in the wrong direction starts with an event you first have to prove. You don't seem to have a good grasp of the testimony presented by prosecution and defense witnesses. 

The metal room offered far more privacy than Frank’s front office.

It seems like you have never looked at the factory diagrams in the exhibits. You say workers coming down from the fourth floor were just as likely to enter the metal room as Frank’s office. 

What evidence proves this?

Defense engineer I. U. Kauffman measured the factory and placed Frank’s desk roughly 150 feet from the metal room.

Herbert Schiff, another defense witness, testified Frank’s office door had clear glass in its upper half and a person could see into the office (AC, 3).

The metal room was far toward the rear of the second floor, near the women’s dressing room and toilets.

Monteen Stover also testified the metal-room door was closed during her visit around 12:05 to 12:10. 

The legal record states:

“The door to the metal room was closed” (AST, 4).

So why treat these two locations as equally exposed?

One was a front office with glass visibility.

The other was about 150 feet farther back, behind a closed door during the critical noon period.

Where is your evidence workers were equally likely to enter both places?

“Mary’s hair was not there” is contradicted by the witnesses who saw it.

Robert P. Barrett found hair on the handle of his bench lathe Monday morning.

The official trial record states:

“I found some hair on the handle of a bench lathe” (BOE Barrett, 5).

Barrett also testified the hair had not been there Friday, April 25, 1913.

Several workers saw the hair after he found it.

Mell Stanford saw it.

N. V. Darley saw it.

Magnolia Kennedy saw it.

And Kennedy was not a stranger trying to identify Mary from a photograph.

She worked beside Mary, while Mary worked there for a year.

Her machine was next to Mary’s.

When Dorsey asked whose hair it looked like, Kennedy answered:

“It looked like Mary Phagan’s” (AJ, 6).

Kennedy also testified the lathe hair was light brown and Mary’s hair was light brown / auburn.

So how can you state as a fact:

“Mary’s hair was not there”?

The record says hair was found there.

Several people saw it.

A woman who worked beside Mary testified it looked like Mary’s hair.

Mary’s stepfather also identified the lathe hair.

There is another witness your statement leaves out.

J. W. Coleman, Mary Phagan’s stepfather, later gave sworn testimony concerning the same hair.

Coleman had lived with Mary for about four years.

He testified he examined the hair recovered from the factory shortly after the murder.

His sworn statement said the hair “resembled in every way” Mary’s hair, and he concluded to the best of his knowledge and belief it was hers (Georgia Supreme Court Record, 7).

So now we have Magnolia Kennedy, who worked beside Mary, saying it looked like Mary’s hair.

We have J. W. Coleman, who lived with Mary, saying the recovered hair resembled Mary’s hair.

We have Barrett finding it on the lathe immediately after the murder weekend.

We have Stanford and Darley seeing it.

Against all of this, you simply declare:

“Mary’s hair was not there.”

Where is the proof for your certainty?

Dorsey did not give up on the hair.

This claim is directly contradicted by what Dorsey did in 1914.

Months after Frank’s trial, Dr. Henry Harris questioned whether a later hair sample matched the hair found on Barrett’s lathe.

Dorsey responded by calling undertaker William Gheesling during Jim Conley’s February 1914 trial.

The Atlanta Journal reported Dorsey specifically questioned Gheesling about Mary’s hair.

Gheesling testified:

“I washed it with pine tar soap.”

Asked what effect the soap had on its color, he answered:

“Made it lighter” (AJ, 8).

Why was Dorsey still calling witnesses about Mary’s hair in February 1914 if he had “given up” on it?

The following day, The Atlanta Georgian reported Dorsey arguing the hair evidence again.

Dorsey reminded the jury the hair was found Monday morning and said Magnolia Kennedy testified it looked like Mary’s (AG, 9).

He also used Gheesling’s pine-tar testimony to answer the difference in appearance raised later.

Dorsey did not abandon the hair.

He continued arguing it.

The pine-tar soap matters because it changed Mary’s hair.

Gheesling did not simply say Mary’s hair was washed.

His sworn statement in the Georgia Supreme Court record was stronger.

He said pine-tar soap changed Mary’s hair color and “rendered the hair lighter” (Georgia Supreme Court Record, 7).

That is important to the evidence given by people who did not know Mary and later said the hair looked different in shade or color.

A later visual comparison was not being made against Mary’s untouched hair as it appeared while she was alive on Saturday morning.

Her hair had been washed with a substance the undertaker swore changed its color.

So the later difference in appearance does not justify your flat statement that the lathe hair was not Mary’s.

There was evidence pointing the other way.

“The larger splotch was paint” directly conflicts with George W. Jefferson’s sworn testimony.

This is one of the clearest problems with your reply.

George W. Jefferson had worked at the National Pencil Company for five years.

He worked in the polishing room.

He knew the paints used in the factory.

He named the red paints: maroon red, red line, and bright red.

Then he testified about the suspicious spot in front of the girls’ dressing room.

His sworn statement was:

“That spot that I saw was not one of these three paints” (BOE Jefferson, 10).

So where does your statement come from:

“The larger splotch was paint, not blood”?

A factory worker with five years of experience who knew the red paints testified it was not one of them. Why would you in 2026, know better than a factory employee who worked there in 1913 and their job was to work with paints? 

Jefferson also testified he had not seen the spot there Friday, April 25, 1913.

So if you are going to call it paint, show the evidence proving Jefferson was wrong.

Robert Barrett testified it was blood.

Barrett found the suspicious area Monday morning.

The Atlanta Journal reported he discovered a large spot surrounded by smaller spots near the dressing room.

Under cross-examination, Barrett remained positive the spots were blood spots (AJ, 11).

The sworn trial record is even plainer:

“It was blood” (BOE Barrett, 5).

Barrett also said the spot had not been there Friday.

He described a white substance spread over it.

So this was not simply a random red mark somebody noticed months later.

It was found Monday morning after Mary’s murder, in the area where the State placed the crime.

Mell Stanford also said it looked like blood and had not been there Friday.

Stanford worked in the metal room and swept the floor.

His sworn testimony said he found a spot near the dressing room Monday with white haskoline over it.

He said:

“The spot looked like it was blood” (AST, 4).

Stanford also testified it had not been there when he swept Friday.

The Atlanta Journal reported Stanford was certain the haskoline smear had not been there Friday morning and said the spots led back toward the dressing room (AJ, 11).

So now the list grows.

Barrett saw it and called it blood.

Stanford saw it and said it looked like blood.

Jefferson saw it and testified it was not one of the factory’s red paints.

Magnolia Kennedy saw the blood stain too.

Kennedy, the same worker who said the lathe hair looked like Mary’s, also testified about the floor.

The Atlanta Journal reported:

“She testified further that she saw the blood stain on the floor and the white substance over it” (AJ, 6).

Kennedy had worked in the factory four years.

The newspaper also reported she had never seen blood spots like those there before.

So this was not one witness.

Barrett.

Stanford.

Jefferson.

Kennedy.

All saw the suspicious area.

Dr. Claude Smith found actual blood corpuscles in the floor sample.

Then there is the laboratory evidence.

Dr. Claude Smith was Atlanta’s city bacteriologist and chemist.

He examined chips taken from the floor.

The legal record states he found blood corpuscles in one of the samples (AST, 4).

This directly undercuts the simple statement:

“The larger splotch was paint, not blood.”

Jefferson said it was not one of the factory paints.

Barrett called it blood.

Stanford said it looked like blood.

Kennedy saw the blood stain.

And Dr. Claude Smith found blood corpuscles in the floor sample.

So where is the evidence proving this entire area was nothing but paint?

The newspaper record described the hair and blood as part of the State’s case before the trial even began.

This evidence was not invented later.

On May 25, 1913, more than two months before Frank’s trial, the Atlanta Journal reported Barrett had told the grand jury about “the girl’s hair and the supposed blood” found in the machine room (AJ, 12).

That date matters.

May 25.

This evidence was already being presented during the grand-jury phase.

So the hair and blood were not some story patched together at the end of the trial.

They were part of the investigation from the beginning.

Dorsey was still arguing both the hair and blood in 1914.

The February 24, 1914 Atlanta Georgian gives another direct answer to the idea Dorsey abandoned this evidence.

Dorsey told the Conley jury:

“Blood was found on the second floor.”

Then he turned to the hair and reminded them Barrett found it Monday morning and Kennedy said it looked like Mary’s (AG, 9).

Again, where is the abandonment?

He was still using both pieces of evidence the following year.

A nosebleed or cut finger is an explanation without an identified person.

You say the blood might have come from a nosebleed or cut finger.

Whose nosebleed?

Whose cut finger?

What day?

What time?

Which witness saw it happen?

Where is the worker who testified he bled in that exact spot?

Where is the injury connected with the place where Barrett found the spots?

Where is the testimony explaining the fresh white material Stanford said had not been there Friday morning?

You have proposed possible explanations.

Where is the evidence showing either one actually happened?

Your claim that Conley copied the story from newspapers also needs a paper trail.

You say Conley patched his account together from newspapers.

Show it.

Which newspaper?

Which date?

Which article?

Which fact appeared in print before Conley gave it?

Then show Conley using the same fact afterward.

If the claim is that he learned about the metal room, the hair, the blood, or some other important detail from the press, there should be a trail.

Where is it?

The claim cannot prove itself.

The physical evidence you dismiss was seen by a long list of witnesses.

Your reply makes the metal-room evidence sound like one questionable hair and a meaningless red mark.

The record is larger than that.

Robert P. Barrett found the hair and blood-like spots.

Mell Stanford saw the hair and the suspicious floor area.

N. V. Darley saw the hair.

Magnolia Kennedy said the hair looked like Mary’s and saw the blood stain.

J. W. Coleman said the recovered hair resembled Mary’s hair.

George W. Jefferson said the large red spot was not one of the factory paints.

Dr. Claude Smith found blood corpuscles in the floor sample.

William Gheesling testified Mary’s hair had been washed with pine-tar soap and made lighter.

Dorsey continued using the hair and blood evidence in 1914.

So the questions for your reply are straightforward.

Where is the sworn testimony saying Mary screamed inside Frank’s office?

Where is the testimony saying she fled toward the metal room?

Where is the proof the lathe hair was not Mary’s?

How do you explain Magnolia Kennedy?

How do you explain J. W. Coleman?

How do you explain Dorsey still arguing the hair in 1914 if he had supposedly abandoned it?

How can the large spot be dismissed as factory paint when Jefferson, who knew the paints, testified it was not one of them?

How do you explain Dr. Claude Smith finding blood corpuscles?

Whose nosebleed was it?

Whose cut finger?

Where is the witness?

And where is the newspaper trail proving Conley copied the important parts of his story from published reports?

Those claims need evidence too.

News Flashback

Early 2026

Jan-March

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

News Flashback

Early 2026

Jan-March

Streaming Wars
The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

$YI: A take-private bid now has a funding schedule on paper, and no bank sits behind any of it.

The 13D filed today puts the terms in writing. Huadeng Tech BioArray Ventures commits $20.69 million in cash for a contemplated 55.43% of the post-transaction company, under a consortium agreement dated September 16. Co-founders Gang Yu and Junling Liu roll over 73,630,886 shares instead. The same schedule values those shares at roughly $16.6 million.

No financing condition. Cash plus rolled equity is the entire funding, which takes the key execution risk off the table. The deal is still non-binding, pending definitive agreements and special committee approval.

Exclusivity runs six months from September 16. Consortium members must vote against competing transactions and cannot acquire or dispose of company securities. The buyers have agreed not to buy.

The offer is $4.52 per ADS, a 29.5% premium to the September 15 close and 20% above the 60-day average.

Bank Of Volatility Market Commentary
Thursday 17 September 2026, 12:30 CEST

MARKETS
• The morning after the hike, futures have taken back most of the presser selloff. /ES trades 7,686.50 on the December contract (+0.83%), which is now the active one; the September contract at 7,619 expires tomorrow morning. /NQ 29,278 (+1.09%), Dow futures +0.75%, Russell +0.80%.
• Wednesday's cash close was uneven: the Dow lost 1.21% to 51,462, the S&P 0.44%, the Nasdaq finished flat. Energy fell 3% and financials were the worst major group. Tech carried the tape while everything tied to rates took the hit.
• The post-Fed premium is coming out of volatility fast. VIX 15.99, down 9.7% from 17.71 this morning; the October future 18.25, December 19.18. The equity put/call ratio closed at 0.92 on Wednesday, up 23% on the day, the biggest one-day rise of the month, as the crowd hedged after the fact.

RATES AND THE FED
• The Fed hiked 25 to 3.75 to 4.00, twelve to nothing, the first hike since 2023. Sixteen of eighteen officials see at least one more this year. Warsh refused forward guidance, said he did not submit a dot, called inflation too high for too long, and said the Committee was hard-pressed to describe financial conditions as restrictive. That last line is why the market sold the presser rather than the statement. October hike odds sit near 50%.
• The curve flattened on the news, 2s30s near 61 basis points, and the long end rallied. This morning the 10-year is back under 5% at 4.99, the 2-year 4.72, the 30-year 5.33. Real yields did not follow: 10-year TIPS 2.66, 5-year TIPS 2.49, both at cycle highs, so breakevens are compressing. That is the market believing the Fed on inflation.
• The President has now spoken twice: a call for lower rates hours after the decision, then a line that he wants Warsh independent but the chair has an antagonistic board. Pressure has moved from the man to the Committee.
• Foreign money is voting with its feet in two directions. Treasury data showed long-term foreign purchases of US assets flipped to minus 27.9 billion dollars in July after a record June, with China's holdings down to 618 billion. In Japan, foreigners bought a record 2.2 trillion yen of JGBs last week while selling Japanese stocks.
• Today: claims, Philly Fed, housing starts at 14:30 CEST, the Bank of England at 13:00 with a hold at 3.75% expected, the Bank of Japan tomorrow with a hike expected. Eurozone final CPI 3.3%, core 2.4%, in line.

ASIA AND EUROPE
• Asia mixed: Nikkei +0.33%, KOSPI flat at 6,715, Hang Seng −0.44%, Shanghai −0.41%, ASX +0.41%. Europe green: DAX +0.58%, FTSE +0.43%, CAC +0.17%.
• Carney offered the EU critical minerals, LNG and hydrogen at scale and pooled sovereign compute, and said Canada is not proposing a third bloc. Trump floated EU tariffs if the arrangement looks anti-American.

Turkish artist uses AI to revamp Road Runner cartoons

We’re looking at how one Turkish artist is blending classic cartoons with cutting-edge artificial intelligence to create something truly unique.
Turkish artist uses AI to revamp Road Runner cartoons

Emre Altay, known on Instagram as @emrealtay.ai, has been making waves with his innovative use of AI in film and advertising projects. His latest venture? A modern take on the beloved Road Runner & Coyote cartoons, reimagined through the lens of Seedance2.5 from @dreamina_ai.
The Classic Meets the Cutting Edge

The original Road Runner cartoons first appeared way back in 1949, a time when computers were still a far-off dream for most people. Fast forward to today, and we’re seeing how far animation has come with Emre’s project. But what makes this particular blend of old-school charm and new technology so special?
The Technical Marvel

Emre isn’t just using AI to generate video from text or images; he’s combining several techniques into one complex pipeline. This includes classic retargeting of animations, references for Seedance2.5, neural rendering, and compositing. It’s a mix that requires both technical expertise and artistic vision.

For instance, Emre starts by inputting the original Road Runner & Coyote sequences into Seedance2.5. The AI then analyzes these frames to understand the movements and expressions of the characters. This analysis is crucial for retargeting animations, where classic scenes are reinterpreted with modern techniques. Neural rendering comes next, allowing Emre to enhance the visual quality while maintaining the original spirit of the cartoons.
A Question of Animation vs. Generation

Is this project animation or generation? The answer isn’t clear-cut. Without the original animated sequences to work from, creating something like this would be nearly impossible. Emre is not just generating video; he’s animating with a twist of modern tech. This blend showcases how AI can enhance traditional animation techniques rather than replace them.
What Does This Mean for You?

If you’re into animation or AI, this project shows how these two worlds can collide and create something truly unique. It's about more than making old cartoons look new—it’s about pushing the boundaries of what we think is possible when it comes to blending art and technology. How does Emre’s work inspire your own creative projects?
The Future of Animation

So why should you care? Emre’s work isn’t just a cool project; it’s a sign of things to come. As AI continues to evolve, expect more artists and animators to find innovative ways to use these tools in their craft. This isns't about replacing human creativity—it's about augmenting it.

For example, imagine an animator using AI to quickly prototype character movements or facial expressions before finalizing them manually. Such advancements could save time and resources while still allowing for the creative input that makes each project unique.
The Nostalgic Appeal

The nostalgic aspect is hard to ignore. For those who grew up watching Road Runner & Coyote, seeing them through the lens of modern AI technology brings a sense of wonder and familiarity at once. It’s like looking back at your childhood with fresh eyes. How does this project resonate with you personally?
Technical Limitations and Challenges

Creating something as complex as this isn’t without its challenges. Emre had to navigate technical limitations and ensure that the new version respects the original spirit of the cartoons while adding modern flair. This balance is crucial for maintaining both artistic integrity and audience appeal.

One major challenge was ensuring that the AI-generated animations felt natural and true to the characters’ personalities. Emre spent countless hours tweaking parameters and refining algorithms to achieve this delicate balance.
The Role of Seedance2.5

Seedance2.5 from @dreamina_ai plays a pivotal role in this project. text:
One of the advantages of travelling as much as I have this year is that you start to see the differences between markets that can be difficult to pick up from a distance.

So far, I’ve spent time in El Salvador, Hong Kong, Korea and Brazil, meeting investors, banks, asset managers, regulators and potential partners.

The most interesting part has been seeing how differently each market is approaching the same transition.

We started the year in El Salvador at Tether’s Plan B Forum and the Tether event. We spent the week meeting institutions and potential partners across LATAM.

There is a growing focus on where digital assets fit into existing financial markets rather than treating them as a separate ecosystem.

Hong Kong offered a different perspective.

At Consensus, we hosted a discussion with Animoca Brands and Alumni Ventures around Rayls Commodity Vaults and met investors looking at Brazilian tokenized assets.

What stood out to me was the importance of market structure. The capital is there, the interest is there, but building in Asia requires a much deeper understanding of the local financial ecosystem and how institutions actually operate within it.

Korea has probably been the clearest example of accelerating institutional interest.

I made two trips this year, initially focused on investor relationships and later around Bitcoin and the broader digital asset market. I spent time with banks, asset managers, VCs and financial institutions, both at the conference and in their offices.

The conversations were notably more practical than they were a few years ago.

There is a clear desire to understand the regulatory direction, the infrastructure being built and which partners can help institutions move from exploration to implementation. Korea is also moving quickly on tokenization, which makes the market particularly relevant to what we are building at Parfin and Rayls.

Brazil provides an interesting contrast.

Blockchain Rio has grown significantly, and it is increasingly attracting participants from outside the country. Having grown up in Rio and attended four editions, it has been interesting to watch the event, and the ecosystem around it.

Febraban Tech was probably the clearest indicator of how far the Brazilian market has come.

We had one of our largest presences yet alongside Tether, launched Rayls Sovereign, and spent three days meeting banks, regulators, and financial institutions.

Parfin and Rayls are now known quantities across much of the Brazilian financial sector. We are no longer spending the first part of every meeting explaining who we are or why this infrastructure matters. The discussion is increasingly about implementation, use cases, and how institutions can deploy it.

That is a meaningful change.

Across these markets, I’m seeing the same broad direction but very different paths to get there. Regulation, existing financial infrastructure, institutional readiness and local market dynamics are all determining the pace of adoption.

That makes being on the ground increasingly important. The difference between a market that is genuinely moving and one that is simply generating headlines becomes much easier to identify when you are speaking directly with the institutions involved.

There is plenty more data to gather.

Korea Blockchain Week is next, followed by a packed conference season across Asia, LATAM and other key financial markets.

The next few months should provide an even better read on which institutional use cases are moving from narrative to real adoption, and where the infrastructure requirements are beginning to take shape.

text:
Nicht verpassen! Ein neuer Artikel von mir: HCTGS v37 Japan — The Tower That Sells What Japan Buys . Japan consumes 1,005 TWh of electricity a year, from every source combined. That is 77 to 115 towers. Two-thirds of it is burned from fuel landed by ship — 654 TWh a year standing on an import contract — and that part alone is 50 to 75.

Every earlier article in this series began from a country's water. Japan is the case where that would be the wrong beginning.

Japan has the rain, the utilities and drinking water most countries measure themselves against. What it buys from abroad is energy, minerals and metal, and increasingly the hands to run what it has already built. So the arithmetic runs the other way here: the denominator is the energy balance, and water is what the machine makes on the way.

Three things came out of writing this one that I did not expect.

Japan already built this industry, and then stopped. With no natural magnesite, Japanese chemists built a synthetic magnesia industry out of seawater instead, and at its peak it is reported to have produced over 700,000 tonnes a year before mined imports took the volume. One tower produces 547–703 thousand tonnes a year. One structure matches what a national industry reached at its high-water mark — not as a novelty, but as the continuation of a process that already ran here. The cost step that ended it is the one a cascade removes, because the magnesia is a by-product of making water rather than the object of its own plant.

The customer buys heat, not electricity. Chemicals, steel, cement and ceramics, paper, non-ferrous metals: five sectors whose largest input is process heat, standing on reclaimed coastal land at the water's edge. A power purchase agreement offers one rung of an eight-stage ladder, converted twice on the way. The cascade offers the ladder — 2,200 °C at the top, process steam at 110 °C from the middle, cooling delivered as a product at 4 °C.

And curtailment is a turndown problem before it is a storage problem. Japan turned away 1.74 TWh of solar and wind in the first half of 2025, a record; by March 2026 Tokyo curtailed for the first time. Thermal plant turns down to 30–50 percent and no further, so a floor persists and the variable sources give way. A tower turns down across a factor of seven, and when it turns its electricity down it moves the same energy into hydrogen, water and minerals. Wind and solar then run without being asked to stop.

The conversion efficiency of the vortex stage is a calculated figure — 0.277, against about 0.20 for a natural waterspout — and the electrical numbers are stated on that basis until a pilot returns a measured one.

Thirteen open parameters, both columns of the ledger, and a $10–15 million pilot that publishes either way.
